Quadrant 1- Cells marked in green: -VE for A antigen, +VE for B antigen Quadrant 2- Cells marked in purple: -VE for both the antigens.
Quadrant 3- Cells marked in yellow: +VE for both the antigens Quadrant 4- Cells marked in red: +VE for A antigen, -VE for B antigen

questions.stem: Patients with isolated Ig A deficiency would have associated deficiency of which of the following IgG subtypes?
questions.explanation:
Isolated IgA deficiency is associated with deficiency of IgG subtypes IgG2 and IgG4.
IgA deficiency-affected individuals have extremely low levels of both serum and secretory IgA. It may be familial or acquired in association with toxoplasmosis, measles, or some other viral infection.
Because IgA is the major antibody in external secretions, mucosal defenses are weakened, and infections occur in the respiratory, gastrointestinal, and urogenital tracts. Symptomatic patients commonly have recurrent sinopulmonary infections and diarrhea.
IgA-deficient patients have a high frequency of respiratory tract allergy and a variety of autoimmune diseases, particularly systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.stem: Which of the following are mutated in X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The X-linked lymphoproliferative syndrome is due to mutations in the gene encoding an adaptor molecule called SLAM-associated protein (SAP).
It is characterized by an inability to eliminate Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), eventually leading to fulminant infectious mononucleosis and the development of B-cell tumors.
In about 80% of cases, the disease is due to mutations in the gene encoding the adaptor molecule SAP. Defects in SAP contribute to attenuated NK cell and T-cell activation, resulting in increased susceptibility to viral infections.
Option B: LYST gene is associated with Chediak-Higashi syndrome.
Option C: BTK gene is associated with Isolated growth hormone deficiency type III. Option D: TBX1 gene is associated with 22q11.2 deletion syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following lymphoid tissue findings is seen most commonly in patients with common variable hypogammaglobulinemia?
questions.explanation:
Normal B-cell count is most commonly seen in lymphoid tissues of individuals with the common variable hypogammaglobulinemia.
It is a heterogeneous group of disorders in which the common feature is hypogammaglobulinemia, generally affecting all the antibody classes, but sometimes only IgG.
In contrast to X-linked agammaglobulinemia, most individuals with common variable immunodeficiency have normal or near-normal numbers of B-cells in the blood and lymphoid tissues. These B cells, however, are not able to differentiate into plasma cells.
FDA approved XEMBIFY in 2019, 20% immunoglobulin solution for subcutaneous injection. It is indicated for the use of primary humoral immunodeficiency disorders in patients 2years of age and older.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy is brought with complaints of red rashes over his skin. His mother says that the child will be constantly scratching the rashes. On asking any previous history she says the child keeps getting recurrent infections which mostly require hospitalization. Blood investigations showed a low platelet count. Which of the following is false regarding this syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The given history with eczema, recurrent infections, and thrombocytopenia points towards Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome. In this condition, IgM levels in the serum are low.
Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP), which is located on Xp11.23. The X-linked disease is characterized by thrombocytopenia, eczema, and a marked vulnerability to recurrent infection, resulting in early death.
Platelets are small in size. The thymus is morphologically normal, at least early in the course of the disease, but there is the progressive loss of T lymphocytes in the peripheral blood and in the T-cell zones (paracortical areas) of the lymph nodes, with variable defects in cellular immunity.
Patients do not make antibodies to polysaccharide antigens, and the response to protein antigens is poor. IgM levels are low, IgG is usually normal, while the levels of IgA and IgE are often elevated. Patients are prone to developing B-cell lymphomas.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl was brought to the OPD with complaints of repeated falls while walking for the past 1 year. She had difficulty in eating, gripping, or holding things. On examination, hand mouth incoordination and slurring of speech were noted. On ocular examination, the following finding was seen. All are true about this condition except:  [[IMG:1]]
options: There is defective production of IgA and IgG2
Affected gene is located on chromosome 11
There is increased risk of malignancy
questions.explanation:
The above clinical scenario and image showing telangiectasia are diagnostic of ataxia-telangiectasia. It is an autosomal-recessive disorder, not autosomal dominant.
The most prominent humoral immune abnormalities are defective production of IgA and IgG2. The gene responsible for this disorder is located on chromosome 11 and encodes a protein called ATM. The ATM protein is a sensor of DNA damage (double-strand breaks), and it activates p53 by phosphorylation.
Ataxia-telangiectasia is characterized by abnormal gait (ataxia), vascular malformations (telangiectases), neurologic deficits, increased incidence of tumors, and immunodeficiency. It may affect both B and T cells.
There is a high incidence of lymphomas and leukemias.

questions.stem: Human immunodeficiency virus affects CD4 cells due to their interaction with which protein?
questions.explanation:
The CD4 cells are affected by HIV due to their interaction with gp120.
HIV-1 virion is spherical and contains an electron-dense, cone-shaped core surrounded by a lipid envelope derived from the host cell membrane. Target cells of HIV include CD4+ helper T cells (worst affected), monocyte-macrophages, and dendritic cells.
The virus core contains:
Major capsid protein p24
Nucleocapsid protein p7/p9
Two copies of viral genomic RNA
The three viral enzymes (protease, reverse transcriptase, and integrase)
The viral core is surrounded by a matrix protein called p17, which lies underneath the virion envelope. The viral envelope is studded by two viral glycoproteins, gp120 and gp41, which are critical for HIV infection of cells.
Viral glycoprotein gp120 binds to CD4+ cells in the host. CXCR4 and CCR5 function as coreceptors for HIV-1 entry into CD4+ cells. This binding leads to a conformational change in gp41 causing exposure of a hydrophobic region called the fusion peptide at the tip of gp41. This peptide inserts into the cell membrane of the target cells (e.g., T cells or macrophages), leading to the fusion of the virus with the host cell.
The image below shows the pathogenesis of HIV infection.

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]
[[IMG:6]]

questions.stem: Which of the following cell types is not a target for the initiation and maintenance of HIV infection?
questions.explanation:
The neutrophil is not a target for the initiation and maintenance of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection.
HIV enters the body and affects T cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages. Particularly, memory and activated T cells are infected, but it is inefficient at productively infecting naive (unactivated) T cells.
Completion of the viral life cycle in latently infected cells occurs only after cell activation, and in the case of most CD4+ T cells, virus activation results in cell lysis.
The image below shows the pathogenesis of HIV infection.

questions.stem: Which is the most common CNS neoplasm in HIV patients?
questions.explanation:
The most common central nervous system (CNS) neoplasm in patients with HIV infection is primary CNS lymphoma.
Lymphomas are the most common CNS neoplasm in immunosuppressed individuals, including those with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) and immunosuppression after transplantation. They are associated with latent infection with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV). The vast majority of primary brain lymphomas are of B-cell origin.
At least two mechanisms appear to underlie the increased risk of B-cell tumors in HIV-infected individuals. They are:
The unchecked proliferation of B cells infected with oncogenic herpes viruses in the setting of profound T-cell depletion (AIDS).

Germinal center B-cell hyperplasia in the setting of early HIV infection.
The most common site for lymphoma in patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome
(AIDS) is the central nervous system (CNS).

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man, who is HIV-positive, presents with generalized lymphadenopathy. Which of the histopathological features is least likely to be seen on lymph node biopsy?
options: Collection of monocytoid B Cells in sinuses
questions.explanation:
Hematoxylin bodies are seen in lymph nodes in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE).
Features of AIDS-related lymphadenopathy:
Early stages of HIV infection:
Florid hyperplasia of B cell follicles
Follicle lysis
Monocytoid B cells in sinuses
Neutrophils and dermatopathic lymphadenopathy
The interfollicular zone shows vascular proliferation, which may progress to Kaposi sarcoma Late stages of HIV infection:
Severe lymphoid involution
Possible hyalinization of the germinal centers
Burnt-out lymph nodes, which become atrophic and may harbor numerous opportunistic pathogens, often within macrophages

questions.stem: A 50-year-old HIV-seropositive man presents with raised violaceous plaques over the legs. Microscopy shows a lesion in the dermis with dilated, jagged vascular channels lined and surrounded by plump spindle cells. It contains red cells with marked hemorrhage, hemosiderin pigment, and mononuclear inflammation. Mitotic figures are also seen. Which organism is associated with this tumor?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is Kaposi sarcoma, caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8).
Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm, that is highly associated with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). It is the most common cancer seen in patients having AIDS. Though the
incidence of Kaposi carcinoma reduced, it still occurs in 2-3% of HIV-infected individuals. The pathogenesis of Kaposi sarcoma that is caused by HHV8 includes:
A virally encoded G protein that induces VEGF production, stimulating endothelial growth
The lytic infection caused by HHV8 increases the pro-inflammatory cytokines
HHV8 encoded proteins inhibit the p53 induced apoptosis
The given images show coalescent red-purple macules and plaques of the skin and the histologic appearance of Kaposi sarcoma, demonstrating sheets of proliferating spindle cells:

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: A 45 -year-old HIV-positive patient has patchy pneumonia. Smears of induced sputum and sedimented cells from lavage fluid stained with methenamine silver are as seen below. Which is the most likely organism implicated?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The smears stained with methenamine silver show black-colored stained cysts resembling the crushed ping pong balls of Pneumocystis jirovecii.
Approximately 15% to 30% of untreated HIV-infected people develop pneumonia during the course of the disease. It is mainly caused by the fungus P. jirovecii (reactivation of prior latent infection).

[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: Which among the following best describes an amyloid?
questions.explanation:
Amyloid can be best described as a proteoglycan.
Amyloidosis refers to the extracellular deposition of fibrillar proteins.
Abnormal fibrils are produced by the aggregation of misfolded proteins. The fibrillar deposits bind a wide variety of proteoglycans and glycosaminoglycans (heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate), and plasma proteins (serum amyloid P component).
The abundant charged sugar groups in these adsorbed proteins give the deposits staining characteristics that resemble starch (amylose). Therefore, these deposits are called amyloid.
Amyloid appears as an amorphous, eosinophilic, hyaline, extracellular substance.

questions.stem: In a patient with reactive systemic amyloidosis, which of the following proteins are likely to get deposited in the tissues?
questions.explanation:
There is the deposition of AA proteins in reactive systemic amyloidosis (secondary amyloidosis).
In inflammatory states, there is a release of IL-1 and IL-6, which act on the liver cells. The liver increases the production of SAA (serum amyloid-associated) proteins which circulate bound to high-density lipoproteins. This gives rise to AA proteins, which get deposited in tissues causing reactive systemic amyloidosis or secondary amyloidosis.
The most common sites are the kidney and heart. It is usually seen secondary to:
Rheumatoid arthritis (most common)
Tuberculosis
Bronchiectasis
Chronic osteomyelitis
Inflammatory bowel disease
Ankylosing spondylitis
Malignancies - renal cell cancer, Hodgkin’s lymphoma

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of reactive amyloidosis worldwide?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of reactive amyloidosis worldwide is rheumatoid arthritis.
Amyloidosis is reported to occur in 3% of patients with rheumatoid arthritis and is clinically significant in one-half of those affected.

Conditions associated with reactive systemic (secondary) amyloidosis:
Rheumatoid arthritis (most common)
Ankylosing spondylitis
Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis)
Tuberculosis
Bronchiectasis
Chronic osteomyelitis
Malignancies - renal cell cancer, Hodgkin’s lymphoma

questions.stem: An elderly woman is brought with worsening memory for the past 3 years. Recently, she has been unable to carry out her daily chores and frequently gets lost in the neighborhood. There is no history of personality changes, rigidity, or gait disturbances. MRI brain shows temporal lobe atrophy. Which of the following deposits is likely to be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Alzheimer's disease. A amyloid deposition is seen in this condition.
A constitutes the core of cerebral plaques found in Alzheimer's disease. It also gets deposited in the walls of cerebral blood vessels. The A protein is derived by proteolysis from a much larger transmembrane glycoprotein, called amyloid precursor protein (APP).

questions.stem: A diabetic patient with chronic kidney disease has been undergoing hemodialysis for the past 4 years. Deposition of which of the following is likely in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Patients on long-term hemodialysis for renal failure can develop amyloidosis as a result of the deposition of  2-microglobulin.
This protein is present in high concentrations in the serum of persons with renal disease. The protein is retained in the circulation because it cannot be filtered through the dialysis membranes.
It gets deposited in the synovium, joints, and tendon sheaths. When this deposition takes place in the carpal ligament of the wrist, it leads to the development of carpal tunnel syndrome.
With new dialysis filters, the incidence of this complication has decreased substantially.

questions.stem: Which type of amyloidosis is caused by the mutation of the transthyretin protein?
questions.explanation:
Familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy (FAP) is associated with the deposition of mutant transthyretin protein (TTR).
FAP is an autosomal dominant condition. The deposition occurs as amyloid fibrils in peripheral and autonomic nerves. Mutated TTR is prone to misfolding and aggregation, and shows resistance to proteolysis.
Systemic senile amyloidosis (amyloid of aging) refers to the systemic deposition of normal

TTR amyloid in elderly patients. Symptomatic patients present with restrictive cardiomyopathy and arrhythmias. Another rare form affecting predominantly the heart results from the deposition of a mutant form of TTR.
Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) is an autosomal-recessive condition seen in individuals of Mediterranean descent (Armenian, Sephardic Jewish, and Arabic). The affected gene encodes a protein called pyrin, which is involved in cytokine production. The amyloid fibril proteins in this condition are made up of AA proteins. It presents with attacks of fever and serositis.
Isolated atrial amyloidosis is associated with AANP (atrial natriuretic peptide) amyloid deposition

questions.stem: Who among the following patients is at increased risk for developing amyloidosis?
options: A patient with maturity-onset diabetes of the young
A 15-year-old diabetic boy who is on insulin therapy
A 50-year-old diabetic patient with insulin resistance
A patient with autosomal dominant non-insulin dependent form of diabetes
questions.explanation:
Older individuals with insulin resistance are likely to have type 2 diabetes mellitus. These patients are at increased risk of developing amyloidosis.
Microscopic deposits of localized amyloid may be found in certain conditions such as:
Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid gland
Islet tumors of the pancreas
Pheochromocytomas
Undifferentiated carcinomas of the stomach
Islets of Langerhans in individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus

questions.stem: A middle-aged woman presents with thyroid swelling. The histological examination of the swelling is shown below. What type of amyloid deposits are seen in this condition?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]]
questions.explanation:
The slide is showing the presence of amyloid-rich stroma (pinkish material) and nests of polygonal cells, suggestive of medullary carcinoma thyroid. The major fibril protein that gets deposited is A Cal, which is derived from calcitonin.

[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]
Microscopic deposits of localized amyloid may be found in certain conditions such as:
Medullary carcinoma of the thyroid gland
Islet tumors of the pancreas
Pheochromocytomas
Undifferentiated carcinomas of the stomach
Islets of Langerhans in individuals with type 2 diabetes mellitus

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common organ involved in AL amyloidosis?
questions.explanation:
The most common organ involved in AL amyloidosis is renal tissue (Kidneys). They are affected in 70–80% of patients with amyloidosis.
Heart is the second most commonly affected organ (50–60%), and cardiac involvement is the leading cause of death from AL amyloidosis.
Renal amyloidosis usually manifests as proteinuria, often in the nephrotic range, and is associated with hypoalbuminemia, secondary hypercholesterolemia, hypertriglyceridemia, and edema or anasarca.

questions.stem: A bone marrow examination is being planned for a patient with AL amyloidosis. Which of the following is likely to be seen?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Bone marrow examination in AL amyloidosis shows plasmacytosis.
The AL type of amyloid or primary amyloidosis is associated with immunocyte dyscrasias like multiple myeloma or other B cell neoplasms. The tumor cells in multiple myeloma secrete light chains of the immunoglobulins of either the lambda or kappa type, which get deposited in the tissues as amyloid.
The chemical nature of the amyloid is AL (A for amyloid and L for light chain).

questions.stem: In lardaceous spleen, deposition of amyloid occurs in which of the following sites?
questions.explanation: Lardaceous spleen is due to the deposition of amyloid in sinusoids of the red pulp. Sago spleen is due to the deposition of amyloid in splenic follicles (white pulp).

questions.stem: Match the following.
questions.explanation:
The correct match is:
Condition | Amyloid prot ein
Familial Mediterranean fever | AA
Alzheimer's disease | A
Systemic senile amyloidosis | ATTR
Hemodialysis-associated amy loidosis | A 2m

questions.stem: In a patient with suspected systemic amyloidosis, which of the following is the initial investigation of choice?
questions.explanation:
In suspected systemic amyloidosis, the initial investigation of choice is abdominal fat aspirate staining.
Diagnosis of amyloidosis involves the following:
Localized amyloidosis - biopsy the organ involved. e.g., kidney
Systemic amyloidosis - deposits can be found in any tissue of the body
Initial test - non-invasive test on easily accessible tissue (eg: abdominal fat) which is positive in
>80% of cases
If this is negative - more invasive biopsies of the kidney, heart, lung or GI tract (rectal biopsy)
Suspected AL amyloidosis - serum and urine electrophoresis and immunoelectrophoresis
The histological examination of the biopsy material is the commonest confirmatory method for the diagnosis in a suspected case of amyloidosis. The next best step is to determine the type of precursor protein by immunohistochemistry, immunoelectron microscopy, or extraction and biochemical analysis employing mass spectrometry.
Scintigraphy with radiolabeled serum amyloid P component is a rapid and specific test, which gives the extent of the disease. It can be used to follow up on patients undergoing treatment.

questions.stem: A kidney biopsy sample is obtained from a patient with high suspicion of amyloidosis. All of the following can be used to stain this sample, except:
questions.explanation:
Sudan Black is used for staining lipids, not amyloid. Staining for amyloid:
Congo red - most widely used and specific
Iodine staining -
Used for unfixed specimens or histological sections
Amyloid stains mahogany brown and turns violet on adding sulfuric acid
Thioflavin T and S -
Secondary immunofluorescence with ultraviolet light
Thioflavin T is useful for demonstrating the juxtaglomerular apparatus of the kidney
Metachromatic stains (crystal violet and methyl violet) - rose-pink appearance.
Periodic-acid Schiff (PAS) positive
The image given below shows the amyloid appearance on congo red under plain microscopy.

questions.stem: A pathologist is examining a sample from a patient with amyloidosis. Which of the following is false about the specimen's appearance?
options: Rose pink appearance under crystal violet stain
Mahogany brown color on iodine staining
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Amyloid shows apple-green birefringence under polarised microscopy, after staining with Congo red.
The appearance of amyloid:
Light microscopy - amorphous, eosinophilic, hyaline, extracellular substance
Congo red stain - the characteristic appearance using this stain is due to the cross- -pleated sheet conformation
Under ordinary light, it appears pink or red color (as shown below)

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]
- Under the polarizing microscope - imparts apple-green birefringence to amyloid deposits (as shown in the image below)
Electron microscopy - continuous, nonbranching fibrils with a diameter of approximately 7.5 to 10 nm
X-ray crystallography and infrared spectroscopy - Characteristic cross- -pleated sheet conformation.
It appears mahogany brown on iodine staining and rose-pink on staining with crystal violet.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not directly involved in graft rejection?
questions.explanation:
Macrophages present foreign graft antigens to the T-cells but are not directly involved in graft rejection.
Graft rejection is both humoral and cell-mediated in nature. It is a process in which T-cells and antibodies produced against graft antigens react against tissue grafts and destroy it.
The major antigenic differences that result in the rejection of transplants are differences in HLA alleles. The recipient T-cells are involved in the recognition of the donor MHC molecules and mount an immune response. Depending on the antigen-presenting cells (APCs) that are involved in T-cell activation, there are 2 pathways:
Direct pathway of allorecognition - MHC antigens are presented by the APCs in the graft
Indirect pathway of allorecognition - MHC antigens are presented by the recipient’s own APCs
(e.g., macrophages)
The early activation of NK cells kill allogeneic target cells directly or via antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity and release various chemokines and immunomodulatory cytokines.

questions.stem: A man is receiving a matched blood group kidney allograft. While closing the abdomen, the surgeon notices a sudden color change to pale-white in the transplanted kidney. He decides to remove it. Which of the following is responsible for graft rejection in this patient?
questions.explanation: The given clinical scenario within minutes of transplant is suggestive of hyperacute rejection and is due to preformed antibodies from the recipient.

questions.stem: A patient underwent kidney transplantation due to severe diabetic nephropathy. A few months later, he presented with fever, malaise, and flank pain. During evaluation, oliguria and an acute rise in creatinine levels were observed. A biopsy of the kidney showed endotheliitis. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and the biopsy findings of endotheliitis suggest a diagnosis of acute cell-mediated graft rejection.
In acute cell-mediated graft rejection, CD8+ CTLs directly destroy graft cells or CD4+ cells secrete cytokines that damage the graft.
On histopathology, it produces two different patterns of injury in the graft:
Tubulointerstitial pattern (type I): extensive interstitial and tubular inflammation associated with focal tubular injury
Vascular pattern - Inflammation (type II) and necrosis (type III), endotheliitis (swollen endothelial cells with lymphocytes between endothelium and vessel wall)
Immunosuppressive therapy aims to prevent and reduce acute rejection by blocking the activation of alloreactive T cells. In the absence of humoral rejection, patients respond well to immunosuppressive therapy.

questions.stem: In patients with acute graft-versus-host disease, which of the following organs is least likely to be involved?
questions.explanation:
The lung is least likely to get affected in acute graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).
GVHD occurs when immunologically competent cells or their precursors are transplanted into immunologically crippled recipients. The transferred cells recognize alloantigens in the host and attack host tissues.
It is seen most commonly in the setting of hematopoietic stem cell (HSC) transplantation. Rarely, it may occur following transplantation of solid organs rich in lymphoid cells (e.g., the liver) or transfusion of unirradiated blood.
It is of two types, acute and chronic.
Acute GVHD develops within days to weeks. There is the involvement of the immune system and epithelium of the skin, liver, and intestines. It presents with:
Generalized rash
Jaundice
Bloody diarrhea due to mucosal ulceration

Non-infectious pulmonary infiltrates (rarely), the outcome is generally poor Chronic GVHD may follow the acute syndrome or occur insidiously. It presents with:
Skin - extensive cutaneous injury, with the destruction of skin appendages and dermal fibrosis
(may resemble systemic sclerosis)
Liver - chronic liver disease, manifested as cholestatic jaundice
GIT - esophageal strictures
Immune system involvement - involution of the thymus and depletion of lymphocytes GVHD is mediated by T lymphocytes contained in the transplanted donor
cells. Therefore, depletion of donor T cells before transfusion virtually eliminates the disease.

questions.stem: Graft from identical twin is called:
questions.explanation:
A graft from an identical twin is called an isograft.
Isograft is defined as an organ or tissue that is taken from a donor and is transplanted to a recipient who has the same genetic constitution as the donor. For example, graft between identical twins.

questions.stem: Which is the most common type of anemia worldwide?
questions.explanation:
The most common type of anaemia worldwide is iron deficiency anemia. It is also the most common type of nutritional anemia in India.
WHO recommendations for diagnosing anemia (g/dl) are:
Population | Nor mal | Mild Ane mia | Moderate Ane mia | Severe Ane mia
Men 15 years | 13 | 11 - 12.9 | 8 - 10.9 | <8
Non-pregnant wo men | 12 | 11 - 11.9 | 8 - 10.9 | <8
Pregnant women | 11 | 10 - 10.9 | 7 - 9.9 | <7

questions.stem: What is the most common hematologic manifestation seen in patients with HIV infection?
questions.explanation:
Anaemia is the most common hematologic abnormality associated with HIV infection. It affects 60–80% of patients during the late stage.
In most cases, the cause of anaemia in HIV-infected patients is multifactorial. It is often associated with infection, inflammation, malignancy, malnutrition, and polypharmacy.
Note: Prior to the use of potent antiretroviral therapy (ART), thrombocytopenia was a common finding in individuals infected with HIV. With use of potent ART, the incidence of thrombocytopenia is far lower.

questions.stem: Which of the following anemia is not due to diminished erythropoiesis?
questions.explanation:
Hereditary spherocytosis is not due to diminished erythropoiesis. It is a type of hemolytic anemia. Classification of anemia according to underlying mechanism:
Anemias of diminished erythropoiesis - decreased red cell production

Hemolytic anemias - increased red cell destruction
Anemia due to blood loss
Anemias due to diminished erythropoiesis:
Iron deficiency anemia
Megaloblastic anemia
Anemia of chronic diseases
Aplastic anemia
Myelophthisic anemia
Fanconi's anemia

questions.stem: In a patient with MCV of 109 fl, which of the following is least likely?
questions.explanation:
MCV >100 fl indicates macrocytic anaemia which is not seen in anaemia of chronic disease. RBCs in anemia of chronic disease are initially normocytic and normochromic, becoming microcytic and hypochromic over time.
Vitamin B12 deficiency, thiamine deficiency, and orotic aciduria cause macrocytic anaemia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with iron deficiency anaemia is prescribed oral iron supplements. Foods containing which of the following can she take to increase its absorption?
questions.explanation: Absorption of iron is increased by ascorbic acid. It is decreased by phosphates, oxalates, and carbonates.

questions.stem: Which of the following contains most of the functional iron in the body?
questions.explanation:
Most of the functional iron (80%) in the body is found in hemoglobin.
The storage pool represented by hemosiderin, and ferritin contains about 15% to 20% of total body iron. Myoglobin and iron-containing enzymes such as catalase and the cytochromes contain the rest.

questions.stem: Which transporter is required for the transport of iron into the enterocyte?
questions.explanation:
DMT1 (divalent metal transporter 1) is required for the transport of iron into the enterocyte.
Dietary iron is mostly in Fe3+ (ferric state) and must be reduced to Fe2+ (ferrous state) by ferrireductases. Fe2+ iron destined for circulation is transported from the cytoplasm across the basolateral enterocyte membrane by ferroportin 1.

[[IMG:1]]
Hephaestin is an iron oxidase that converts Fe2+ to Fe3+

questions.stem: Which of the following is involved in iron metabolism?
questions.explanation:
Ceruloplasmin is involved in iron metabolism.
Ferritin is the storage form of iron in the body. Ceruloplasmin and hephaestin help in oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ at the basolateral border of enterocytes. This is coupled with transport through ferroportin. In plasma, iron is transported by transferrin.
Haptocorrin and cubulin are involved in vitamin B12 absorption. Selenoprotein is involved in selenium metabolism.

questions.stem: Hepcidin inhibits iron transfer from the enterocyte to the plasma by binding to
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Hepcidin inhibits iron transfer from the enterocytes into the plasma by binding to ferroportin, which is an iron efflux channel in the enterocyte.
Iron metabolism is regulated by hepcidin, a protein and acute phase reactant produced by the liver. It binds to ferroportin and degrades it. This inhibits the transfer of iron from the enterocyte to the plasma via ferroportin. As a result, iron becomes trapped within the duodenal cells (enterocytes) in the form of mucosal ferritin and is lost in feces when these cells are shed off.
Transcription of hepcidin is increased by the following factors:
Increased levels of iron
Inflammatory cytokines
Transcription of hepcidin is decreased by the following factors:
Iron deficiency
Hypoxia
Ineffective erythropoiesis
Hepcidin is encoded by the HAMP gene and its mutations are associated with hereditary hemochromatosis.

questions.stem: What is the main site of iron absorption?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Absorption of iron mainly occurs in the proximal duodenum.

questions.stem: Which of the following is true regarding the internal iron homeostasis in iron-deficiency anaemia?
options: Ferritin mRNA concentration iron-responsive element increases and ferritin synthesis decreases
Transferrin receptor 1 iron-responsive elements increases transferrin receptor mRNA concentration and synthesis
Transferrin receptor 1 iron responsive elements decreases transferrin receptor mRNA concentration and synthesis
Ferritin mRNA concentration iron responsive element decreases and ferritin synthesis increases
questions.explanation:
In iron deficiency anaemia, there is an increase in transferrin receptor mRNA concentration and synthesis.
Iron absorbed through diet or which is released from circulation is bound to transferrin (iron transfer protein). When erythropoiesis is stimulated, iron-transferrin complexes act as transferrin receptors on the surface of bone marrow erythroid cells. Through receptor-mediated endocytosis, this complex is internalised.
This iron is then made available for heme synthesis while the transferrin-receptor complex is recycled to the surface of the cell, from where the transferrin is released back into circulation and the transferrin receptor re-anchors into the cell membrane. The excess iron after hemoglobin synthesis binds to apoferritin (storage protein), forming ferritin.
Senescent RBCs undergo phagocytosis in the cells of the reticuloendothelial system. The hemoglobin is broken down, the globin and other proteins are returned to the amino acid pool, and the iron is shuttled back to the surface of the reticuloendothelial cell, where it is taken up by transferrin via ferroportin (iron export channel).
There is no regulated excretory pathway for iron, and the only mechanisms by which iron is lost are blood loss (via gastrointestinal bleeding, menstruation, or other forms of bleeding) and the loss of epithelial cells from the skin, gut, and genitourinary tract. The normal daily iron loss from the body is 1-2 mg.
Variables | Iron-deficient state | Iron-excess stat e
Iron uptake |  | 
Transferrin receptor synthesi s |  | 
Transferrin receptor mRNA c oncentration |  | 
Iron storage |  | 
Ferritin synthesis |  | 
Ferritin mRNA concentration | No change | No change

questions.stem: Peripheral smear of a patient with koilonychia is given below. Which of the following lab findings is consistent with her likely diagnosis?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation: The given peripheral smear showing microcytic and hypochromic picture with pencil cells is suggestive of iron-deficiency anaemia. In this condition, TIBC is increased, transferrin saturation is decreased, and ferritin is decreased.

questions.stem: You would expect iron-deficiency anaemia in all of the following patients except:
options: A 54-year-old woman after Billroth II operation
questions.explanation:
Maize rich diet is not one of the causes of iron deficiency anaemia. It can cause pellagra.
Iron deficiency anaemia can be caused by hookworm infestation, carcinoma of the cecum and in Billroth II operation.

questions.stem: Which of the following laboratory findings is seen in a patient with sideroblastic anaemia?
questions.explanation: In sideroblastic anemia, the transferrin saturation is increased. Serum iron and serum ferritin are also elevated.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not included in the triad of the Plummer-Vinson syndrome?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The triad of the Plummer-Vinson syndrome does not include koilonychia (marked as 2). Triad of Plummer–Vinson syndrome:
Esophageal webs
Microcytic hypochromic anaemia
Atrophic glossitis
Koilonychia is a symptom of iron deficiency anaemia. It may or may not be present in Plummer Vinson syndrome. Hence, it is not a part of the triad.

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with severe anaemia was started on parenteral iron. Which of the following would occur first in this patient as a response to therapy?
questions.explanation:
One of the earliest responses to the correction of iron deficiency anaemia is increase in serum iron.
Responses after initiation of treatment:
12 to 24 hours - Replenishment of intracellular iron enzymes; decreased irritability; increased appetite; increase in serum iron.
36 to 48 hours - Erythroid hyperplasia in bone marrow
48 to 72 hours - Reticulocytosis, peaking at 5-7 days
4 to 30 days - Increase in hemoglobin level, increase in ferritin, increase in MCV
1 to 3 months - Repletion of stores


[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman who is taking OCPs presents with weakness and fatigue. Her laboratory investigations and peripheral smear are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of megaloblastic anaemia due to the following reasons:
History of OCP use
Hemogram shows decreased hemoglobin and increased MCV
Peripheral smear shows anisopoikilocytosis, macroovalocytes, and hypersegmented neutrophils

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a history of bowel resection for Crohn's disease develops megaloblastic anaemia. Which component of the vitamin B12 metabolism is likely to be affected in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Ileal resection for Crohn's disease can cause megaloblastic anaemia due to the decrease in cubilin receptors. They are the vitamin B12 receptors on the ileum.
Absorption of vitamin B12 involves the following steps:
Pepsin in the stomach releases vitamin B12 from the binding proteins in the food
Released B12 binds to haptocorrin, which is a salivary protein
In the duodenum, pancreatic proteases release B12 from haptocorrin
B12 binds to intrinsic factor to form IF-B12 complex
In the ileum, ileal enterocytes that contain cubulin receptors (IF receptor) endocytose the complex
In the ileal cells, B12 is associated with transcobalamin II, which is a carrier protein
B12 is delivered to the liver, bone marrow and GIT

questions.stem: In which of the following patients would you not suspect megaloblastic anaemia caused by vitamin B12 deficiency?  [[IMG:1]]
options: A 5-year-old child with fish tapeworm infestation
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:2]]
Phenytoin therapy causes folate deficiency leading to megaloblastic anaemia. It does not cause vitamin B12 deficiency.
Dietary folate is in polyglutamate form, which is then converted into monoglutamates by the intestinal conjugase. Phenytoin acts by inhibiting this enzyme, thereby causing folate deficiency, and thus megaloblastic anaemia.
Options A, B and C: They cause megaloblastic anemia due to vitamin B12 deficiciency.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old female with easy fatiguability and pallor presented to the OPD. The image of her hand is as given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Skin hyperpigmentation especially on the dorsum of hands involving the knuckles is seen in cyanocobalamin or vitamin B12 deficiency which is a causative factor of megaloblastic anaemia.
In megaloblastic anaemia, there is impairment of DNA synthesis that leads to ineffective hematopoiesis. It also causes distinctive morphologic changes, including abnormally large erythroid precursors and red cells.
Clinical features of megaloblastic anaemia (cyanocobalamin and folate deficiency) include: Peripheral smear findings:
Macro-ovalocytes
Most macrocytes lack the central pallor of normal red cells and even appear hyperchromic, but the MCHC is not elevated.
Reticulocyte count is low
Nucleated red cell progenitors occasionally appear in the circulating blood when anaemia is severe
Neutrophils are also larger than normal (macro polymorphonuclear) and show nuclear hypersegmentation, having five or more nuclear lobules
The image given below shows hypersegmented neutrophils seen in megaloblastic anaemia.

[[IMG:1]]
System | Clinical features
Oral | GlossitisAngular cheilosis
Gastrointestinal | AnorexiaWeight lossDiarrhea Constipation
Skin | Hyperpigmentation(reversibl e)
Hematological | ThrombocytopeniaLeucopeni aIneffective erythropoiesis an d unconjugatedjaundice
Cardiovascular | Atherosclerosis leading to PV D, CAD (due to elevated hom ocysteine)
Neurological (only B12) | Peripheral neuropathySubac ute combined degeneration ( degeneration of the posterior and pyramidal tracts of the s pinal cord)
Pregnancy (only folate) | Recurrent fetal lossNeural tu be defects
Others | Mildfeverin severe casesPsyc hiatric disturbances
Bone marrow findings:
Markedly hypercellular as a result of increased hematopoietic precursors.
Sieve-like pattern of chromatin of immature precursors (Megaloblasts)
Granulocytic precursors also display dysmaturation in the form of giant metamyelocytes and band forms
Megakaryocytes can be abnormally large and have bizarre, multilobate nuclei
The derangement in DNA synthesis causes most precursors to undergo apoptosis in the marrow
(ineffective hematopoiesis) and leads to pancytopenia

questions.stem: What is your diagnosis with respect to the findings shown in the peripheral smear given below?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]]
questions.explanation:
The peripheral smear showing macro-ovalocytes and a hypersegmented neutrophil are suggestive of megaloblastic anaemia. Vitamin B12 deficiency is a cause of megaloblastic anaemia.

Peripheral smear findings in megaloblastic anaemia:
Macro-ovalocytes
Most macrocytes lack the central pallor of normal red cells and even appear hyperchromic, but the MCHC is not elevated.
Reticulocyte count is low
Nucleated red cell progenitors occasionally appear in the circulating blood when anaemia is severe
Neutrophils are also larger than normal (macro polymorphonuclear) and show nuclear hypersegmentation, having five or more nuclear lobules

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would you not expect to see in patients with megaloblastic anaemia?
questions.explanation:
The reticulocyte count is decreased in megaloblastic anaemia.
The reticulocyte count is indicative of bone marrow function and its ability to produce healthy erythrocytes. In megaloblastic anemia, there is intramedullary hemolysis leading to raised indirect bilirubin and impaired erythroid maturation leading to a low reticulocyte count.

questions.stem: A patient is suspected to have megaloblastic anaemia. Which of the following will not be helpful in differentiating vitamin B12 deficiency from folate deficiency?
questions.explanation: Increased serum homocysteine levels are common to both vitamin B12 deficiency and folate deficiency. Hence, it cannot be used to differentiate between them.

questions.stem: You are examining the peripheral smear of a patient with anaemia and see the following finding. Name the finding and its pathogenesis.  [[IMG:1]]
options: Howell Jolly body - ineffective RBC enucleation
questions.explanation:
The marked structure in this peripheral smear showing figure of 8 appearance is a Cabot ring. They are RBC inclusion bodies seen in conditions due to ineffective erythropoiesis. It is considered a remnant of microtubules during cell division.
Cabot rings can be seen in the following conditions:
Megaloblastic anaemia
Post-splenectomy patients
Lead poisoning
Hemolytic anemias
Option A: Heinz bodies are due to oxidative damage, seen in G6PD deficiency.
Option B: Basophilic stippling is due to ribosomal precipitation, seen in heavy metal poisoning, thalassemia and sickle cell disease.
Option D: Howell Jolly bodies are due to ineffective RBC enucleation, characteristic of asplenia.

questions.stem: Schilling's test can be used for all the following except
options: To differentiate between vitamin B12 and folate deficiency
To identify the cause of vitamin B12 deficiency
To identify the extent of megaloblastic anaemia
questions.explanation: Schilling test cannot identify the extent of megaloblastic anaemia.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false regarding the antibodies of pernicious anaemia?
options: Type I antibodies are found in both plasma and gastric juice
Type I antibody blocks the binding of vitamin B12 to intrinsic factor
Type II antibodies prevent the binding of the IF-B12 complex to ileal receptors
Type III antibodies are against haptocorrin
questions.explanation:
Type III antibodies are not against haptocorrin. They recognize the  and  subunits of the gastric proton pumps.
Pernicious anaemia is a specific form of megaloblastic anaemia caused by autoimmune gastritis. It impairs the production of intrinsic factor, which is required for vitamin B12 uptake from the gut.
Types of antibodies in pernicious anaemia are:
Type I antibodies - block the binding of vitamin B12 to intrinsic factor. They are found in both plasma and gastric juice
Type II antibodies - prevent binding of the intrinsic factor-vitamin B12 (IF-B12) complex to its ileal receptor
Type III antibodies - recognize the  and  subunits of the gastric proton pump of parietal cells

questions.stem: A 53-year-old woman presents with complaints of light-headedness every time she stands up. She is a known case of rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate. On examination, she has pallor and brittle nails. Which of the following statements is true regarding her condition?  [[IMG:1]]
options: Serum iron and tissue iron levels are normal
Anemia can be normocytic and normochromic
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of anaemia of chronic diseases (ACD). In this condition, the anaemia initially can be normocytic normochromic.
ACD occurs in the setting of persistent systemic inflammation. It is associated with
Low serum iron
Reduced total iron-binding capacity
Abundant stored iron in tissue macrophages
Inflammatory mediators like IL-6 stimulate an increase in the production of hepcidin.
This inhibits ferroportin function in the macrophages and reduces the transfer of iron from the storage pool to developing erythroid precursors in the marrow. As a result, erythroid precursors are starved for iron despite the availability of plenty of iron in tissue macrophages.

questions.stem: Identify the cell in the given peripheral blood smear and the likely diagnosis.
options: Acanthocyte in anemia of renal disease
Acanthocyte in anemia of liver disease
Echinocyte in anemia of renal disease
Echinocyte in anemia of liver disease
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Acanthocyte or spur cells are seen in anaemia of liver disease. These cells are characterized by only a few spicules of varying sizes that project from the cell surface at irregular intervals.
Conditions where acanthocytes can be seen include:
Severe liver disease
Abetalipoproteinemia
Post splenectomy
Hyposplenism
The image given below shows a peripheral smear with acanthoctye.

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
Echinocytes or burr cells are seen in anaemia of renal disease. These cells are characterized by smaller, regularly spaced projections, smoothly rounded crenulations which are uniform in shape and distribution compared to acanthocytes.
Conditions where echinocytes can be seen include:
Anaemia of renal disease (uremia)
In premature infants, after exchange transfusion
Storage artefact
The image given below shows a peripheral smear with echinocytes.

questions.stem: [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]] Which of the following is the most common cause of aplastic anemia?
questions.explanation:
From the given options, the most common cause of aplastic anemia is drugs. Causes of aplastic anemia:
Acquired
Idiopathic - most common cause (about 65% of the cases)
Acquired stem-cell defects

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman presents with progressive weakness and fatigue. Her hemogram is given below. What is the best investigation to arrive at the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given hemogram is suggestive of pancytopenia. Cause of pancytopenia can be aplastic anaemia (hypocellular bone marrow) or myeloid neoplasms (hypercellular bone marrow). Hence, the best investigation is bone marrow biopsy to differentiate between them.
Findings in bone marrow biopsy in aplastic anaemia:
Markedly hypocellular bone marrow largely devoid of hematopoietic cells
Abundant fat cells
Fibrous stroma, scattered lymphocytes, and plasma cells
Bone marrow aspiration often yields a dry tap, so biopsy is preferred.

questions.stem: Bone marrow biopsy of a patient with pancytopenia is given below. What is the most common infectious cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given bone marrow biopsy shows a hypocellular bone marrow with abundant fat cells which is suggestive of aplastic anaemia. In this condition, the most common infectious cause is viral hepatitis of the non-A, Non-B, Non-C, and Non-G type.

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
The images given below show the normal and hypocellular bone marrow.
Note- Viral hepatitis, parvovirus B19, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), cytomegalovirus and Epstein-Barr virus can cause aplastic anemia. Viral hepatitis is however the most common cause.

questions.stem: Which of the following is likely to develop in a patient with aplastic anaemia?
questions.explanation: Aplastic anaemia can transform into both acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS).

questions.stem: Which of the following causes pure red cell aplasia?
questions.explanation:
Causes of pure red cell aplasia include:

Neoplasms - thymomas and large granular lymphocytic leukemia
Drug exposure - phenytoin, azathioprine and isoniazid
Auto-immune disorders - neutralizing antibodies against erythropoietin
Parvovirus infection
Hereditary - Diamond Blackfan syndrome

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of myelophthisic anaemia?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of myelophthisic anaemia is metastatic cancer from the breast, lung, and prostate.
Myelophthisic anaemia describes a form of marrow failure in which space-occupying lesions replace normal marrow elements. Causes include:
Metastatic cancer
Granulomatous diseases
Myeloproliferative neoplasms.
This leads to the release of nucleated erythroid precursors and immature granulocytic forms into peripheral blood (leukoerythroblastosis) and tear-drop shaped red cells.
The image given below shows a peripheral smear with teardrop cells.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man presents with progressive weakness and chronic fatigue. Physical examination reveals a hard nodule of about 1cm in the prostate. His lab reports reveal low Hb and elevated PSA. Peripheral blood smear shows a normocytic normochromic picture. There are some occasional myelocytes, a few tear-drop cells and 2 nucleated RBCs per 100 white cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of myelophthisic anaemia. Prostatic mass with elevated PSA and age suggestive of prostatic carcinoma, which could be the likely cause in this case.
It is a form of marrow failure in which space-occupying lesions replace normal marrow elements. The most common cause is metastatic cancer from the breast, lung, and prostate.
Lab findings of myelophthisic anaemia include:
Myelocytes + nucleated RBCs = leukoerythroblastic image
Presence of tear-drop cells

questions.stem: A 52-year-old male patient comes with complaints of abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. A peripheral blood smear reveals macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils and an endoscopy reveals atrophic gastritis. Which of the following conditions is likely to be seen this patient?
questions.explanation:
The given findings are suggestive of pernicious anemia, which is associated with atrophic gastritis and vitamin B12 deficiency.
Anemic patient with a peripheral smear showing macrocytic RBCs and hypersegmented neutrophils are important characteristic features of megaloblastic anemia. Vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency are the main causes of megaloblastic anemia.
Pernicious anemia is an autoimmune disease characterized by the presence of autoantibodies which impairs the production or activity of the intrinsic factor (IF). This is required for the uptake of vitamin B12. There are three types of autoantibodies namely, type I, II, and III. The action of each of these include:
Autoantibody type I prevents the binding of vitamin B12 to the intinsic factor (IF).
Autoantibody type II prevents the binding of vitamin B12-IF complex to the ileal receptors.
Autoantibody type III acts against the  and  subunits of the gastric proton pump, which impairs the production of intrinsic factor.
These patients also develop chronic atrophic gastritis, characterized by loss of parietal cells, infiltration of lymphocytes and plasma cells and megaloblastic changes in mucosal cells.

questions.explanation:
The types of hemoglobin along with their globin chains are:
The image given below shows the graphical representation of the globin chain synthesis.

questions.stem: Enzyme deficiency in which of the following pathways can cause hemolysis?
questions.explanation:
Enzyme deficiency in the glycolytic pathway can cause hemolysis. The following enzyme deficiencies can cause hemolysis:
In the glycolytic pathway:
Pyruvate kinase deficiency
Hexokinase deficiency
In the HMP shunt pathway:
G6PD deficiency
Glutathione synthetase deficiency
Note: Orotic aciduria causes megaloblastic anaemia.

questions.stem: What is the normal reticulocyte count?
questions.explanation:
Normal reticulocyte count is 0.5–1.5% of total red cells. Causes of increased reticulocyte count:

Hemolytic anaemia
Acute and chronic blood loss
Causes of decreased reticulocyte count:
Iron deficiency anaemia
Megaloblastic anaemia
Aplastic anaemia
Anaemia of chronic diseases
Myelodysplastic syndromes

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false about reticulocytes?
options: They are larger in size than red cell
questions.explanation:
Reticulocytes are red cell precursors, which are non-nucleated.
They have blue-red polychromatophilic cytoplasm due to the presence of a reticular (mesh-like) network of ribosomal RNA. They can be visualized using supravital stains like methylene blue and brilliant cresyl blue, which stain the ribosomal RNA.
Reticulocytosis (increased reticulocytes) indicates effective erythropoiesis i.e. good bone marrow response to anaemia. It is seen in:
Hemolytic anaemias
Acute blood loss
Reticulocytopenia (decreased reticulocytes) indicates ineffective erythropoiesis i.e. poor bone marrow response to anaemia. It is seen in:
Chemotherapy
Aplastic anaemia
Bone marrow malignancy
Anaemia of chronic disease
Iron-deficiency anaemia
Vitamin B12 and folate deficiency

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
The peripheral smear shows reticulocytosis and spherocytosis seen in non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman had severe blood loss during delivery 2-days ago. Her current hemoglobin is 5 gm/dL and reticulocyte count is 9%. What is her corrected reticulocyte count?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the corrected reticulocyte count is 3. It is given by the following formula:
Corrected reticulocyte count = Reticulocyte count × (patient's hemoglobin or hematocrit  standard hemoglobin or hematocrit)
So, in this case, the corrected reticulocyte count = 9×5/15 = 9/3 = 3
This formula corrects for hemoglobin. It will show you if the patient is making enough reticulocytes for the degree of anemia present. As the hemoglobin drops, reticulocytes increase from the normal range of 0.5–2.0%.
The standard reference range of hemoglobin concentration in females is 12-15 g/dl. Accordingly, in this scenario, corrected reticulocyte count would range between 3-3.75%. So, the best answer to this question remains option C.
Absolute reticulocyte count is the percentage of red cells that are reticulocytes (normal is about 0.5 – 2.0%). However, it does not reflect the fact that as the hemoglobin drops, there should be more reticulocytes, percentage-wise (for example, at a hemoglobin of 5, you should have a much higher percentage of reticulocytes than you should at a hemoglobin of 10). To take this into account, we use corrected reticulocyte count.
Reticulocyte Index = Corrected reticulocyte count / maturation factor
This corrects for the longer life span of prematurely released reticulocytes in the blood which is a phenomenon of increased red blood cell production.
Hematocrit | Maturation fact or
 35% | 1.0
35% > Hct  25% | 1.5
25% > Hct  20% | 2.0
< 20% | 2.5

questions.stem: In a patient with microcytic hypochromic anaemia, red cell distribution width was measured. What is this parameter used to identify?
questions.explanation:
Red cell distribution width (RDW) deals with anisocytosis of RBCs. It refers to the unequal size of the RBCs.
Normal values are:
RDW-SD (Standard deviation) - 39-46 fL
RDW-CV (Coefficient of variation) - 11.6-14.6%
RDW is of great use in two clinical situations. They are:
To differentiate between thalassemia and iron deficiency anaemia (IDA)
Thalassemia - the RBCs are small (low MCV) and of uniform size (normal RDW)
IDA - the RBCs are small (low MCV) but vary greatly in size (high RDW).
To diagnose dimorphic anaemia (anaemia due to both iron and vitamin B12 deficiency)
High RDW
Normal MCV

questions.stem: Which of the following is not increased in intravascular hemolysis?
questions.explanation:
Haptoglobin is decreased in intravascular hemolysis. Types of hemolysis based on location:
Intravascular hemolysis - hemolysis that occurs mainly within the blood vessels
Extravascular hemolysis - hemolysis that occurs via macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system in the spleen, liver, bone marrow, and lymph nodes
Features of intravascular hemolysis are:
Decreased haptoglobin
Increased lactate dehydrogenase
Hemoglobinemia
Hemoglobinuria
Hemosiderinuria
Methemoglobinemia
Methemoglobinuria
Indirect hyperbilirubinemia

questions.stem: Which of the following does not cause intravascular hemolysis?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Thalassemia causes extravascular hemolysis. Causes of intravascular hemolysis:
Mechanical injury
Trauma caused by cardiac valves
Microangiopathic hemolytic anaemias (hemolytic uremic syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura )
Repetitive physical trauma
Complement fixation (antibody-mediated destruction)
Hemolytic disease of the newborn
Transfusion reaction
Drug-induced
Infections of red blood cells
Malaria
Babesiosis
Exogenous toxic factors - Clostridial sepsis
Causes of extravascular hemolysis:
Hereditary spherocytosis
Thalassemia
Sickle cell anaemia
Causes of both intravascular and extravascular:
G6PD deficiency
Autoimmune hemolytic anaemia

questions.stem: Which of the following pairs of mutation and involved genes describes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) is a disease that results from acquired mutations in the phosphatidylinositol glycan complementation group A gene (PIGA).
This gene codes for an enzyme that is essential for the synthesis of certain membrane-associated complement regulatory proteins. It is the only hemolytic anaemia caused by an acquired genetic defect.
PNH blood cells are deficient in 3 GPI-linked proteins that regulate complement activity:
Decay Accelerating Factor or CD55
Membrane Inhibitor of Reactive Lysis or CD59
C˜-binding protein
CD59, a potent inhibitor of C3 convertase, prevents the spontaneous activation of the alternative complement pathway. Red cells deficient in these GPI-linked factors are abnormally susceptible to lysis or injury by C5b-C9 membrane attack complex of the complement system.

questions.stem: Which of the following cells are involved in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?
questions.explanation:
All three cell lines, RBCs, WBCs, and platelets are affected in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).
PNH occurs from acquired mutations in the gene PIGA which affect GPI-linked proteins.
These causative mutations occur in a hematopoietic stem cell. Hence, all of its clonal progeny, i.e., red cells, white cells, and platelets, are deficient in GPI-linked proteins.
Clinical features of PNH include:
Intravascular hemoglobinuria - cola-colored urine
Pancytopenia + hypercellular bone marrow

Thrombosis (if hepatic vein involved  Budd–Chiari syndrome)

questions.stem: A 23-year-old man with pancytopenia is suspected to have PNH. Which of the following findings is inconsistent with this condition?
questions.explanation:
In PNH, the leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score is decreased.
Alkaline phosphatase activity is found predominantly in mature segmented neutrophils. LAP score is obtained by assessing the staining intensity in 100 consecutive neutrophils, with each neutrophil scored on a scale of 1–4. Conditions that result in an increase in leukocytes in all stages of maturity will reflect a corresponding increase in LAP.
Increased LAP | Decreased LAP
Leukemoid reactionPregnanc yPolycythemia veraHodgkin's disease | CMLPNHSickle cell ane mia

questions.stem: Which of the following is most likely the cause of death in a patient with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?
questions.explanation:
Among the following, Budd-Chiari Syndrome is the most likely the cause of death in a patient with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH).
Thrombosis (particularly venous thrombosis) is the leading cause of disease-related death in patients with PNH. 40% of PNH patients suffer from venous thrombosis, which commonly affects the hepatic, portal, or cerebral veins.
The pathophysiology of thrombosis in PNH is not completely understood, but two main mechanisms may be responsible:
Nitric oxide (NO) is absorbed by free hemoglobin (which is released during hemolysis).
Endothelial damage caused by the C5-9 membrane attack complex (due to deficiency of CD59).

questions.stem: Flow cytometric analysis in a patient with pancytopenia shows a deficiency of GPI-linked proteins on blood cells. Which of the following is not a complication of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The deficiency of GPI linked proteins on blood cells is seen in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). Cryoglobulinemia is not a complication of this condition.
Thrombosis is the leading cause of disease-related death in individuals with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH). About 5% to 10% of patients eventually develop acute myeloid
leukemia (AML) or myelodysplastic syndrome.

questions.stem: What is the gold standard for the diagnosis of paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria?
questions.explanation:
The gold standard for the diagnosis of PNH is flow cytometry. It provides a sensitive means for detecting red cells that are deficient in GPI-linked proteins such as CD59.
Investigations in PNH include:
Flow cytometry (gold standard) - deficiency of CD59 and CD55
Ham test (acidified serum lysis) - lysis of RBCs in a mildly acidic pH due to complement fixation
Bone marrow biopsy -
Hypercellularity with erythroid hyperplasia is seen in classical presentations
Patients who develop pancytopenia will have hypocellular bone marrow
Imaging - to evaluate venous thrombosis

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man presents with a history of dark coloured urine in the morning for 2 months. His lab investigations and flow cytometry are given below. What is the curative therapy for this condition?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of PNH (paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria). The curative therapy for this condition is a hematopoietic stem cell transplant.
Pancytopenia is seen in this condition. Flow cytometry shows 2 populations of red cells:
Marked red in the left lower quadrant - deficient in both CD55 and CD59, characteristic of PNH.
Marked black in the right upper quadrant - CD55+ and CD59+ cells from the residual normal hematopoietic cells
Eculizumab is a monoclonal antibody that can be used in PNH. It prevents the conversion of C5 to C5a and reduces hemolysis.
Immunosuppressive drugs are sometimes beneficial for those with evidence of marrow aplasia. Note: FDA has approved the following drugs for treatment of adults with PNH:
Ravulizumab injection, a long-acting C-5 complement inhibitor
Pegcetacoplan, which acts by binding to complement protein C3 and increasing hemoglobin concentration

questions.stem: The peripheral smear of a patient with chronic fatigue is shown below. This marked finding is seen in all of the conditions except  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given peripheral smear shows Howell–Jolly bodies. They are not seen in paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria.
They are small nuclear remnants seen as inclusions in red cells and are characteristic of asplenia. They are seen in the following conditions:
Sickle cell anaemia - due to auto splenectomy
Hereditary spherocytosis
Thalassemia post-splenectomy
The images given below show Howell–Jolly bodies in peripheral blood smear.

questions.stem: Match the types of thalassemia with their most common mutations.
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
The most common types of mutations causing thalassemia are:
The different splicing mutations are:
Mutations that destroy the normal RNA splice junctions - completely prevent the production of normal  -globin mRNA resulting in  0-thalassemia
Mutations that create an ectopic splice site within an intron with normal splice regions - some normal  -globin mRNA is made resulting in  + thalassemia
There are two subtypes of chain terminator mutations:
New stop codon within an exon
Small insertions or deletions that shift the mRNA reading frames
Thalassemia | Most common mut ation
 + thalasse mia | Splicing mutation
 0thalassem ia | Terminator mutati on
 thalassemi a | Gene deletion

questions.stem: Which chromosome is affected in alpha-thalassemia?
questions.explanation:
Chromosome 16 contains an identical pair of -globin genes which is affected in alpha-thalassemia. This condition is due to decreased synthesis of alpha chains.
The two  chains are encoded by a single  -globin gene on chromosome 11.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false regarding -thalassemia?
options: Free  and  chains are more soluble than free  chains
 chains are coded by a pair of genes
Hb Barts is the most severe form
questions.explanation:
 chains are coded by 4 genes i.e. two pairs of genes located on chromosome 16.
Free  and  chains are more soluble than free  chains. They also form more stable homotetramers. Hence, hemolysis and dyserythropoiesis in  thalassemia are less severe when compared to  thalassemia.

[[IMG:1]]
In HbH disease, excess  -globin chains form  4 tetramers. They are seen in older children with -thalassemia.
Hydrops fetalis is the most severe form of -thalassemia. It is caused by the deletion of all four
-globin genes. This leads to excess -globin chains forming -globin tetramers (hemoglobin Barts).

questions.stem: A woman with an obstetric score of G3P2A0L0, in a consanguinous marriage, delivered a hydropic stillborn at 32 weeks of gestation. Further evaluation revealed the presence of Hb Barts in the fetal blood. Which of the following globin chains tetramer is found in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Hb Barts is a tetramer of -globin chains (4). This type of hemoglobin is seen in newborns with the most severe form of -thalassemia and results in hemoglobin Barts hydrops fetalis. There is no production of  chains.
Hb Barts has a higher affinity for oxygen. This leads to intrauterine hypoxia, eventually leading to stillbirth.
The image given below shows (a) immature red cell precursors in peripheral smear and (b)
stillborn hydropic infant in Hb Barts hydrops syndrome.
In HbH disease, excess  -globin chains form  4 tetramers. They are seen in older children with -thalassemia.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old Chinese translator presents with fever, jaundice and splenomegaly. His Hb is 6 g% and peripheral smear with brilliant cresyl blue is given below. Which of the following globin chains would you expect to see in this patient?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of extravascular hemolysis (jaundice and splenomegaly) and peripheral smear showing golf ball cells is suggestive of HBH disease. It is a type of  thalassemia where the HbH is composed of tetramers of  chains ( 4).
Hb-H disease is one type of alpha-thalassaemia with inactivation of 3 of the 4 alleles. It is more common in the Asian population. It usually manifests in the 1st year of life. It causes acute episodes of hemolysis when triggered by infections or oxidant drugs.

The decreased  chain production leads to a relative excess of  chains. This leads to the formation of HbH which has a high affinity for oxygen. Such RBCs are more prone to oxidation which causes precipitation of HbH to form golf ball inclusion bodies. This leads to increased sequestration and phagocytosis in the spleen.

questions.stem: A patient has a HbA2 of 3% and HbF of 97%. A peripheral blood smear is taken. Which of the following blood pictures will be seen in this patient?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]]
questions.explanation:
The presence of HbA2 3% and HbF 97% indicates that it is a case of thalassemia major. In thalassemia major, hematological findings in image 1 showing poikilocytes and image 3 showing target cells are seen. Image 2 showing Howell Jolly bodies are seen in post-splenectomy thalassemia patients and not in this case.
Hematological findings in thalassemia major include the following:
Anisopoikilocytosis
Target cells (codocytes)
Nucleated RBC’s
Dacrocytes
Basophilic stippling
Polychromatophilic cells

[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]
[[IMG:6]]

questions.stem: Given below is the hemogram of a patient. Calculate the Mentzer index.
questions.explanation:
From the given hemogram, the Mentzer index is 10.
The formula for Mentzer index is MCV (fL) / TRBC (millions/mm3) i.e. 60/6 = 10
This index is used to differentiate between iron-deficiency anemia and beta-thalassemia trait. If the index is <13, it is most likely to be a thalassemia trait.
Differences between iron deficiency anemia and beta-thalassemia minor (beta-thalassemia trait) are given below.

Feature | Iron-deficiencyanemi a | Beta-thalassemia min or
Peripheral blood sme ar | Microcytic hypochro mic | Microcytic hypochro mic
Retic count | Low | Low
RDW | Wide | Narrow
TRBC | Low | High
Mentzer index | >14 | <12
Serum ferritin | Low | Normal
Serum iron | Low | Normal
TIBC | High | Normal
HbA2 | 2-3%(normal) | >3.5%

questions.stem: The following test was performed with blood sample from a patient with anaemia. What is this test used for?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows NESTROFT i.e. Naked Eye Single Tube Red cell Osmotic Fragility test. It is a very useful screening tool for thalassemia, particularly in poor resource settings.
The principle is based on the decreased osmotic fragility of red cells in thalassemia. It is performed as follows:
Mix EDTA blood and 0.36% buffered saline solution.
Shake the tube and leave it at room temperature for 30 minutes.
Shake the tube again and immediately hold the tube in front of a piece of paper with text or lines.
The image given below shows the NESTROFT.
NESTROFT | Inference | Reason
Lines visible (negative) | Normal | Hemolysis has occurred

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
NESTROFT | Inference | Reason
Lines not seen (positive) | Thalasse mia | Stable RBC, unable to lyse

questions.stem: A couple with a family history of thalassemia comes for genetic counselling. Their HPLC reports are given below. What is the risk of their offspring having thalassemia major?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
In the given clinical scenario, the risk of their offspring having thalassemia major is 0%.
From the given HPLC reports, the husband is normal (normal value of HbA2 is 2.5%±0.3%) and the wife has  thalassemia minor (HbA2 level 4.9%). This disease is transmitted with an autosomal recessive inheritance. Hence, the chance of their offspring having full blown thalassemia is zero.
In  thalassemia minor, the Hb A2 levels are increased to 4–8%. This is due to an elevated ratio of
 chain to  chain synthesis. Hb F levels are generally normal or slightly increased.
Note: Increased HbF (diagnostic) and normal HbA2 levels are features of thalassemia major.

questions.stem: A 25-year old man presents with chronic anemia and gall stones. His family history is significant for a similar illness. His peripheral blood smear is given below. What is the mode of the inheritance of the given clinical condition?
questions.explanation:
The given peripheral smear showing spherocytes, along with the history, is suggestive
of hereditary spherocytosis. Inheritance of this condition is mainly autosomal dominant.
Hereditary spherocytosis is a structural RBC disorder making the RBCs more spheroid. The RBCs are less deformable and more vulnerable to splenic sequestration and destruction. This decreases the lifespan of RBCs.

questions.stem: What is the most common protein deficiency associated with hereditary spherocytosis?
questions.explanation:
Ankyrin is the most common protein deficiency associated with hereditary spherocytosis (HS).
The chief protein component of the RBC membrane skeleton is spectrin. It consists of two polypeptide chains, alpha and beta. These dimers associate with actin oligomers. The spectrin–actin skeleton is then connected to the cell membrane by two distinct interactions.
Ankyrin and band 4.2 binds spectrin to the transmembrane ion transporter, band 3
Protein 4.1 binds the tail of spectrin to the transmembrane protein glycophorin A
Defect in any of the components of the red cell membrane skeleton results in hereditary spherocytosis. The image given below shows the pathogenesis of this condition.
Note: Few one-liners on membrane skeleton -

[[IMG:1]]
Most abundant integral proteins - glycophorin, band 3
Responsible for biconcave shape of RBC - spectrin
Most severe deficiency - spectrin
Hereditary elliptocytosis is due to deficiency of alpha spectrin
Mushroom cells appearance due to deficiency of band 3
Never involved in HS - glycophorin

questions.stem: The peripheral smear of a patient with anaemia, jaundice and splenomegaly shows pincer cells. Which protein deficiency is responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: Pincer cell or mushroom cell is seen in hereditary spherocytosis associated with deficiency of cytoskeletal protein band 3.

questions.stem: Which of the following features would you least expect to see in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Hemoglobinuria is not seen in hereditary spherocytosis where extravascular hemolysis occurs. It is a feature of intravascular hemolysis. Pigment gallstones, pallor and splenomegaly can be seen in this condition.
Cinical features of extravascular hemolysis include:
Anaemia
Jaundice
Splenomegaly
Causes of extravascular hemolysis:
Hereditary spherocytosis
Thalassemia
Sickle cell anaemia
Note: G6PD deficiency and autoimmune hemolytic anaemia can cause both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis.

questions.stem: What is the life span of affected red cells in patients with hereditary spherocytosis?
questions.explanation: The life span of affected red cells in hereditary spherocytosis is 10 to 20 days. The normal life span of RBC is 120 days.

questions.stem: In a patient with hereditary spherocytosis, MCHC of 38 g/dL was noted. What could be the probable reason for this finding?
questions.explanation:
Increased MCHC in hereditary spherocytosis is due to dehydration caused by the loss of K+ and H2O.
MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration) is given by the formula hemoglobin / PCV
(g/dL). It indicates the amount of hemoglobin per unit volume. Note:
MCV (mean corpuscular volume) is given by the formula PCV / RBC (fL). It denotes the size of the RBCs.
MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) is given by the formula hemoglobin / RBC (pg). It quantifies the hemoglobin in the RBCs.

[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: [[IMG:1]] In the following osmotic fragility curve, A occurs in .
questions.explanation:
Osmotic fragility curve shifts to the right in hereditary spherocytosis.
In hereditary spherocytosis, the cells are spherocytic in normal plasma (0.9% NaCl)
and hemolyse readily at higher concentrations than normal discoid red cells do, hence shifting the curve to the right.
Osmotic fragility is the susceptibility of the RBC to rupture under osmotic stress.
In hypotonic solutions, RBCs swell to become spherical and eventually hemolyse. In the graph, the x-axis represents the saline concentration while the y-axis represents the percentage of red cells that have undergone hemolysis. When osmotic fragility is normal, red cells begin to hemolyse at 0.5% saline, with 50% of hemolysis occuring at 0.40-0.42% saline and complete hemolysis occuring at 0.35% saline as represented in the curve.
In thalassemia and sickle cell anemia on the other hand, the cells are resistant to hemolysis and don’t hemolyse unless the concentration of saline is very low, shifting the graph to the left.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl presents with fever and jaundice for 5 days. On examination, splenomegaly is noted. Her lab reports are given below. What is the likely trigger to have caused this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given hemogram showing pancytopenia and spherocytes in peripheral smear is suggestive of aplastic crisis in hereditary spherocytosis. It is usually triggered by parvovirus infection.
Parvovirus infects and kills the red cell precursors. This creates a transient arrest of erythropoiesis
i.e. aplastic crisis as the life span of RBCs are shortened. The immune response clears the virus in 1-2 weeks.
Blood transfusions may be necessary during acute phases of the infection. This crisis can also occur in other hemolytic anaemias.

questions.stem: Which amino acid lies at the sixth position of the beta chain of hemoglobin?
questions.explanation:
Glutamate lies at the 6th position of the beta chain of hemoglobin.
Sickle-cell disease is caused by a point mutation in the sixth codon of  -globin. This leads to the replacement of a glutamate residue with a valine residue.

questions.stem: A blood sample is taken from a suspected case of sickle cell anaemia. Which of the following properties can be used to differentiate HbS from HbA?
questions.explanation:
Solubility can be used to differentiate as HbS is less soluble than HbA. The function, stability and affinity of HbS are similar to that of HbA.
In HbS, glutamic acid, which is a polar amino acid, is replaced by a non-polar amino acid valine at the 6th position. HbS molecules have the tendency to stack into polymers when
deoxygenated. This process converts the red cell cytosol from a free-flowing liquid into a viscous gel. This causes a change in the solubility of the hemoglobin.
The major pathologic manifestations of decreased solubility and polymerisation of HbS are chronic hemolysis, microvascular occlusions, and tissue damage.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man was diagnosed to have heterozygous sickle cell trait. What will be the approximate percentage of HbS in this patient?
questions.explanation:
In heterozygotes with sickle-cell trait, about 40% of the hemoglobin is HbS. The rest of hemoglobin (60%) is HbA.
