questions.stem: Which of the following is not considered as a myeloma-defining event, according to the revised criteria for the diagnosis of multiple myeloma?
options: More than one focal lesionon MRI of 5 mm or more
60% or more clonal plasma cells on bone marrow examination
Serum involved/uninvolved free light-chain ratio of 100 or greater
questions.explanation:
Biopsy-proven plasmacytoma is not considered as a myeloma-defining event (MDE).
Revised International Myeloma Working Group criteria for the diagnosis of multiple myeloma: Clonal bone marrow plasma cells 10% (or) Biopsy-proven bony or extramedullary plasmacytoma.
AND
Myeloma defining events (one or more): Evidence of end-organ damage attributable to the underlying plasma cell proliferative disorder, specifically-
HyperCalcemia: Serum calcium level >1 mg/dL higher than the upper limit of normal or >11 mg/dL
Renal insufficiency: Creatinine clearance <40 mL/min or serum creatinine >2 mg/dL
Anemia: Hemoglobin level of >20 g/L (2gm/dl) below the lowest limit of normal, or Hb <10 g/dL
Bone lesions: One or more osteolytic lesions on skeletal radiography, computed tomography
(CT), or positron emission tomography (PET)/CT.
Any one or more biomarkers of malignancy: Clonal bone marrow plasma cells 60%; Serum involved/uninvolved free light-chain ratio  100; >1 focal lesion on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) that is  5 mm in size.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old lady presents with complaints of pallor, recurrent UTI, and bone pain in lower limbs. Peripheral smear shows rouleaux formation. X-ray done is given below. Which is the best immunohistochemical marker for this condition?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and X-ray showing lytic lesions on the bone are suggestive of multiple myeloma. The best immunohistochemical (IHC) marker for this condition is cyclin D1.
Multiple myeloma is associated with diverse translocations involving the IgH locus; overexpression of D cyclins—cyclin D1 and D3. Plasma cell tumors are positive for CD138 and often express CD56.

questions.stem: A patient diagnosed with multiple myeloma develops features of restrictive cardiomyopathy and macroglossia. Which of the following amyloid is responsible for this?
questions.explanation: The given clinical scenario is suggestive of amyloidosis. The amyloid of the AL type is produced from free Ig light chains secreted by a monoclonal population of plasma cells and its deposition is associated with multiple myeloma.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of death in patients with myeloma?
questions.explanation:
Infections are the most common cause of death in patients with myeloma. Complications of multiple myeloma include:
Infections
Renal failure
Cardiac failure
Hypercalcemia
Anemia

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with complaints of fatigue, pain over the ribs, and confusion. Lab investigations reveal anemia, hypercalcemia, and increased serum creatinine. X-ray shows lytic lesions on the bones. Which of the following is the most powerful prognostic indicator of this condition at the time of diagnosis?
options: Number of myeloma cells in the marrow
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of multiple myeloma. The most powerful prognostic indicator of this condition at the time of diagnosis is serum  2 microglobulin.
Beta-2 microglobulin is a low-molecular-weight protein found on the surface of all nucleated cells. It is the light chain of the HLA histocompatibility complex.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not associated with poor prognosis in a patient with multiple myeloma?
questions.explanation:
t(11;14) is associated with a good prognosis in patients with myeloma.
t(4;14), high serum beta-2 microglobulin, and low serum albumin are all poor prognostic factors in myeloma.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man presents with chronic low back pain. On examination, he has pallor and bony tenderness. A skeletal radiographic survey reveals several punched-out lytic lesions. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an M band in the gamma globulin region. Which of the following is not associated with a poor prognosis in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is highly suggestive of multiple myeloma. Translocations involving cyclin D1 are associated with a good outcome in this condition.
t(14;16), deletions of 17p, and t(14;20) are associated with a more aggressive course.

questions.stem: Which among these is not diagnostic of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance?
questions.explanation:
Bence–Jones proteinuria is not diagnostic of monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) because it is seen in multiple myeloma also.
MGUS is the most common monoclonal gammopathy.
Diagnostic criteria of MGUS according to International Myeloma Working Group guidelines
(2014):
Serum monoclonal protein <3g/dL

Clonal bone marrow plasma cells < 10%
Absence of end-organ damage such as hypercalcemia, renal failure, anemia and bone lesions
(CRAB)
No amyloidosis
The three distinct clinical types of MGUS are:
Non-IgM MGUS:
Most common subtype of MGUS
Approximately 1% of patients with MGUS develop a symptomatic plasma cell neoplasm, usually multiple myeloma, per year
IgM MGUS:
IgM MGUS accounts for approximately 15% of MGUS cases
It can progress to Waldenström macroglobulinemia, but progression to multiple myeloma is rare
Bence–Jones proteinuria has been reported in approximately 20% of these cases
Light chain MGUS (LC-MGUS):
LC-MGUS is a unique subtype of MGUS in which there is no immunoglobulin heavy-chain component
Urinary M protein <500 mg/24 hour
LC-MGUS may progress to light-chain smoldering multiple myeloma (idiopathic Bence–Jones proteinuria) and to light-chain multiple myeloma

questions.stem: A patient with complaints of blurred vision, bleeding gums, and tingling sensation over the extremities is diagnosed with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Which of the following immunoglobulins is this condition associated with?
questions.explanation:
High levels of IgM are seen in lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma.
In lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, high levels of IgM lead to symptoms related to hyperviscosity of the blood. This is known as Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinemia. ‘M’ or monoclonal spike is seen in this condition. Here, it is caused by IgM; in multiple myeloma, it is caused by IgG. It is characterized by the absence of lytic lesions and normal serum calcium levels.
IgM greatly increases the viscosity of the blood, giving rise to a hyperviscosity syndrome characterized by the following:
Visual impairment
Neurologic problems
Bleeding
Cryoglobulinemia
The normal relative viscosity of the serum is 1.8. Hyperviscosity is seen in:
Multiple myeloma

Waldenstrom’s macroglobulinemia
Cryoglobulinemia
Myeloproliferative disorders

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man is diagnosed with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Which of the following genes is mutated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
Virtually all cases of lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma are associated with acquired mutations in MYD88.
The most common cytogenetic abnormality associated with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma is deletion of 6q.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not seen in patients with Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia?
options: M spike in serum protein electrophoresis
Absence of lytic lesions on imaging
questions.explanation:
Serum calcium levels remain normal in Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a syndrome characterised by the following:
Hyperviscosity syndrome due to high levels of IgM
Most commonly occurs in association with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma
‘M’ or monoclonal spike
Absence of lytic lesions
Normal serum calcium levels
Diffuse marrow infiltration by plasma cells, plasmacytoid lymphocytes, and lymphocytes (all from the same clone)
Cells do not form tumor masses or produce lytic lesions
Lymphocytes commonly contain Dutcher bodies (intranuclear inclusions)
Bence–Jones proteins in 20–30%

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common site for extramedullary plasmacytoma?
questions.explanation:
Extramedullary plasmacytomas are seen in the upper respiratory tract. Most of them are seen in the nasopharynx, oropharynx, sinuses, and larynx.
Plasmacytoma is a tumor of plasma cells of bony or soft tissue. It can occur anywhere in the body without evidence of systemic disease.

questions.stem: What is Seligmann's disease?
questions.explanation:
- heavy chain disease (HCD) is known as Seligmann's disease. There are three heavy chain diseases:

- heavy chain disease - Seligmann's disease
- heavy chain disease - Franklin's disease
- heavy chain disease - Associated with light-chain secretion (Bence–Jones proteinuria) in a few cases

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with a history of bone pain, weakness, and loss of weight for 3 years. On examination, enlarged lymph nodes and organomegaly are noted. Peripheral smear shows 22% plasma cells, which are -chain restricted. Serum IgE level is elevated. X-ray image of the lumbar vertebra shows lytic punched-out lesions. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario points to the diagnosis of plasma cell leukemia. In this case, the peripheral blood smear shows 22% of plasma cells and presents with organomegaly.
Plasma cell leukemia is defined by the observation in blood of more than 20% clonal plasma cells by differential count of the leucocytes or by counting more than 2 × 109 per liter circulating clonal plasma cells. Plasma cell leukemia (PCL) is a rare and aggressive form of leukemia and plasma cell dyscrasia. PCL can be divided into primary PCL (PCL) and secondary PCL (sPCL) following previously diagnosed multiple myeloma (MM); the latter typically occurring at a late and advanced stage of MM.
Patients with plasma cell leukemia are more likely to have extramedullary involvement of liver and spleen, causing organomegaly than in multiple myeloma. (Option A)

chapters.title: Myelodysplastic Syndrome, Myeloproliferative Syndromes and Histiocytosis

questions.stem: A 73-year-old woman presents with chronic fatigue and easy bruising. She has had surgery for ovarian cancer 7 years ago along with chemoradiation. Her lab reports reveal pancytopenia and bone marrow biopsy shows the following finding. What is the most probable diagnosis?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of therapy-related myelodysplastic syndrome (t-MDS).
The bone marrow biopsy stained with Perl's Prussian blue shows ringed sideroblasts. They are erythroblasts with iron-laden mitochondria visible as perinuclear granules as shown in the image below.

[[IMG:2]]
Myelodysplastic syndrome is a group of clonal stem cell disorders characterized by maturation defects, associated with ineffective hematopoiesis.
It is of two types:
Primary MDS - develops slowly, usually after 50 years of age.
Secondary or therapy-related MDS (t-MDS) - develops 2 to 8 years after toxic drug or radiation exposure with poor prognosis
Patients usually present with weakness, infections and hemorrhages due to pancytopenia. Both types of MDS have a high risk of transformation to acute myeloid leukemia (AML). However, most frequent and rapid transformation occurs in therapy-related MDS (t-MDS).

questions.stem: What is the most common cytogenetic change in children with myelodysplastic syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Monosomy 7 is the most common cytogenetic change seen in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) in children.
5q deletion is the most common cytogenetic change seen in MDS in adults.
The del(5q) abnormality is the dominant clone in most cases of MDS. This involves the stem-cell compartment and hence occurs as an early or initiating event in disease pathogenesis.

questions.stem: Which of these histopathological findings would you not expect to see in patients with myelodysplastic syndrome?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
Pseudo–Pelger–Huet cells are seen in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) and not Pelger–Huet cells.

[[IMG:2]]
Pelger–Huet cells are seen in Pelger–Huet syndrome, which is due to mutations in the lamin B-receptor gene. It is a neutrophil differentiation disorder with leukocyte appearance as:
Dumbbell-shaped bilobed nuclei
Reduced number of nuclear segments
Coarse clumping of the nuclear chromatin
In MDS, pseudo-Pelger Huet cells are seen due to abnormal nuclear budding i.e. neutrophils with only 2 nuclear lobes.

questions.stem: Which of the following bone marrow and peripheral blood findings is not seen in patients with myelodysplastic syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Image 3 showing hypocellular bone marrow is not seen in myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS.) In this condition, bone marrow is hypercellular. However, pancytopenia results from ineffective hematopoiesis.
The image given below shows the histopathological findings seen in MDS.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with complaints of fatigue, weight loss, and heaviness in the left hypochondrium for 6 months. His hemogram and peripheral smear are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML).
In this condition, the peripheral smear contains neutrophils and their precursors of various sizes and configurations like band cells, myelocytes, metamyelocytes, and blasts. Hence, the histological picture is described to have garden party or college girl appearance.
The image given below shows the peripheral smear in CML showing garden party or college girl appearance.
CML is a myeloproliferative disorder with peak incidence in the 5th to 6th decades of life. It occurs due to the chimeric BCR-ABL gene.

[[IMG:2]]
Clinical features of CML:
Hypermetabolism
Fatigability
Weakness
Weight loss and anorexia
Extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis causing -
Splenomegaly
Mild hepatomegaly
Lymphadenopathy Hematological findings include:
Mild-to-moderate anemia
Leukocytosis
Platelets - usually increased
DLC shows predominantly neutrophils, band forms, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, eosinophils, and basophils and blasts (>10%)
Note: Convent girl appearance is seen in CLL.

questions.stem: What mutation results in Philadelphia chromosome?
questions.explanation:
Philadelphia chromosome results from t(9;22)(q34;q11). It is most commonly seen in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).

[[IMG:1]]
CML is due to the formation of a chimeric BCR-ABL gene or Philadelphia chromosome. This gene is derived from a reciprocal translocation (9;22)(q34;q11).
The image given below shows the formation of the Philadelphia chromosome.
This translocation can be identified on fluorescence in situ hybridisation (FISH).
The image given below shows (9;22) translocation as seen on FISH.

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
[[IMG:4]]

questions.stem: Bone marrow biopsy in a patient shows pseudo-Gaucher cells. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Psuedo-Gaucher cells are characteristic of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML). These cells are scattered macrophages with abundant wrinkled, green-blue cytoplasm. Their presence indicates a good prognosis.
Bone marrow findings in CML:
Markedly hypercellular marrow - increased maturing granulocytic precursors
Elevated eosinophils and basophils
Increased megakaryocytes - include small, dysplastic forms
Erythroid progenitors - normal or mildly decreased
Increased reticulin deposition
Overt marrow fibrosis - rare early in the course
Pseudo-Gaucher cells
Sea blue histiocytes
The image given below shows pseudo-Gaucher cells in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with fever and splenomegaly was diagnosed to have chronic myeloid leukemia. She was started on imatinib therapy. After a few months of therapy, she had persistent progressive splenomegaly and fatigue. Which of the following will not be seen in this phase?
questions.explanation:
In a patient with chronic myeloid leukemia (CML), progressive splenomegaly, not responsive to therapy is suggestive of an accelerated phase. In this phase, blasts are <20% in blood or marrow.
Diagnosis of an accelerated phase of CML requires one of the following criteria:
Persistent or increasing WBC (>10 × 109/L), unresponsive to therapy
Persistent or increasing splenomegaly, unresponsive to therapy
Persistent thrombocytosis (>1000 × 109/L), unresponsive to therapy
Persistent thrombocytopenia (<100 × 109/L) unrelated to therapy
20% or more basophils in the peripheral blood
10%-19% blasts in the peripheral blood or bone marrow
Additional clonal chromosomal abnormalities in Ph+ cells at diagnosis that include “major route” abnormalities (second Ph, trisomy 8, isochromosome 17q, trisomy 19), complex karyotype, or abnormalities of 3q26.2
Any new clonal chromosomal abnormality in Ph+ cells that occurs during therapy

questions.stem: What is the percentage of blast cells in the blast phase of CML?
questions.explanation:
In the blast phase of chronic myeloid leukemia, there are >20% blasts in the bone marrow. The 3 phases of CML are:
Chronic phase is the most common presentation. It is characterized by:
Leukocytosis - bimodal distribution with higher proportions of mature segmented neutrophils and myelocytes
Blast cells <10%
Increased basophils and eosinophils
Monocytosis <3%
Accelerated phase occurs in 50% of the patients who present with increasing anemia, thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly. It is characterized by:
Blast count 10-19%
Basophilia >20%

Blast phase in CML occurs in an average of 3 years after the diagnosis. It is characterized by:
Large foci or clusters of blasts on the bone marrow biopsy >20%.
Presence of extramedullary blastic infiltrates (e.g., myeloid sarcoma or chloroma)

questions.stem: Which of the following is not seen in a patient with Myelodysplastic/Myeloproliferative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia?
questions.explanation:
Myelodysplastic/Myeloproliferative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia (previously named as atypical chronic myeloid leukemia) shows minimal absolute basophilia, i.e., <2% of total WBCs.
Myelodysplastic/Myeloproliferative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia is a leukemic disorder having features of both myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative features at the time of diagnosis. It is classified under the WHO 5th edition (2022) MDS/MPN category.
Characteristics of myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia:
Peripheral blood leukocytosis with an increased number of mature and immature neutrophils
Prominent dysgranulopoiesis
Philadelphia chromosome-negative
Neutrophil precursors (promyelocytes, myelocytes, metamyelocytes) >10% of WBCs
Minimal absolute basophilia <2% of WBCs
Absolute monocytosis <10% of WBCs
Hypercellular bone marrow
<20% blasts in blood and bone marrow
Thrombocytopenia
Differences between CML and myelodysplastic/myeloproliferative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia:
Feature | CML | Myelodysplastic/Myeloprolife rative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia
BCR-ABL gene | Present | Absent
Feature	CML	Myelodysplastic/Myeloprolife rative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia | Feature	CML	Myelodysplastic/Myeloprolife rative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia | Feature	CML	Myelodysplastic/Myeloprolife rative syndrome (MDS/MPN) with neutrophilia
Basophilia | Present | <2%
Myeloblasts in peripheral blo odMyeloblasts in bone marro w | <2%<5% | <20%<20%
Granulocytic dysplasia | Minimal/ abs ent | Prominent

questions.stem: Which of the following patients will have a decreased leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score?
options: A 65-year-old-man with garden party appearance on peripheral smear
A 50-year-old man with Reed Sternberg cells on LN biopsy
A 35-year-old woman with Hb level of 23 g/dL
A 43-year-old woman with smudge cells on peripheral smear
questions.explanation: Leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) score is decreased in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) i.e. garden party appearance on peripheral smear.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not cause relative polycythemia?
questions.explanation:
High altitude produces absolute polycythemia and not relative polycythemia.
Polycythemia denotes an abnormally high red cell count, usually with a corresponding increase in the hemoglobin level (> 16 ±2 g/dL). It is 2 types:
Relative - hemoconcentration due to decreased plasma volume
Absolute - increase in the total red cell mass Causes of relative polycythemia include:
Dehydration - deprivation of water, prolonged vomiting or diarrhea, excessive use of diuretics
Gaisböck syndrome - stress polycythemia where affected individuals are usually hypertensive, obese, and anxious
Causes of absolute polycythemia include:
Primary - intrinsic abnormality of hematopoietic precursors
Polycythemia vera
Inherited erythropoietin receptor mutations
Secondary - red cell progenitors responding to increased levels of erythropoietin
Compensatory due to cyanotic heart and lung disease, high altitude
Paraneoplastic erythropoietin secreting tumours
Note: In dengue hemorrhagic fever, increased vascular permeability causes plasma leakage and volume loss. Hence, relative polycythemia is seen.

questions.stem: A young boy from high altitude came with fever and weakness and had the following reports - Hemoglobin 17 g%, TLC is 21,000 with neutrophils 25, lymphocytes 30, eosinophils 5, myelocytes and metamyelocytes 40 in peripheral smear. Next step in the investigation should be:
options: Bone Marrow biopsy with reticulin stain
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of polycythemia (Hb>16 g/dL). Hence, erythropoietin levels (EPO) are estimated next, to differentiate between primary or secondary polycythemia.
Based on EPO levels:
Primary polycythemia - normal/ decreased
Secondary polycythemia - increased
Options A and B: JAK 2 mutation and Philadelphia chromosome analysis is only done as a last resort.
Option D: Bone marrow estimation with reticulin is done for myelofibrosis which can be seen in the spent/ late stage of the disease. However, peripheral smear findings are not suggestive of primary myelofibrosis. Leukoerythroblastic reaction with dacrocytes is seen in myelofibrosis.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman who presented with aquagenic pruritis had a Hb level of 20 g/dL. Her lab investigations are given below. Which of the following is not seen in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of polycythemia vera. Hepatic failure is not seen in this condition.
Polycythemia vera is strongly associated with activating point mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2. In this condition, clonal erythrocytosis occurs autonomously i.e. independent of erythropoietin.
Clinical features of polycythemia vera:
Headache
Hypertension
Dizziness
Intense pruritis, aquagenic pruritis
Peptic ulcer
Venous thrombosis - Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic vein thrombosis), bowel infarction, stroke, myocardial infarction
Minor hemorrhages - epistaxis, gum bleeding Laboratory findings in polycythemia vera:
Panmyelosis - increased marrow production of red cells, granulocytes, and platelets
Low erythropoietin
Elevated hematocrit
Hyperuricemia
Complications of polycythemia vera:
Myelofibrosis and extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis - spent /late phase
Acute myeloid leukemia

questions.stem: A 63-year-old woman complains about throbbing pain over both palms. Her examination findings and lab reports are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of essential thrombocythemia (ET). The image showing erythematous hands is suggestive of erythromelalgia.
Essential thrombocythemia (essential thrombocytosis) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm. It is associated with mutations that increase JAK-STAT signaling.
WHO criteria for diagnosis of essential thrombocythemia:
Major criteria -

Platelet count 450 × 109/L
Bone marrow biopsy showing proliferation mainly of the megakaryocyte lineage with increased numbers of enlarged, mature megakaryocytes with hyperlobulated nuclei
Not meeting WHO criteria for BCR-ABL1 chronic myeloid leukemia, PV, PMF, myelodysplastic syndromes, or other myeloid neoplasms
Presence of JAK2, CALR, or MPL mutation
Minor criteria - the presence of a clonal marker or absence of evidence for reactive thrombocytosis
Diagnosis of ET requires meeting all 4 major criteria or the first 3 major criteria and the minor criterion
Option A: Polycythemia vera can also present with erythromelalgia. However, it also presents with increased Hb levels.
Option C: Fibrosis (not reticulin fibrils) is seen in bone marrow biopsy of primary myelofibrosis. Option D: WBC counts are increased in leukemoid reactions.

questions.stem: Patients with which of the following conditions do not have a leukoerythroblastic picture on peripheral smear?
questions.explanation:
Leukoerythroblastic picture is not seen in patients with thalassemia as it is a hemoglobinopathy and does not involve myeloid precursors.
Abnormal presence of immature precursors of blood in the peripheral blood smear is called leukoerythroblastosis. Findings include:
Nucleated red cells
Dacryocytes (or teardrop RBC) - formed due to damage to red cell membrane caused by fibrous tissue in the marrow
Immature cells of granulocytic series
It occurs due to conditions causing marrow replacement like:
Primary myelofibrosis - fibrosis of bone marrow
Myelophthisic anemia - space occupying lesions of bone marrow
Gauchers disease
Spent phase of polycythemia vera
The image given below shows a leukoerythroblastic blood picture with nucleated RBCs, tear-drop cells, and immature myeloid cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not included under MDS/MPN overlap syndromes?
options: MDS/MPN with SF31B mutation and thrombocytosis
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Myelodysplastic syndrome/ myeloproliferative neoplasm (MDS/MPN) overlap syndromes are a group of chronic clonal myeloid malignancies in which there are features of both MDS and MPN at the time of presentation. According to the 5th edition WHO classification (2022), it includes:
Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia
MDS/MPN with neutrophilia (previously atypical chronic myeloid leukemia)
MDS/MPN with SF31B mutation and thrombocytosis
MDS/MPN not otherwise specified

questions.stem: Which of the following is not compatible with a diagnosis of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia?
options: More than 20% blasts in blood or bone marrow
Absent or minimal dysplasia in myeloid lineages
questions.explanation:
More than 20% of blasts in the blood or bone marrow are not compatible with a diagnosis of chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML). In this condition, blasts are less than 20%.
WHO 5th edition diagnostic criteria (2022_for chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML)
include:
Prerequisite criteria:
1. Persistent absolute (0.5 × 109/ L) and relative (10%) peripheral blood monocytosis.
2. Blasts constitute <20% of the cells in the peripheral blood and bone marrow.
3. Not meeting diagnostic criteria of chronic myeloid leukemia or other myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPN).b
4. Not meeting diagnostic criteria of myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with tyrosine kinase fusions.c Supporting criteria:
1. Dysplasia involving 1 myeloid lineage.d
2. Acquired clonal cytogenetic or molecular abnormality.
3. Abnormal partitioning of peripheral blood monocyte subsets.e Pre-requisite criteria must be present in all cases:
If monocytosis is  1 × 109/ L: one or more supporting criteria must be met.

If monocytosis is 0.5 and <1 × 109/ L: supporting criteria 1 and 2 must be met. Subtype criteria:
Myelodysplastic CMML (MD-CMML): WBC < 13 × 109/L
Myeloproliferative CMML (MP-CMML): WBC  13 × 109/L
Blasts and blast equivalents include myeloblasts, monoblasts, and promonocytes.
MPN with monocytosis can mimic CMML. In these instances, a documented history of MPN excludes CMML. The presence of MPN features in the bone marrow and/or a high burden of
MPN-associated mutations (JAK2, CALR, or MPL) tends to support MPN with monocytosis rather than CMML.
Criteria for myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with tyrosine kinase fusions should be specifically excluded in cases with eosinophilia.
Morphologic dysplasia should be present in 10% of cells of a hematopoietic lineage in the bone marrow.
Based on the detection of increased classical monocytes (>94%) in the absence of known active autoimmune diseases and/or systemic inflammatory syndromes.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with Noonan syndrome presents with hepatosplenomegaly and lymphadenopathy. You are suspecting juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia. Which of the following is not seen in this condition?
questions.explanation:
HbF levels are increased in juvenile myelomonocytic leukemia (JMML), not Hb A2.
JMML is a hematopoietic stem cell-derived myeloproliferative neoplasm of early childhood. It is one of the myeloproliferative neoplasms. It is associated with mutations in the RAS pathway.
Neurofibromatosis 1, Noonan syndrome, and trisomy 8 mosaicism can predispose to this condition. Aggressive types include PTPN11 mutation and neurofibromatosis type 1.
WHO diagnostic guidelines of JMML:
*Germline mutation (indicating Noonan syndrome) needs to be excluded.
It is associated with a poor prognosis and only a few patients undergo spontaneous regression.
Category I (Mandatory):Clini cal and hematologic features | Category II:Genetic (only 1 re quired) | Category III: Category I + the se findings:
SplenomegalyPeripheral bloo d monocyte count 1 × 109/L Blast percentage in periphera l blood and bone marrow <2 0%No Philadelphia chromos ome (BCR/ABL1 rearrangeme nt)Exclusion of KMT2A muta tion | Somatic mutation inPTPN11 * orKRAS* orNRAS*Clinical d iagnosis of Neurofibromatosi s type 1 or NF1 mutationGer mline CBL mutation | Hemoglobin F increased for ageMyeloid or erythroid prec ursors on the peripheral bloo d smearHypersensitivity to G M-CSF by colony assay and S TAT5 hyperphosphorylationT hrombocytopenia with hyper cellular bone marrow

questions.stem: JAK2 mutation is most commonly associated with
questions.explanation:
Polycythemia vera is strongly associated with activating point mutations in the tyrosine kinase JAK2.
A mutation in JAK2, a key member of the cytokine intracellular signaling pathway, can be found in 90–95% of patients with polycythemia vera.
It is characterized by :
Increased marrow production of red cells, granulocytes, and platelets (panmyelosis)
Low erythropoietin levels and elevated hematocrit
Blood viscosity and sludging lead to both thrombosis and bleeding.
Headache, dizziness, hypertension, dizziness, venous thrombosis (Budd Chiari syndrome due to hepatic vein thrombosis), bowel infarction, and stroke.
Intense pruritus especially aquagenic pruritus
Peptic ulceration, hyperuricemia
15% to 20% of patients after an average period of 10 years ->Myelofibrosis and extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis,
PCV transforms into AML in 2% of patients. Primary myelofibrosis
Marrow fibrosis associated with extramedullary hemopoiesis in the spleen.
Activating mutation in JAK2 (more commonly) or MPL.
Presence of neoplastic megakaryocytes, which are responsible for the release of fibrogenic factors like PDGF (platelet-derived growth factor) and TGF- .
Bone marrow aspiration yields dry tap due to fibrosis of the bone marrow.
So, bone marrow biopsy is the investigation of choice, which shows the presence of hypocellularity with increased deposition of reticulin inside the marrow, abnormal megakaryocytes and the characteristic finding of dilated marrow sinusoids.
Blood shows mild leukocytosis, decreased Hb and hematocrit levels, and elevated LAP scores.
Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) occurs in 5% to 20% of cases.
Essential thrombocytosis (ET) may also be associated with JAK2, MPL, or CALR mutations.
Essential thrombocytosis (ET) is often associated with activating point mutations in JAK2 (50% of cases) or MPL (5% to 10% of cases), a receptor tyrosine kinase that is normally activated by thrombopoietin.
In addition, recent DNA sequencing studies have revealed that most of the remaining cases have mutations in calreticulin (CALR), a protein with several functions in the endoplasmic reticulum and the cytoplasm. Since JAK2 and calreticulin mutations are mutually exclusive, it is hypothesized that the calreticulin mutations also increase JAK-STAT signaling through mechanisms that are currently unknown.
CML is the consequence of the balanced translocation between chromosomes 9 and 22 (t[9;22]).

PV, PMF, and ET are characterized by driver mutations that directly or indirectly constitutively activate JAK2, a tyrosine kinase essential for the function of the erythropoietin andthrombopoietin receptors and also utilized by granulocyte colony stimulating factor receptor.

questions.stem: Which of the following patients is least likely to have leukemoid reaction?
options: A patient with acute myocardial infarction
questions.explanation:
Myocardial infarction does not cause leukemoid reaction.
Leukemoid reaction is defined as persistent leukocytosis above 50000 cells /mm3, where the cause is other than leukemia.
Causes of leukemoid reaction include:
Severe infections
Malignancy
Severe hemorrhage
Acute hemolysis
Trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
Asplenia
Diabetic ketoacidosis

questions.stem: Electron microscopic picture of which of the following conditions is shown below?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given electron microscopy image shows tennis racket shaped Birbeck granules. These granules are characteristic of Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
These granules are pentalaminar tubules with dilated terminal ends. This gives a characteristic tennis racket appearance on electron microscopy. They contain the protein langerin (CD207).
The image given below shows the Birbeck granules as seen on electron microscopy.
On peripheral smear, the proliferating Langerhans cells are characterised by:

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
Abundant vacuolated cytoplasm
Vesicular nuclei containing linear grooves or folds - coffee bean nuclei
The image given below shows Langerhans cells with coffee bean nuclei and moderately abundant pale cytoplasm mixed with a few eosinophils.
Note: Tennis racket cells in light microscopy seen in sarcoma botryoides.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a histiocytic neoplasm?
questions.explanation:
Rosai–Dorfman disease is not a histiocytic neoplasm. It is sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy.
WHO classification of histiocytic/ hematolymphoid neoplasm 2016 includes the following:
Histiocytic sarcoma
Langerhans cell histiocytosis
Langerhans cell sarcoma
Indeterminate dendritic cell tumour
lnterdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma
Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma
Fibroblastic reticular cell tumour

Disseminated juvenile xanthogranuloma
Erdheim–Chester disease

questions.stem: You are suspecting Langerhans cell histiocytosis in a child with an enlarging scalp lesion. Which of the following markers will you test to confirm your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
S-100 is a marker for Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
Tumour cells in this condition typically express the following:
HLA-DR
S-100
CD1a

questions.stem: A 5-year-old girl is brought to you by her father, who states that the girl is drinking a lot of water lately. Physical examination reveals exophthalmos. Further workup shows the presence of multiple lytic bone lesions involving her calvarium and the base of her skull. What is the most likely diagnosis?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Hand–Schüller–Christian disease. Langerhans cell histiocytosis presents as multiple clinicopathological entities:
Hand–Schüller–Christian disease is a multifocal unisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis. It usually affects young children. It is characterized by the triad of:
Diabetes insipidus (excessive thirst) - involvement of the posterior pituitary stalk of the hypothalamus
Exophthalmos
Multiple lytic bone lesions
It usually undergoes spontaneous regression. It is treated with local excision or irradiation.
Letterer–Siwe disease is a multifocal multisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis. It occurs most frequently before 2 years of age, but occasionally affects adults.
It is characterized by the following features:
Cutaneous lesions, resembling a seborrheic eruption - caused by infiltrates of Langerhans cells over the front and back of the trunk and on the scalp
Hepatosplenomegaly
Lymphadenopathy
Pulmonary lesions
Destructive osteolytic bone lesions
Due to marrow infiltration - anemia, thrombocytopenia, predisposition to recurrent infections
(otitis media and mastoiditis)
Treatment involves intensive chemotherapy. This condition is fatal if left untreated.
Eosinophilic granuloma is a unifocal unisystem Langerhans cell histiocytosis. It is characterized by the proliferation of Langerhans cells admixed with variable numbers of eosinophils, lymphocytes, plasma cells, and neutrophils.

These lesions occur in the following sites:
Medullary cavities of bones - most commonly the calvarium, ribs, and femur
Skin
Lungs
Stomach
Bone lesions can manifest as:
Asymptomatic
Pain
Tenderness
Pathologic fractures.
Treatment is by local excision or irradiation.
Pulmonary Langerhans cell histiocytosis is most often seen in adult smokers. It regresses spontaneously upon cessation of smoking.

questions.stem: The X-ray of a 65-year-old man is given below. Clinical examination, and hematological and urinary tests were normal. Which of the following is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given image showing a solitary punched-out lytic lesion without a sclerotic rim
with a beveled edge appearance, along with the age of the patient with history of normal hematological and urinary tests is suggestive of Langerhans cell histiocytosis.
Langerhans cell histiocytosis occurs due to the proliferation of a special type of immature dendritic cells, called Langerhans cells. Their normal function is to present antigens.
It is characterized by single or multiple osteolytic bone lesions. It can also infiltrate the skin (of the scalp), lungs, liver, spleen, bone marrow, or the central nervous system.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true regarding the procedure done using the instrument given in the image below?  [[IMG:1]]
options: Procedure can be done in both lateral & prone position
Diagnosing an infiltrative or granulomatous disease
questions.explanation:
The image shows a bone marrow biopsy needle. Thrombocytopenia is not in itself a contraindication for bone marrow biopsy. However, a platelet count >20,000 is ensured for safety purposes.
Indications of bone marrow biopsy:
Evaluation of unexplained anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia
Evaluation of polycythemia, thrombocytosis, leukocytosis
Diagnosis and staging of lymphoma or solid tumors
Diagnosis and evaluation of plasma cell disorders and leukemias
Evaluation of suspected infiltrative and storage diseases

[[IMG:2]]
Evaluation of fever of unknown origin, suspected mycobacterial, fungal, or parasitic infections, or granulomatous diseases
Contraindications of bone marrow biopsy:
Severe hemophilia
Severe disseminated intravascular coagulopathy
Severe bleeding disorders Procedure for bone marrow biopsy:
Prone or lateral position is chosen for the procedure. Posterior superior iliac spine is identified. After disinfection and local anaesthesia, the patient is asked to inhale slowly through the nose and exhale slowly through the mouth to relieve anxiety .The needle is inserted and rotated on its axis.
On reaching the desired depth, the stylet is removed and needle is advanced. The needle is rotated in the opposite direction to loosen the specimen. It is then withdrawn using the same rotational movement.

questions.stem: Blood examination shows pancytopenia, which can be correct?
questions.explanation:
Megaloblastic anemia (hypocellular phase), hairy cell leukemia, and hypocellular MDS can show pancytopenia. Acute promyelocytic leukemia is not associated with pancytopenia.
Causes of pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow:
Acquired aplastic anemia
Hypocellular myelodysplastic syndrome
Rare aleukemic leukemia
Some acute lymphoid leukemia
Rare lymphomas of bone marrow
Copper deficiency

Causes of pancytopenia with cellular bone marrow:
Myelodysplastic syndromes
Systemic lupus erythematosus
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
Hypersplenism
B12, folate deficiency, Copper deficiency
Myelofibrosis
Aleukemic leukemia
HIV, Brucellosis, Leishmaniasis, Tuberculosis Sepsis
Myelophthisis
Bone marrow lymphoma
Sarcoidosis
Hairy cell leukemia

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions will have the least chances of a dry tap on bone marrow aspiration?
questions.explanation:
Follicular lymphoma is the least likely cause of a dry tap on bone marrow aspiration. Causes of dry tap are:
Metastatic carcinoma infiltration
Chronic myeloid leukemia
Myelofibrosis
Hairy cell leukemia
Acute leukemia
Hodgkin's lymphoma
AML- M7
Causes of pancytopenia with cellular marrow are:
Primary disease of marrow-
Myelodysplastic syndrome
Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH)
Myelofibrosis
Aleukemic leukemia
Myelophthisis
Bone marrow lymphoma

Hairy cell leukemia Secondary to systemic disease-
SLE, sarcoidosis
B12, folate deficiency
Copper deficiency
Hypersplenism
Alcohol
HIV infection, TB
Brucellosis, leishmaniasis
Note: Although marrow is hypercellular in CML, MDS etc., extensive marrow fibrosis (rare) has been proposed to account for a dry tap on bone marrow biopsy.

questions.stem: From which period of embryogenesis does the liver become the chief site of hematopoiesis?
questions.explanation:
From the 3rd month of embryogenesis, the liver becomes the chief site of hematopoiesis. Development of hematopoietic tissues:
Yolk sac - blood cell progenitors first appear during the 3rd week
Liver - hematopoietic stem cells migrate to the liver during the 3rd month of embryogenesis
Bone marrow - hematopoiesis starts in bone marrow during the 4th month of intrauterine life and becomes the predominant site after birth

questions.stem: Which cells in the bone marrow are referred to as nurse cells?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Nurse cells are specialized macrophages in the bone marrow that assist in the development of red blood cells (RBCs).

questions.stem: Bone marrow biopsy of a normal adult is given below. What is the ratio of structures marked A and B? [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The structures marked A are fat cells and B are hematopoietic elements. The normal ratio of fat cells to hematopoietic elements in a normal adult is 1:1.
In hypoplastic states (like aplastic anemia), the proportion of fat cells is greatly increased
(increased fat to cell ratio).
Conversely, fat cells often disappear in conditions like hematopoietic tumors and in diseases with compensatory hyperplasias (like hemolytic anemias) and neoplastic proliferations such as leukemias (decreased fat-to-cell ratio).

questions.stem: Which of the following is a marker for pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
CD34 is an antigen of pluripotent hematopoietic stem cells and progenitor cells of many lineages.

questions.stem: Which of the following is called leukocyte common antigen?
questions.explanation: CD45 is called leukocyte common antigen because it is found in all leukocytes.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a characteristic feature of Kostmann syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Kostmann syndrome is characterized by neutropenia.
It is a rare congenital condition in which inherited defects in specific genes impair granulocytic differentiation. This results in severe congenital neutropenia.
It presents in young children as recurrent bacterial infections (such as otitis media, cellulitis) and oral ulcers. It is associated with an increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of agranulocytosis?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of agranulocytosis is drug toxicity. Causes of agranulocytosis include:
Inadequate or ineffective granulopoiesis -
Suppression of hematopoietic stem cells - aplastic anemia, infiltrative marrow disorders
Suppression of committed granulocytic precursors
Ineffective hematopoiesis - megaloblastic anemia, myelodysplastic syndromes
Congenital conditions - Kostmann syndrome
Increased destruction or sequestration of neutrophils -
Immunological injury to neutrophils - idiopathic, systemic lupus erythematosus, drug exposure
Increased peripheral utilization - bacterial, fungal, or rickettsial infections
Splenomegaly

questions.stem: A patient who was started on chemotherapy 2 weeks ago is found to have a neutrophil count of 2000/mm3. Below what neutrophil count is he at risk of developing serious infections?
questions.explanation: Serious infections are most likely when the neutrophil count falls below 500/mm3.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy is brought with complaints of episodes of severe, violent coughs, followed by a high-pitch intake of breath that sounds like a whoop. These coughing episodes are usually followed by vomiting. He and his family are refugees and his prior vaccination records are not available. Lab investigations of this child will likely reveal which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of whooping cough or pertussis. It is due to Bordetella pertussis infection and results in lymphocytosis.
Causes of lymphocytosis include:
Pertussis
Tuberculosis
Brucellosis
Hepatitis A
Cytomegalovirus
Epstein-Barr virus

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man admitted to ICU develops sepsis 3 days after insertion of a central venous catheter. A peripheral blood smear reveals the following. What does the structure marked by the arrow indicate?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given peripheral smear, prepared from an individual with bacterial sepsis, shows reactive changes in neutrophils. The arrow-marked structure is a Döhle body.

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
Reactive changes in neutrophils associated with leukocytosis in severe inflammatory disorders are:
Toxic granules, which are coarser and darker than the normal neutrophilic granules, represent abnormal azurophilic (primary) granules
Döhle bodies are patches of the dilated endoplasmic reticulum that appear as sky-blue cytoplasmic puddles
Toxic cytoplasmic vacuoles
The image given below shows a neutrophil with cytoplasmic vacuoles.

[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]

questions.stem: Which of the following does not cause follicular hyperplasia of the lymph nodes?
questions.explanation:
B-cell lymphoma results in malignant proliferation within the lymph node, not follicular hyperplasia.
Follicular hyperplasia is a benign condition caused by stimuli that activate humoral immune responses. It may occur in:
Rheumatoid arthritis
Toxoplasmosis
Early stages of HIV infection
It is defined by the presence of large oblong germinal centres (secondary follicles), which are surrounded by a collar of small, resting naive B cells (mantle zone).

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a feature of reactive lymphoid hyperplasia?
options: No variation in shape and size of the follicles
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
In reactive lymphoid hyperplasia, there is marked variation in the shape and size of follicles. Features favoring reactive lymphoid hyperplasia, which are absent in neoplastic follicles are:
Preservation of the lymph node architecture, including the interfollicular T-cell zones and the sinusoids
Marked variation in the shape and size of the follicles
Presence of frequent mitotic figures and phagocytic macrophages
Recognizable light and dark zones

questions.stem: In which of the following organs are tingible body macrophages found?
questions.explanation:
Tingible-body macrophages are found in lymph nodes.
A tingible-body macrophage is a type of macrophage predominantly found in germinal
centers containing many phagocytosed apoptotic cell debris. This debris is referred to as tingible bodies (tingible meaning stainable). The presence of these macrophages suggests non-neoplastic reactive hyperplasia of the lymph node, or can be seen as the stars in the starry sky appearance of Burkitt lymphoma.

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: A 16-year-old boy presented with complaints of fever, sore throat, and enlarged lymph nodes. Paul Bunnell's test was done and found to be positive. What type of lymphoid hyperplasia is seen in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of infectious mononucleosis. Acute viral infections, like infectious mononucleosis, produce paracortical hyperplasia.
There are three types of lymph node hyperplasia. They are:
Follicular hyperplasia
Paracortical hyperplasia
Sinus histiocytosis (reticular hyperplasia)
Paracortical hyperplasia is seen in the T-cell-containing paracortical region of the lymph node. It is caused by stimuli that trigger T-cell–mediated immune responses. The involved regions typically contain:
Immunoblasts
Activated T-cells 3-4 times the size of resting lymphocytes t
Round nuclei
Open chromatin
Several prominent nucleoli
Moderate amounts of pale cytoplasm
Hypertrophy of sinusoidal and vascular endothelial cells, with infiltrating macrophages and eosinophils

[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: In patients with breast cancer with lymph node metastases, which of the following changes is seen in affected lymph nodes?
questions.explanation:
In the case of lymph node metastases, there is prominent reticular hyperplasia.
Reticular hyperplasia or sinus histiocytosis refers to an increase in the number and size of the cells that line lymphatic sinusoids. Although nonspecific, this form of hyperplasia may be particularly prominent in lymph nodes draining cancers such as carcinoma of the breast.
The lining lymphatic endothelial cells are markedly hypertrophied and macrophages are greatly increased in numbers, resulting in the expansion and distension of the sinuses.
The image given below shows reticular hyperplasia in the lymph node.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is false?
options: There is systemic activation of macrophages and CD8+ T cells
The most common trigger is infection with Epstein-Barr virus
It presents as an acute febrile illness with hepatosplenomegaly
Hemophagocytosis seen in bone marrow is sufficient for diagnosis
questions.explanation:
Hemophagocytosis is usually seen on bone marrow examination, but it is neither sufficient nor required to make the diagnosis of hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH).
HLH is a reactive condition also known as macrophage-activation syndrome. The common feature of all forms of HLH is the systemic activation of macrophages and CD8+ T-cells.
The most common trigger for HLH is an infection, particularly with EBV (Epstein-Barr virus). It is characterized by acute febrile illness associated with splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and cytopenias.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a feature in patients with hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis?
questions.explanation:
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is associated with very high serum ferritin levels. Laboratory findings in HLH include:

Anemia
Thrombocytopenia
High serum ferritin
High plasma IL2 receptor levels
Elevated liver enzyme levels
High triglyceride levels
Features of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
