questions.stem: Pulsating hematoma is associated with which of the following conditions?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
Pulsating hematoma is associated with a false aneurysm.
An aneurysm is a localized abnormal dilation of a blood vessel or the heart. There are 2 types:
True aneurysm
Due to weakened and thinned, but intact arterial wall
False aneurysm
Due to a defect in the vascular wall
Results in an extravascular hematoma that communicates with intravascular space
Causes transmission of arterial pulsations to the hematoma (pulsating hematoma)
Dissection occurs when blood enters a defect in the arterial wall and tunnels/dissects between its layers.
The image below shows a pseudo/false aneurysm of the left ventricle.
False aneurysm | Dissection
Defect across all the layers of the vessel wall | Defect is usually an intimal t ear
Hematoma is extravascular ( outside the vessel wall) | Hematoma is within the laye rs of the vessel wall
Hematoma is lined by extrav ascular connective tissue | Hematoma is lined by the lay ers of the vessel wall

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]

questions.stem: A patient presented with a severe headache and transient loss of consciousness. On examination, neck rigidity was present and blood pressure was 160/110 mmHg. A CT brain was done as shown below. Which type of aneurysm could have been involved in causing this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) in a hypertensive patient. It may occur due to the rupture of Berry aneurysms, which are saccular aneurysms.
Aneurysms are classified as:
Saccular aneurysms are spherical outpouchings involving only a portion of the vessel wall.
Fusiform aneurysms are diffuse, circumferential dilations involving long vascular segments.
Both saccular and fusiform aneurysms are true aneurysms because they have an intact vessel wall.
Dissecting aneurysm is produced when a dissection leads to an aneurysm. The image below shows the CT appearance of a SAH.

questions.stem: A patient who is a known case of hypertension was diagnosed with an abdominal aortic aneurysm. What is the likely underlying pathophysiology causing this condition?
questions.explanation:
The likely underlying pathophysiology causing this condition is increased metalloproteinase expression that degrades extracellular matrix and weakens the vessel wall.
The two most important causes of aortic aneurysms are atherosclerosis and hypertension. Aneurysms occuring as a consequence of atherosclerosis occurs most commonly in the abdominal aorta and common iliac arteries.
Option A: Obliterative end-arteritis of vasa-vasorum occurs in late stage syphilis and can contribute to aneurysms

Option D: Medial hypertrophy of vasa-vasorum occurs in hypertension, which is associated most commonly with ascending aortic aneurysms.

questions.stem: Arterial aneurysms due to underlying cystic medial degeneration are seen in patients with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Cystic medial degeneration leading to aneurysms is a feature of Marfan syndrome.
Cystic medial degeneration refers to the degenerative changes in the media of the vessel wall that lead to aneurysm formation. These include:
Loss of smooth muscle cells
Loss of elastic fibers
Inadequate extracellular matrix synthesis
Increased production of glycosaminoglycan It can be caused due to:
Medial ischemia - atherosclerosis, hypertension
Defective connective tissue - Marfan syndrome, scurvy
The image below (Movat stain) shows a cross-section of the aortic media from a patient with Marfan's syndrome showing elastin fragmentation (stained black) and loss of smooth muscle cells (cells stained red and nuclei stained violet).

questions.stem: Which of the following causes aneurysm formation due to defective elastin?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Loeys–Dietz syndrome leads to aneurysm formation due to defective elastin (due to a defect in TGF- signalling pathway).
Aneurysms are caused due to structural or functional defects in the connective tissue of the vascular wall. The following conditions cause intrinsic defects in connective tissue leading to aneurysm formation:
Syndrome | Defect in
Loeys–Dietzsyndrome | Synthesis ofelastinandcollage ns IandIII
Ehlers–Danlossyndrome | Synthesis oftype III collageni n some subtypes
Marfansyndrome | Synthesis of the proteinfibrill incausing weakening of elasti c tissue
Scurvy(vitamin C deficiency) | Collagencross-linking

questions.stem: What is the most common site of syphilitic aneurysms?
questions.explanation:
Syphilitic aneurysms most commonly involves the ascending aorta.
Late-stage syphilis causes obliterative endarteritis of vasa vasorum of the aorta. This leads to ischemic injury of the aortic media resulting in aneurysmal dilation.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old normotensive patient with dyslipidemia is undergoing a regular check-up. He is at an increased risk of developing all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Dyslipidemia is not a direct risk factor for deep vein thrombosis.
Dyslipidemia is a risk factor for atherosclerosis and its complications, including abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA). AAA can also be associated with smaller aneurysms of the iliac
arteries. Patients with AAA are also likely to have atherosclerotic lesions in other vascular beds that may lead to ischemic heart disease or stroke.

questions.stem: Which of the following myocardial infarcts cause aneurysm as a post-MI complication?
questions.explanation:
Anterior transmural infarcts are involved in causing aneurysm as a post-MI complication.
Posterior transmural infarcts are more likely to be complicated by conduction blocks, right ventricular involvement, or both.

questions.stem: A patient was diagnosed with an asymptomatic abdominal aortic aneurysm of a diameter of 3.6cm. On a follow-up visit 1 year later, the diameter was noted to be 3.8cm. What is the risk of rupture of the aneurysm in this patient at present?
questions.explanation:
Abdominal aortic aneurysms (AAA) of size  4 cm with slow growth have no risk of rupture. The risk of rupture for AAA is directly related to the size of the aneurysm:
4 cm - nil
4–5 cm - 1% per year
5–6 cm - 11% per year
>6 cm - 25% per year
Most aneurysms expand at a rate of 0.2 to 0.3 cm/year. The risk of rupture increases when there is a growth of > 0.5 cm/6 months as well as in active smokers.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man presents with sudden onset chest pain radiating to the back between the scapulae. The CT of this patient is given below. What is the major risk factor for developing this condition?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]] [[IMG:4]]
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with the CT finding of a second column of blood after an intimal tear is the classic presentation of an aortic dissection. The major risk factor for aortic dissection is hypertension.
Dissection occurs when blood enters into the media to form a blood-filled channel between the laminar planes of the media. It usually occurs due to a tear in the intima which allows blood in the lumen to flow into the media. It may also occur due to the rupture of vasa vasorum.
It occurs due to:
Hypertension
Connective tissue defects like Marfan syndrome
Iatrogenic trauma during coronary catheterization or cardiopulmonary bypass

questions.stem: A 2D echocardiography of a patient who presented with chest pain showed the following appearance of the aorta on suprasternal parasagittal view. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]]
options: It is a severe type of dissection
questions.explanation:
The above image shows a double-barreled aorta with a superior and inferior lumen. It is a less severe type of dissection because it is less likely to cause hemorrhage.

[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]
A double-barreled aorta is seen there are two intimal tears. Hence, the hematoma enters the media through an intimal tear but re-enters back into the lumen through another intimal tear present distally. As the blood enters the lumen back, this type of dissection does not progress, thus averting hemorrhage.
This creates a false vascular channel in the blood vessel which, over time, can be endothelialized to become chronic dissections.

questions.stem: How would you classify the following according to the DeBakey classification?
questions.explanation:
The above image shows proximal dissection of only the ascending aorta. This is classified as type II as per DeBakey's classification.
Classification of aortic dissection:
Stanford Type A - proximal lesions. These are more common and dangerous. It may involve:
Both the ascending and descending aorta - DeBakey type I
Only the ascending aorta - DeBakey type II
Stanford Type B or DeBakey type III - distal lesions not involving the ascending part and usually beginning distal to the subclavian artery

[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: Which of the following is a large vessel vasculitis?
questions.explanation: Giant cell arteritis is a large vessel vasculitis.

questions.stem: All of the following vasculitides involves veins except?
questions.explanation:
Giant cell arteritis does not involve the veins. Vasculitides affecting the veins are as follows:
Leukocytoclastic vasculitis
Behcet disease
Buerger disease (Thrombangiitis obliterans)

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man presents with sudden onset blindness. He gives a history of frequent headaches along the sides of his scalp. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of giant cell arteritis.
Giant cell / temporal arteritis is a chronic inflammatory disorder of large to small-sized arteries that especially affects the temporal arteries. It is seen in people over 50 years of age. It usually presents with facial pain or headache along the course of the superficial temporal artery.
It can also affect:
Ophthalmic arteries- leading to sudden onset diplopia or blindness
Aorta- leading to giant-cell aortitis
Vertebral arteries
A biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis.
Giant cell arteritis needs to be promptly diagnosed and treated with steroids to prevent permanent blindness.

questions.stem: An elderly patient presented with temporal headache and jaw claudication. She was diagnosed to be a case of Giant cell arteritis. Which of the following statements about giant cell arteritis is incorrect?
options: A negative biopsy excludes the diagnosis
The classic lesions are medial granulomas
Fragmentation is seen in internal elastic lamina
questions.explanation:
A negative biopsy cannot exclude the diagnosis of giant cell arteritis. It is because the lesions are focally distributed. A biopsy sample may be taken from the normal part of the artery leading to a false-negative report. An adequate biopsy requires at least a 1-cm segment.
Biopsy findings:
Giant cell arteritis is primarily medial granulomatous inflammation.
These lesions involve the internal elastic lamina leading to elastic lamina fragmentation.
There is intimal thickening that reduces the luminal diameter.
Granulomas with multinucleated giant cells, infiltrate of T cells (CD4+ >CD8+), and macrophages.
Note : According to the 21st edition of Harrison's Medicine, as involvement of the vessel may be segmental, getting a biopsy segment of 3–5 cm together with serial sectioning of biopsy specimens would help to increase a positive yield. And Robbin's 10th edition mentions that an adequate biopsy requires at least a 1-cm segment.
Image: Giant-cell arteritis with intimal thickening and internal elastic lamina fragmentation

questions.stem: A 30-year-old lady presents with weakness of the left upper limb. On examination, the blood pressure recorded on the left upper limb was found to be lower than that of the right upper limb. Her aortic arch angiogram showed narrowing of the arch of the aorta and subclavian artery. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
The given clinical scenario and radiological findings are suggestive of Takayasu arteritis.
Takayasu's arteritis is a granulomatous vasculitis affecting medium and large-sized arteries, in this case, the aortic arch and its branches. Clinical manifestations include vision disturbances and profound weakening of the pulses, especially in the upper extremities.
Histopathology:
Irregular thickening of the vessel wall is seen with associated intimal hyperplasia.
Characteristic granulomatous inflammation, with the presence of giant cells and patchy medial necrosis.
Disease progression is associated with collagenous scarring and chronic inflammatory infiltrates across all layers of the vessel wall.
Other options-
Option A: Giant cell arteritis (GCA), also known as temporal arteritis, is an inflammation of medium and large-sized vessels. It is more common in women and people aged >50 years.
The clinical features include headache associated with scalp pain and jaw claudication, fever, fatigue, malaise, and weight loss. Half of the patients have temporal artery abnormalities such as enlargement, tenderness, nodular swelling, and loss of pulse of the temporal artery, either unilateral or bilateral. Gentle pressure on the scalp may elicit focal or generalized tenderness.
Though the arch of the aorta may also be involved in giant cell arteritis (known as giant cell aortitis), it is seen in people more than 50 years of age. Whereas, Takayasu arteritis is seen more commonly in adolescents and young women.
Option C: Thromboangitis obliterans, also known as Buerger's disease, is an inflammatory occlusive vascular disorder involving medium- and small-sized vessels in the distal extremities. It is most frequently seen in male smokers less than 40 years of age.
Option D: Behcet's disease is a neutrophilic vasculitis affecting small- to medium-sized vessels that classically presents as a clinical triad of recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. There can also be gastrointestinal and pulmonary manifestations, with disease mortality related to severe neurologic involvement or rupture of vascular aneurysms.

questions.stem: A young girl with bilaterally unequal pulses is diagnosed with Takayasu Arteritis. Which of the following is the most commonly involved site in Takayasu arteritis?
questions.explanation:
The most commonly involved blood vessel in Takayasu arteritis is sublclavian artery.
Takayasu arteritis is an inflammatory and stenotic disease of medium and large-sized arteries characterized by a strong predilection for the aortic arch and its branches. It is also known

as aortic arch syndrome.
The order of arteries affected in Takayasu arteritis is subclavian artery > common carotid artery > abdominal aorta > renal artery > aortic arch = vertebral > coeliac axis > iliac > pulmonary > coronary artery.
Takayasu arteritis causes irregular thickening of the vessel wall with intimal hyperplasia leading to narrowing of the lumen and organ ischemia.
It may have various clinical presentations depending on the vessel involved:
Arch of aorta and its branches:
Subclavian artery- leads to weak pulses in the upper extremities. Hence it is also known as pulseless disease
Carotid arteries- leads to weak pulses, blindness, neurological deficits
Distal aorta- leads to claudication of the legs
Pulmonary artery- leads to pulmonary hypertension
Coronary arteries- leads to myocardial infarction
Renal arteries- leads to systemic hypertension

questions.stem: A young male presents to the emergency room with severe abdominal pain. The small bowel is found to have a small infarcted area which is surgically removed. Histopathological examination of the biopsy specimen is given below. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the small bowel infarction?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the histopathological findings are suggestive of polyarteritis nodosa (PAN).
PAN affects small or medium-sized muscular arteries. It typically affects young adults. The patient may present with rapidly accelerating hypertension due to renal artery involvement (most common) or abdominal pain and bloody stools caused by involvement of gastrointestinal vessels.
Option A: Hyperplastic arteriosclerosis is a vascular pathology seen in severe hypertension. Option B: Cystic medial degeneration leads to dissecting aortic aneurysm.
Option C: Mönckeberg’s arteriosclerosis does not cause infarction.

questions.stem: Which of the following is characteristically spared in polyarteritis nodosa?
questions.explanation:
Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) characteristically spares the pulmonary circulation.
PAN is a systemic vasculitis of small or medium-sized muscular arteries. It typically involves the renal (most commonly involved) and visceral vessels. It has no association with ANCA, but about 30% of patients have chronic hepatitis-B.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child was brought to the hospital with complaints of fever, rash and swelling of her hands and feet since past 5 days. There is desquamative skin rash, oedema of hands and feet, erythema of palms and soles, oral erythema, and cervical lymphadenopathy. What is the likely condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Kawasaki disease or mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome.

Kawasaki disease is an acute febrile illness associated with arteritis of medium to large-sized vessels. It is commonly seen in infants and children <4 years of age.
Clinical features include:
Fever
Conjunctival and oral erythema
Blistering, edema of hands and feet
Erythema of palms and soles
Desquamative rash
Cervical lymphadenopathy
The disease is usually self-limiting. In some cases, the disease may involve coronary artery leading to thrombosis and acute myocardial infarction. Intravenous immunoglobulin and aspirin may be given to reduce the risk of coronary artery disease.

questions.stem: Which of the following antibodies is associated with vasculitis seen in patients with Kawasaki disease?
questions.explanation:
Antibodies to endothelial cells are associated with vasculitis in Kawasaki disease.
Option A: Immune complex deposition is characteristic of vasculitis due to systemic immunologic disorders such as SLE.
Option B: ANCA-associated vasculitis is seen in microscopic polyangiitis, Churg–Strauss syndrome, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis.
Option D: Autoreactive T cells are seen in giant cell arteritis.
Reports have been described in children with a multisystem inflammatory condition (MIS-C) linked to COVID-19 infection with some features similar to Kawasaki disease and toxic shock syndrome. Although shock is rarely associated with Kawasaki disease, many children with the inflammatory syndrome related to COVID show signs of shock.

questions.stem: Which of the following is known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Kawasaki disease is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome.
Kawasaki disease is an acute febrile illness occurring in children aged 4 years or younger. It is usually self- limiting. This vasculitis affects large to medium-sized vessels and even small vessels.
It is also known as mucocutaneous lymph node syndrome because it can present with
non-purulent conjunctivitis, oral erythema, edema of the hands and feet, desquamative rash, and cervical lymph node enlargement.
It has a predilection for coronary artery involvement and is the leading cause of acquired heart disease in children. Untreated patients may develop coronary artery ectasia or aneurysms, leading to rupture or thrombosis, myocardial infarction, and sudden death.

Espundia is the muco-cutaneous variant of Leishmaniasis

questions.stem: A 27-yr-old woman, presented to OPD with complaints of joint pain and photosensitivity. On examination, you see a butterfly rash on the face and petechial hemorrhages on the lower limbs. On serology ANA, turns out to be positive. Which of the following is the most likely cause of vasculitis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus. The vasculitis occurring in a patient with systemic lupus erythematosus is due to immune complex deposition.
Vasculitis is the inflammation of the vessel wall. The various mechanisms that cause vasculitis are:
Immune-mediated inflammation- Vasculitis caused by immune-mediated inflammation may occur due to the following factors:
Immune complex deposition: Seen in systemic immunological disorders like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA): Seen in Wegener's granulomatosis, Churg–Strauss disease, etc
Anti endothelial cell antibodies: Implicated in Kawasaki disease
Autoreactive T cells
Infectious pathogens- by direct invasion, generating immune complexes or triggering cross-reactivity.
Physical or chemical injury- from irradiation, trauma, toxins, etc.

questions.stem: A 43 year-old-male patient came to the clinic with complaints of occasional hematuria and recurrent upper respiratory tract infections. Examination revealed tiny petechial hemorrhages over his lower limbs. The patient tests positive for the anti-proteinase-3 antibody. Which of the following is true about this major antibody?
options: It is also known as p-ANCA
It shows perinuclear staining on immunofluorescence
questions.explanation:
Anti-proteinase-3/PR3-ANCA / c-ANCA is triggered by certain infections as proteinase 3 shares similarities with many microbial peptides. This is the major antibody responsible for Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA).
Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA) are a heterogeneous group of autoantibodies directed against the constituents of neutrophils or monocytes. Many patients with vasculitis have circulating antibodies that react with neutrophil cytoplasmic antigens.
The two most important ANCAs related to vasculitis are:
Anti-proteinase-3/PR3-ANCA/c-ANCA - Directed against PR3 which is a neutrophil azurophilic granule constituent.
Anti-myeloperoxidase/MPO-ANCA/p-ANCA - Directed against MPO which is a lysosomal granule constituent involved in oxygen free-radical generation. MPO-ANCAs are induced by several therapeutic agents, particularly propylthiouracil.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a pauci-immune rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis?
questions.explanation: Type III or pauci-immune-type of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) may be a component of systemic vasculitis such as Wegener granulomatosis or microscopic polyangiitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about microscopic polyangiitis is not true?
options: It affects capillaries, small arterioles, and venules
It is also known as leukocytoclastic vasculitis
Lesions of different stages of activity coexist in the same vessel
questions.explanation:
All lesions of microscopic polyangiitis tend to be of the same age in any given patient, unlike polyarteritis nodosa where all stages of activity from early to late may coexist in different vessels or even within the same vessel.
Microscopic polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that affects capillaries, small arterioles, and venules. It is associated with MPO-ANCA. It is also called leukocytoclastic vasculitis because of apoptotic neutrophils.
It may involve the skin, mucous membranes, lungs, brain, heart, gastrointestinal tract, kidneys, and muscle. Therefore, the patient may present with hemoptysis, hematuria, proteinuria, bowel pain or bleeding, muscle pain or weakness, and palpable cutaneous purpura. Necrotizing glomerulonephritis (90% of patients) and pulmonary capillaritis are particularly common.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old boy, who is a known case of asthma, presents with wheezing and rhinitis. Laboratory results show peripheral eosinophilia and antibodies against neutrophil myeloperoxidase. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the lab findings are suggestive of Churg–Strauss syndrome.
Churg-Strauss Syndrome / Allergic granulomatosis and angiitis is a small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis classically associated with:
asthma
allergic rhinitis
asymmetric mono neuritis multiplex
lung infiltrates
peripheral hypereosinophilia
extravascular necrotizing granulomata.
It is a multisystem disease with cutaneous involvement (palpable purpura), gastrointestinal tract bleeding, and renal disease. Eosinophilic infiltrates may also be seen in the myocardium giving rise to cardiomyopathy.
p- ANCA (MPO-ANCA) is positive in about 50% of cases. Histological features are similar to those observed in polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) or microscopic polyangiitis but characteristically accompanied by granulomas and eosinophils.
Eosinophilic vasculitis seen in Churg-Strauss syndrome:

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man presents with hematuria, intermittent hemoptysis and chronic sinusitis. His chest radiograph shows multiple opacities and cavities. Renal biopsy suggests focal necrotizing glomerulonephritis. Which of the following is not seen in this condition?
options: Necrotizing granulomas of the upper respiratory tract
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
The given clinical scenario suggests a diagnosis of Wegener's granulomatosis. It is associated with PR3- ANCA (and not MPO- ANCA) in about 95% of cases.
Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis/Wegener granulomatosis is a necrotizing vasculitis characterized by a triad of necrotizing inflammation:
Necrotizing granulomas of the upper respiratory tract or the lung
Necrotizing or granulomatous vasculitis affecting small to medium-sized vessels, most prominently in the lungs
Focal necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis
Males are affected more often than females. The most common clinical features include persistent pneumonitis with bilateral nodular and cavitary infiltrates, chronic sinusitis, mucosal ulcerations of the nasopharynx, and evidence of renal disease.
Image: Chest radiograph showing pulmonary granulomatosis

questions.stem: A 15-year old boy comes to the clinic complaining about recurrent painful oral ulcers. He also experiences repeated episodes of eye redness and pain which subside with medication. On examination, ulcers are seen on his genitals. Which of the following features would you not expect to see in this patient?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Behçet disease. Nail fold capillary abnormalities are typically seen in systemic sclerosis.
Behcet disease is a neutrophilic vasculitis affecting small- to medium-sized vessels that classically presents as a clinical triad of recurrent oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, and uveitis. Other skin findings include erythema nodosa (red tender nodules on legs) and positive pathergy test (pustular reaction 24-48 hrs after sterile needle puncture or normal saline injection).
There can also be gastrointestinal and pulmonary manifestations, with disease mortality related to severe neurologic involvement or rupture of vascular aneurysms. Dural sinus thrombosis is the most common CNS manifestation in children. Pulmonary aneurysms are the most severe feature of pediatric BD.
It is associated with HLA subtype B51. T helper 17 (Th17) cells play an important contribution in the recruitment of neutrophils, which will later infiltrate into the vessel wall.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with colicky abdominal pain and purpuric skin lesions on the extensor surfaces of the arms and legs. Urine analysis reveals hematuria and mild proteinuria. The most probable diagnosis is:
questions.explanation:
The clinical features and the investigations are suggestive of Henoch-Schonlein purpura.
Henoch-Schönlein purpura is a systemic immune disorder, commonly seen in the age group of 3-8 years. The patient may present with the following clinical features:
Skin lesions- characteristically involve the extensor surfaces of arms and legs, and also the buttocks
Abdominal manifestations- include pain, vomiting, and intestinal bleeding.
Renal manifestations- include gross or microscopic hematuria, nephritic or nephrotic syndrome. Renal manifestations are more severe in the adults
It is strongly associated with atopy in a few patients, and the onset often follows an upper respiratory infection. IgA is deposited in the glomerular mesangium in a distribution similar to that of IgA nephropathy.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures are involved in Buerger's disease?
questions.explanation: Arteries, veins and nerves can be involved in thrombangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease). It is a vasculitis of small and medium-sized arteries and secondarily extends into contiguous veins and nerves. With time, all three structures can be encased in fibrous tissue.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old male smoker presents with intermittent claudication and gangrene of the lower extremities. Biopsy of the blood vessels supplying this area shows acute and chronic inflammation, with luminal thrombosis containing small neutrophilic microabscesses.  Granulomatous inflammation appears to extend into the contiguous veins and nerves. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is thromboangiitis obliterans / Buerger disease.
It is the segmental, thrombosing, acute and chronic inflammation of medium-sized and small arteries. It principally involves the tibial and radial arteries.
It is seen in heavy cigarette smokers, usually before the age of 35 years. HLA-A-9 and HLA-B-5 associated with a high risk of TAO.
The patients present with intermittent claudication, chronic ulcerations of the extremity, and later progress to frank gangrene. The microscopy findings include luminal thrombosis (thrombangiitis), that is, thrombus containing microabscesses that occlude the lumen (obliterans). They contain small microabscesses composed of neutrophils.
Berger disease refers to IgA nephropathy. It is seen within 3-5 days of sore throat. It is associated with purpuric rash in the lower limbs.

questions.stem: Which of the following histologic findings would be most suggestive of Buerger’s disease in a patient?
options: Mononuclear infiltrates with perivascular cuffing of the vasavasorum
questions.explanation:
Luminal thrombosis containing small microabscesses composed of neutrophils is seen in thromboangiitis obliterans or Buerger disease.
Option A: Adventitial mononuclear infiltrates with perivascular cuffing of the vasa vasorum has been described in Takayasu arteritis.
Option B: Fragmented neutrophils undergoing apoptosis infiltrating blood vessels termed leukocytoclastic vasculitis are seen in small vessel vasculitis.
Option D: Fibrinoid necrosis is seen in immune reactions involving blood vessels seen in immunologically mediated vasculitis syndromes.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes angiosarcoma?
questions.explanation:
Angiosarcoma is a malignant neoplasm. It is a vascular tumor arising from the endothelial cells.
Benign vascular tumors are characterized by well-formed vascular channels lined by normal endothelial cells. Whereas, malignant vascular tumors are characterized by poorly formed vessels with cellular atypia.

questions.stem: Which of the following vascular tumors are not derived from endothelial cells?
questions.explanation:
Hemangiopericytoma is not derived from endothelial cells. It is a malignant vascular tumor derived from supporting cells of the blood vessels.
Vascular tumors derived from endothelial cells are:
Hemangioma
Lymphangioma
Angiosarcoma
The endothelial origin of vascular neoplasms can be confirmed using endothelial cell-specific markers such as CD31 or von Willebrand factor.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a true neoplasm?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
Cystic hygroma / cavernous lymphangioma is a true neoplasm. It is a benign vascular tumor arising from endothelial cells.
Options A and B: Nevus flammeus and port wine stain are vascular ectasias which are not true neoplasms. They are congenital or acquired malformations.
Option D: Bacillary angiomatosis is non-neoplastic reactive vascular proliferation in response to opportunistic bacilli.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common form of vascular ectasia?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]]
questions.explanation:
The most common form of vascular ectasia is nevus flammeus.
Vascular ectasias are the conditions involving the dilatation of blood vessels. They can be congenital or acquired malformations or hamartomas. Telangiectasia is the permanent dilation of small blood vessels. They lead to red lesions in the skin or mucous membranes.
Various types of vascular ectasias are as follows:
Nevus flammeus (birthmark): Pink/purple flat lesions on the head or neck. They regress spontaneously.
Image showing nevus flammeus in a newborn:
Port-wine stain: A special form of nevus flammeus. It thickens the skin surface. It grows during childhood and does not fade with time.
Image showing port-wine stain in a child:
Spider telangiectasias: They are pulsatile and blanch with pressure. These commonly occur on the face, neck, or upper chest. They are associated with hyperestrogenic states, such as pregnancy or liver cirrhosis.

[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]
Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (Osler–Weber–Rendu disease) is caused by mutations in genes related to the TGF- signaling pathway. It is characterized by dilated blood vessels with thin walls that bleed easily. There can be bleeding from the mucous membranes of the nose (epistaxis), tongue, mouth, eyes, and the gastrointestinal tract.
The image below shows multiple flat non pulsating telengiectasias in a patient with Osler-Weber-Rendu disease:

[[IMG:6]]
[[IMG:7]]

questions.stem: A young girl presents with recurrent seizures, mental retardation and a skin lesion as shown in the image below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and the facial port-wine stain as seen in the image is characteristic of Sturge-Weber syndrome.
This is characterized by a triad of:
Facial port wine nevus - usually found in the distribution of the ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal nerve
Glaucoma
Ipsilateral leptomeningeal angiomatosis (LAM) - can lead to seizures, mental retardation or hemiplegia and are seen as intracranial tram-track calcifications on CT as given below.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about hemangioma is true?
options: Capillary hemangioma is the most common type of hemangioma
Cavernous hemangioma usually regresses completely by 7 years of age
Juvenile hemangioma is infiltrative and does not regress spontaneously
Pyogenic granuloma is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus
questions.explanation:
The most common type of hemangioma is capillary hemangioma.
Hemangiomas are benign vascular tumors of infancy and childhood. They are of the following types:
Capillary hemangiomas are the most common type. They occur in the skin, subcutaneous tissues, and mucous membranes of the oral cavities and lips.
Cavernous hemangiomas are composed of large, dilated vascular channels. They are more infiltrative and frequently involve deep structures. They do not spontaneously regress.
Juvenile hemangiomas/strawberry type hemangiomas of the newborn are extremely common. They arise in the skin and grow rapidly for a few months, and usually regress completely by the age of 7 years.

[[IMG:1]]
Pyogenic granulomas are capillary hemangiomas that present as rapidly growing red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingival, or oral mucosa. They bleed easily and are often ulcerated. It is not caused by bacterial infection.

questions.stem: A child is brought by her parents to the OPD with complaints of a swelling on the right thigh. Further evaluation led to the diagnosis of capillary hemangioma in this patient. What is the most appropriate next best step?
options: Explain about the risk of malignant transformation of the tumor
Test the child for retrovirus infection
Enquire about history of exposure to polyvinyl chloride
Assure the parents about spontaneous regression of the tumor
questions.explanation:
Capillary hemangiomas are present from birth and initially increase in size, but many eventually regress spontaneously. They are generally benign.
Images show the gross and microscopic pictures of capillary hemangioma:

questions.stem: A patient with bilateral pheochromocytoma is diagnosed with von Hippel-Lindau disease. This condition is associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
von Hippel–Lindau disease is associated with cavernous hemangiomas. These vascular lesions are commonly found in the cerebellum, brain stem, retina, pancreas, and liver.
Cavernous hemangiomas are large, cavernous blood-filled vascular spaces separated by connective tissue stroma. They are infiltrative and involve deep structures. They do not regress spontaneously.
The given image shows the microscopic appearance of cavernous hemangioma:

questions.stem: Which of the following vascular lesions are commonly seen in patients with Turner syndrome?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
The vascular lesions commonly seen in Turner syndrome are cavernous lymphangiomas of the neck.
Cavernous lymphangiomas (cystic hygromas) are massively dilated lymphatic spaces lined by endothelial cells and separated by connective tissue stroma. They are typically found in the neck or axilla of children and rarely in the retroperitoneum. They can be enormous causing gross deformities around the neck.
Image shows cavernous lymphangioma of the neck associated with a girl having Turner syndrome:

questions.stem: A middle aged male patient presents with a swelling on his left thumb as shown in the image below. Which of the following statements about this swelling is false?  [[IMG:1]]
options: It is caused by a bacterial infection
It is a type of capillary hemangioma
questions.explanation:
The given image shows a pyogenic granuloma. It is not caused by bacterial infection. The term pyogenic granuloma is a misnomer as it neither contains pus nor is it a granulomatous lesion.
These are capillary hemangiomas that appear as red pedunculated lesions on the skin, gingival, or oral mucosa. They are most commonly benign. They tend to grow rapidly, bleed easily and are often ulcerated.
Histologic image of pyogenic granuloma:

questions.stem: Granuloma gravidarum is a type of .
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Pregnancy tumor or granuloma gravidarum is a type of pyogenic granuloma that occurs infrequently in gingiva of pregnant women.
These lesions may spontaneously regress, especially after pregnancy, or they may undergo fibrosis. Occasionally, they require surgical excision.

questions.stem: Which of the following vascular tumors arising from arteriovenous structures is involved in thermoregulation?
questions.explanation:
The vascular tumor arising from arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation is glomus tumor.
These tumors arise from modified smooth muscle cells of the glomus bodies which are specialized arteriovenous structures involved in thermoregulation. They are benign but extremely painful due to abundant nerve fibers.
Histopathology shows branching vascular channels separated by stroma containing glomus cells in nests:

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
[[IMG:4]]

questions.stem: What is the most common site of glomus tumors?
questions.explanation: Glomus tumors are most commonly found in the distal portion of the digits, especially under the fingernails.

questions.stem: [[IMG:1]] A 46-year-old HIV-positive female patient presents with fever, weight loss, and cutaneous lesions as shown in the image. Microscopic examination reveals capillary proliferation and neutrophilic infiltration. Which of the following is the causative organism?
questions.explanation:
The clinical vignette and the microscopic findings suggest the diagnosis of bacillary angiomatosis caused by Bartonella henselae.
Bacillary angiomatosis is a vascular proliferation in immunocompromised hosts caused by opportunistic gram-negative bacilli of the Bartonella family like Bartonella henselae
and Bartonella quintana.
These lesions can involve the skin, bone, brain, and other organs. They contain stromal neutrophils, nuclear dust, and causal bacteria. Histology shows capillary proliferation with endothelial cells exhibiting nuclear atypia and mitosis.
Modified silver (Warthin-Starry) stain is used for demonstrating clusters of tangled bacilli. The given image shows histologic appearance of bacillary angiomatosis:

questions.stem: A 50-year-old HIV seropositive male presents with skin lesions over the distal portion of the lower limbs as shown in the image below. Biopsy shows a lesion composed of proliferating spindle cells along with small vessels and spaces containing red cells. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:2]]
The given clinical scenario and the histopathological findings are most suggestive of Kaposi sarcoma.
Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular neoplasm caused by human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) and is highly associated with AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome). Classic Kaposi sarcoma occurs
in older men of Eastern European and Meditteranean descent. It has the following three clinical stages:
Patches- red-purple macules on the distal lower extremities
Plaques- patches progress to large violaceous raised plaques. Lesions spread proximally.
Nodules- Lesions become nodular with more neoplastic features. This stage also progresses to involve nodes and viscera.
Diseases caused by HHV-8 infection primarily in patients with HIV infection include:
Kaposi sarcoma
Multicentric Castleman disease (MCD)
Primary effusion lymphoma (PEL)
The given image shows sheets of proliferating spindle cells:

questions.stem: Which type of Kaposi sarcoma is most commonly seen in patients with HIV infection?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
AIDS-associated or epidemic Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is an AIDS-defining illness, and worldwide, it represents the most common HIV-related malignancy.
Four forms of KS are recognized, based on population demographics and risks:
Type | Classic | Endemic African | Transplant-associated | AIDS- associated epi demic KS
Epidemiolo gy | Older men of eastern European and Meditt eranean descentNot a ssociated with HIV | HIV seronegative indi viduals | Solid organ transplan t recipients | HIV-infected individ uals
Clinical feat ures | Skin plaques and nod ules | Lymph node and visc eral involvement | Cutaneous, mucosal a nd visceral lesions | Lymph nodes involve d

questions.stem: A patient with vague upper abdominal pain is diagnosed with hemangioendothelioma of the liver. What is this classified as?
questions.explanation: Hemangioendothelioma is classified as intermediate-grade neoplasm. It encompasses a spectrum of vascular neoplasms with clinical behavior intermediate between benign well-differentiated hemangiomas and anaplastic angiosarcomas.

questions.stem: An elderly male working in a factory manufacturing PVC pipes is at risk of developing which of the following cancers?
questions.explanation:
Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with carcinogenic exposures to polyvinyl chloride.
Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm that primarily affects older adults. The tumor often involves the skin, soft tissue, breast, and liver. Angiosarcomas are locally invasive and can readily metastasize.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common causative agent for lymphangitis?
questions.explanation:
Group A beta-hemolytic streptococci are the most common agents responsible for lymphangitis.
Lymphangitis represents acute inflammation elicited by the spread of bacterial infections into lymphatics. It is manifested by red, painful subcutaneous streaks (the inflamed lymphatics) and painful enlargement of the draining lymph nodes (lymphadenitis).

Filariasis causes obstructive lymphedema and chronic lymphadenitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes Milroy disease?
questions.explanation:
Milroy disease refers to heredofamilial congenital lymphedema. Causes of lymphedema:
Primary lymphedema:
Simple congenital lymphedema
Heredofamilial congenital lymphedema (Milroy disease) Secondary or obstructive lymphedema:
Malignant tumors obstructing lymphatic channels
Surgical removal of regional groups of lymph nodes, e.g., radical mastectomy
Postirradiation fibrosis
Filariasis
Post-inflammatory thrombosis and scarring

questions.stem: Which of the following layers is not present in the cardiac valve?
questions.explanation:
Adventitia is not a layer of the cardiac valves. It is the outermost layer of a blood vessel. It contains connective tissue, a few cells, macrophages, mast cells, fibroblasts, and the nerves and vessels that supply the vascular wall.
Cardiac valves are lined by endothelium and share a tri-layered architecture:
Fibrosa is a dense collagenous core at the outflow surface. It is connected to the valvular supporting structures.
Spongiosa is a central core of loose connective tissue
Ventricularis or atrialis is a layer rich in elastin on the inflow surface.

questions.stem: You are conducting an autopsy of an elderly patient who was found dead in his home. Which of the following changes in the heart will not be suggestive of normal aging?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, an increase in the size of the left ventricle is not normally seen in the heart of an elderly person. The size of the left ventricular cavity is decreased in the aged heart, particularly in the base-to-apex dimension. This change is exacerbated by systemic hypertension.
Changes in the aging heart:
Chambers:
Increased left atrial cavity size
Decreased left ventricular cavity size
Valves:

Fibrous thickening of valve leaflets
Aortic and mitral valve calcific deposits
Epicardial coronary arteries:
Diminished compliance
Calcific deposits
Atherosclerotic plaques
Myocardium:
Increased subepicardial fat
Brown atrophy
Lipofuscin deposition
Basophilic degeneration
Amyloid deposits
Aorta:
Dilated with a rightward shift
Elastic fragmentation and collagen accumulation
Atherosclerotic plaque

questions.stem: What type of cells are heart failure cells?
questions.explanation:
Heart failure cells are hemosiderin-laden macrophages. They are telltale signs of previous episodes of pulmonary edema.
In cardiac failure, red cells and plasma proteins extravasate into the edema fluid within the alveolar spaces. These are then phagocytosed and digested by macrophages. The iron recovered from haemoglobin is stored in the form of hemosiderin.
The image given below shows heart failure cells within alveolar spaces.

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of left-sided diastolic heart failure?
questions.explanation:
Hypertension is the most common cause of left-sided diastolic heart failure.
Left-sided heart failure can be divided into systolic and diastolic failure. Diastolic failure predominantly occurs in patients older than age 65 years. Here, the left ventricle is abnormally stiff and cannot relax during diastole.
Causes of diastolic heart failure:
Hypertension: most common
Diabetes mellitus
Obesity
Bilateral renal artery stenosis
Systolic failure is due to insufficient ejection fraction, i.e., pump failure. It occurs when the contractile function of the left ventricle is deranged.

questions.stem: Which of the following does not cause isolated right-sided heart failure?
questions.explanation:
Isolated right-sided heart failure is not caused by left-sided heart failure.
Isolated right-sided heart failure is not common and usually occurs in patients with disorders affecting the lungs. Therefore, it is often referred to as cor pulmonale. It is caused by disorders of the lung parenchyma and pulmonary vasculature. It is also caused by conditions causing pulmonary vasoconstriction like obstructive sleep apnea and altitude sickness.

Pulmonary hypertension is the common feature of these disorders, which leads to hypertrophy and dilation of the right side of the heart.
Right-sided heart failure is most commonly caused by left-sided heart failure. This is because an increase in pressure in the pulmonary circulation from left-sided failure burdens the right side of the heart.

questions.stem: A massive pulmonary embolism occurs in a patient with acute cor-pulmonale. What pathological changes do you expect in the heart of this patient?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, the patient has acute cor pulmonale. This causes right ventricular dilation without hypertrophy. On cross-section, the normal crescent shape of the right ventricle is transformed to a dilated ovoid.
In chronic cor pulmonale, the right ventricular wall thickens. The hypertrophied right ventricle may compress the left ventricular chamber. It can also cause regurgitation and fibrous thickening of the tricuspid valve.

questions.stem: The liver specimen obtained after the autopsy of a patient is given below. What could be the likely cause of this finding?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
In the image, the liver specimen shows a nutmeg liver appearance, which occurs in congestive hepatomegaly. This is secondary to passive congestion due to right heart failure.
In right heart failure, there is congestion of hepatic and portal vessels, greatest around the central veins. This leads to increased liver size and weight. The pericentral zones become congested and red-brown. The periportal regions are normal coloured and tan. This leads to a nutmeg liver appearance. With longstanding failure, the central areas can become fibrotic, eventually culminating in cardiac cirrhosis.
Pathological changes are also seen in the spleen and the gastrointestinal tract. Portal venous hypertension also causes the enlargement of the spleen, with platelet sequestration. This is known as congestive splenomegaly. This can also contribute to chronic congestion and oedema of the bowel.

questions.stem: Which hormone reduces the risk of myocardial infarction in women of reproductive age?
questions.explanation:
Estrogen reduces the risk of myocardial infarction in women in the reproductive age group.
Accelerated coronary artery disease is associated with the postmenopausal decline in estrogen production. However, postmenopausal hormonal replacement therapy (HRT) has not been shown to be beneficial.
The most common cause of death in older women is ischemic heart disease. Through middle age, males have a relatively increased risk of myocardial infarction.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man presented to the casualty with severe, sudden-onset chest pain radiating to the left arm. ECG showed ST-segment elevation in precordial leads. The person succumbed after 3 hours. On autopsy, the patient's heart was immersed in triphenyl tetrazolium chloride solution. What colour would be imparted to the heart?
options: Viable myocardium appears brick red and infarct appears pale
Viable myocardium appears red and infarct appears dark blue
Viable myocardium appears unstained and the infarct appears dark red
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Triphenyl tetrazolium chloride solution imparts a brick red colour to the viable non-infarcted myocardium. The infarct appears unstained and pale.
Myocardial infarcts < 12 hours old are usually not apparent on gross examination. However, if the infarct preceded death by 2 to 3 hours, it is possible to identify the area of necrosis. This is done by immersing the tissue slices in triphenyl tetrazolium chloride solution.
The histochemical stain imparts a brick-red colour to intact, noninfarcted myocardium. Here, lactate dehydrogenase, LDH, activity is preserved. LDH leaks out through the damaged membranes of dead cells, so an infarct appears as an unstained pale zone.
The image given below shows an ischemic brain after immersion in triphenyl tetrazolium chloride solution. The pale unstained region is the infarcted zone.

questions.stem: What is the approximate time of onset of microvascular injury in ischemic cardiac myocytes?
questions.explanation: Microvascular injury begins >1 hour after the onset of ischemia.

questions.stem: What is the earliest detectable ultrastructural feature of myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation:
Relaxation of myofibrils is the earliest detectable ultrastructural feature of myocardial infarction.
Myofibril relaxation, mitochondrial swelling and glycogen loss can be detected by electron microscopy within half an hour of myocardial infarction.

questions.stem: You are conducting the autopsy of a patient who passed away following myocardial infarction. What would be the earliest light microscopic change that can be observed in the heart of this patient?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
The earliest light microscopic change that can be observed in the heart of this patient is
the waviness of myocardial fibres. This is seen within ½-4 hours at the border of the infarct.
These changes are a result of the forceful contractions of viable fibres. The contractions cause stretching and buckling of immediately adjacent, noncontractile dead fibres.
Myocyte vacuolization or myocytolysis may also be seen in the infarct margins. It is due to the accumulation of salt and water in the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Such myocytes are viable but poorly contractile.
The image below shows microscopic features of myocardial infarction showing wavy myocardial fibres. There are wavy fibres that are elongated and narrow, as compared with normal fibres. The widened spaces between the dead fibres contain edema fluid and scattered neutrophils.

questions.stem: Following myocardial infarction, coagulative necrosis begins at?
questions.explanation: Early coagulative necrosis begins in myocardial infarction by 4–12 hours. However, it is prominent between 1 to 3 days after myocardial infarction.

questions.stem: The heart of a patient who had suffered a myocardial infarction is subjected to a histopathological examination. The microscopic image is given below. What time following infarction would you observe this?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given image shows neutrophilic infiltration into the myocardium. Early neutrophil infiltration starts by 12–24 hours following the infarction. It can be visualised by examination with a light microscope.
The necrotic myocardium elicits acute inflammation most prominent between 1 and 3 days. During this time, there is a brisk interstitial infiltrate of neutrophils.
The image given below shows neutrophilic infiltration into the myocardium following MI.

questions.stem: A patient was admitted four days back following acute myocardial infarction. What type of cells would you expect to see in the infarcted area in this patient?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
In the given scenario, 4 days after MI, macrophages are seen in the infarcted area.
They phagocytose dead myocytes at the border of the infarct earliest by 72 hours. Removal of the necrotic myocytes is most noticeable by 3 to 7 days.
The image below shows a macrophagic infiltrate in the infarcted area.

questions.stem: Match the following:
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
The correct match is:
Well established granulation - 10 - 14 days
Complete scarring - > 2 months
Myocyte hypereosinophilia - 12 - 24 hours
Grey white scar - 2-8 weeks
Loss of nuclei and striations - 1 - 3 days

questions.stem: A 67-year-old woman is found dead in her home. On autopsy, hemopericardium secondary to ventricular wall rupture is seen. How long before her death did she probably have a myocardial infarction?
questions.explanation:
The given autopsy finding of hemopericardium secondary to ventricular wall rupture occurs most frequently 3-7 days after myocardial infarction (MI). During this time, the lysis of the necrotic myocardium is maximum. Thus most of the infarct has been converted to friable granulation tissue.
The risk factors for free-wall rupture are:
Age > 60 years
Female gender
First MI
Large, transmural and anterior MI
Absence of left ventricular hypertrophy
Preexisting hypertension
It is less frequent in patients with prior MI because associated fibrotic scarring inhibits myocardial tearing.
Complications of MI:
Heart failure -
This is due to ventricular dysfunction caused by the infarct and ventricular remodeling
Usually occurs within a day
Cardiogenic shock -
This is usually seen in severe multivessel coronary artery disease due to extensive involvement of myocardium

Usually occurs within a day
Arrhythmias - most common complication, occurring usually 2 days after infarction
Most common arrhythmia within one hour of MI - ventricular fibrillation
Most common arrhythmia after one hour of MI - supraventricular tachycardia
Myocardial rupture - occurs when there is transmural necrosis of a ventricle. It includes the following -
Left ventricular free wall rupture (most common) - leads to cardiac tamponade
Interventricular septal rupture - leads acute ventricular septal defect (VSD)
Papillary muscle rupture - leads to severe mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation (MR) - this can occur due to -
Transient papillary muscle dysfunction - mid-systolic or late-systolic murmur
Rupture of papillary muscle - pansystolic murmur
Dressler syndrome (post-MI syndrome) -
This is an immune-mediated reaction and presents as pericarditis, pleurisy, and fever
It can occur even 48 hrs after MI but usually occurs 1–6 weeks after MI and often subside after a few days
Ventricular aneurysm
Infarct expansion associated with mural thrombus

questions.stem: What causes tigered myocardium?
questions.explanation: Tigered myocardium appearance occurs as a result of prolonged moderate hypoxia due to fatty change. It is the gross appearance of the heart with bands of yellow myocardium alternating with normal myocardium.

questions.stem: Which of the following causes the maximum damage in reperfusion injury?
questions.explanation:
In reperfusion injury, the maximum damage is caused by free radicals.
Reperfusion is the restoration of blood flow to the ischemic myocardium threatened by infarction. Reperfused infarcts are usually hemorrhagic because the vasculature is injured during ischemia. Once the flow is restored, there is bleeding.
On microscopic examination, the irreversibly injured myocytes exhibit contraction bands that are intensely eosinophilic intracellular stripes. These contraction bands are composed of closely packed sarcomeres.
Reperfusion injury may be mediated by:
Oxidative stress
Calcium overload

Inflammatory cells recruited after tissue reperfusion

questions.stem: What creatine kinase isoenzymes do the heart muscle contain?
questions.explanation:
Heart muscle contains MM and MB isoenzymes of creatine kinase. Creatine kinase (CK) has three isoenzymes:
CK-1 (BB) - brain, nerve tissue, prostate (small amounts), intestine, lung, bladder, kidney, uterus, thyroid
CK-2 (MB) - heart and skeletal muscle
CK-3 (MM) - skeletal and heart muscle
Elevation of the CK-MB isoforms is seen in MI. CK-MB is less
sensitive and less specific, therefore, troponins are preferred for the diagnosis of MI. CK-MB begins to rise within 3-12 hours of the onset of MI. It peaks at about 24 hours and returns to normal within approximately 48-72 hours.

questions.stem: A patient comes to the hospital after 3 hours of the onset of chest pain. ECG reveals ST-segment elevation in the precordial leads. Which of the following enzymes would be elevated in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of acute myocardial infarction (MI). Enzymes elevated after 4 to 8 hours of MI are CK-MB (creatine kinase MB) and troponins.
When cardiac troponin is available, CK-MB should not be used for the initial diagnosis of acute MI. If it is the only assay available, it can be used, but it is far less sensitive and less specific.

questions.stem: A 56-year-old man presented to the emergency department with progressive dyspnoea. His wife reports that he had chest pain 7 days back which had lasted for 2 days. You suspect that the patient's chest pain was due to myocardial infarction. If so, blood levels of which of the following enzymes would be elevated now?
questions.explanation:
In the given scenario, on post-MI day 7, troponin and LDH will be raised. Troponins are highly specific for MI and remain elevated for 7 to 10 days.
Troponins are proteins that regulate calcium-mediated contraction of the cardiac and skeletal muscles. It is the single biomarker preferred for diagnosing MI, late diagnosis of MI, and diagnosis of reinfarction. Troponin I is more important than troponin T.
Cardiac troponin increases rapidly in patients with reinfarction. Sometimes, the cardiac troponin concentration is elevated, but stable or decreasing at the time of suspected reinfarction. Then
the diagnosis of reinfarction requires a 20% or greater increase in the cTn measurement.
Myoglobin is the earliest enzyme to increase after MI. It is a protein that is found in the skeletal and cardiac muscles, which binds oxygen. It is a very sensitive indicator of muscle injury. But it is not specific to cardiac muscle and can be elevated to any form of injury to skeletal muscle.
Myoglobin and SGOT levels come to baseline before day 1.

[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: The blood levels of various cardiac biomarkers are measured in a patient following myocardial infarction. This is represented in the given graph. Which biomarker does the yellow curve depict?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The yellow curve here shows the levels of CK-MB which starts rising around 4 to 8 hrs post-MI, peaks at 24 hours and becomes normal at 48 to 72 hrs.
The post-myocardial infarction blood levels of the different cardiac biomarkers are shown in the image given below.

questions.stem: Loss-of-function mutation in potassium channel gene KCNQ1 results in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Loss of function mutation in K+ channel genes KCNQ1 and KCNH2 produces the long QT syndrome. The gain-of-function mutation produces the short QT syndrome.
Long QT syndrome manifests as arrhythmias associated with excessive prolongation of cardiac repolarization. Stress-induced syncope or sudden cardiac death (SCD), are common presentations.
Short QT syndrome presents with arrhythmias associated with abbreviated repolarization intervals. They also present with palpitations, syncope, and SCD.
Brugada syndrome manifests as ECG abnormalities like ST-segment elevations and right bundle-branch block. This occurs in the absence of structural heart disease. Here, patients classically present with syncope or SCD during rest or sleep or after large meals.
Familial atrial fibrillation is caused by a gain of function mutation in genes coding potassium channels.

questions.stem: What is the most common mechanism behind sudden cardiac death?
questions.explanation:
The mechanism behind sudden cardiac death (SCD) is most often a lethal arrhythmia, e.g., asystole or ventricular fibrillation.

Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of SCD, responsible for 80% to 90% of cases. But, the mechanism of SCD is most often a lethal arrhythmia. Infarction need not occur. Most of the patients who have SCD but are successfully resuscitated do not show any enzymatic or ECG evidence of myocardial necrosis.
Ischemic injury can directly affect the major components of the conduction system. But, most cases of fatal arrhythmia are triggered by electrical irritability of the myocardium.

questions.stem: Patients with which of the following conditions have an increased susceptibility to coronary artery disease?
questions.explanation:
Patients with hyperlipidemia have an increased susceptibility to coronary artery disease (CAD).
Hyperlipidemia is considered the second most common risk factor for CAD worldwide after hypertension. Hypercholesterolemia was implicated in 55% of cases with combined hyperlipidemia in 41% cases.

questions.stem: What is lipoprotein a [Lp (a)] composed of?
questions.explanation:
Lipoprotein a [Lp(a)] contains the apolipoprotein B-100 portion of LDL linked to apolipoprotein A
(apo A). It is an altered form of low-density lipoprotein (LDL).
Increased Lp(a) levels are associated with coronary and cerebrovascular disease risk. It is independent of total cholesterol or LDL levels.

questions.stem: Histology of reperfused myocardium:
questions.explanation:
Reperfused myocardium shows eosinophilic contraction bands on light microscopy. They occur in irreversibly injured myocytes with damaged membranes, when blood supply is restored 12-24 hours after MI.
During ischemia, the intracellular levels of calcium are increased due to impaired calcium cycling and sarcolemmal damage. This leads to augmented and uncontrolled contraction of myofibrils
after reperfusion.
On microscopic examination, the irreversibly injured myocytes exhibit contraction bands that are intensely eosinophilic intracellular stripes. These contraction bands are composed of closely packed sarcomeres.
Reperfused infarcts are usually hemorrhagic because the vasculature is injured during ischemia. This leads to bleeding after the flow is restored.

questions.stem: Most congenital heart diseases arise between what weeks of embryogenesis?
questions.explanation:
Most congenital heart diseases arise from faulty embryogenesis during gestational weeks 3 to 8 when major cardiovascular structures form and begin to function.
The most common congenital heart disease is ventricular septal defect (VSD), whereas the 2nd most common is atrial septal defect (ASD).

questions.stem: What congenital heart defect is associated with Char syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Char syndrome is associated with patent ductus arteriosus (PDA).
The clinical presentation of this syndrome includes PDA with facial dysmorphism and abnormal fifth digits.
The following images show the facial dysmorphism associated with Char syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following cardiac defects is not associated with Down's syndrome?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Coarctation of the aorta is a feature of Turner's syndrome, not Down's syndrome.
Down's syndrome (trisomy 21) is the most common cause of congenital heart disease (CHD).
Cardiac defects in Down's syndrome are due to endocardial cushion defects. Cardiac defects in various chromosomal anomalies are as follows:
Syndrome | Cardiac defects

questions.stem: What is the most common type of atrial septal defect?
questions.explanation:
Secundum atrial septal defect (ASD) is the most common type of ASD.
ASDs are abnormal, fixed openings in the atrial septum caused by incomplete tissue formation that allows communication of blood between the left and right atria.
It results in a left-to-right shunt. Excess blood flow through the ASD and/or the pulmonary valve results in a murmur. They are generally well-tolerated and usually do not become symptomatic before the age of 30 years.
ASDs are classified according to their location:
Secundum ASD (90%) - usually isolated defects, can be of any size, multiple or fenestrated
Primum anomalies (5%) - occur adjacent to the AV valves, often associated with AV valve defects and/or VSD
Sinus venosus defects (5%) - located near SVC entrance and can be associated with anomalous pulmonary venous return to the right atrium

[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a feature of tetralogy of Fallot?
questions.explanation:
Right ventricular hypertrophy (RVH) is a feature of the tetralogy of Fallot (TOF), not left ventricular hypertrophy.
The four cardinal features of tetralogy of Fallot are as follows:
Ventricular septal defect (VSD)
Obstruction of the right ventricular outflow tract (subpulmonary stenosis)
An aorta that overrides the VSD
Right ventricular hypertrophy
It is the most common type of cyanotic congenital heart disease (CHD). The heart is typically enlarged and is classically boot-shaped due to marked right ventricular hypertrophy.

[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child was brought to the OPD for evaluation of cognitive impairment. Parents report that the child is overly-friendly with strangers. On examination, elfin facies and hypotonia are noted. Investigations reveal hypercalcemia. Which of the following cardiac defects is associated with this syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The given features are suggestive of Williams (Williams–Beuren) syndrome. It is associated with supravalvular aortic stenosis.
This condition is due to deletions on chromosome 7 which includes the gene for elastin. These mutations may cause supravalvular stenosis by disrupting elastin–smooth muscle cell interactions during aortic morphogenesis. There is thickening of ascending aortic wall and consequent luminal constriction.
Other features of the syndrome include:
Elfin facies - wide mouth, chubby cheeks, long philtrum, small nose, and delicate chin (as shown in the image)
Cognitive abnormalities
Intellectual disability (usually mild)
Personality changes - over-friendliness to strangers
Hypotonia
Connective tissue abnormalities
Endocrine abnormalities (hypercalcemia, hypercalciuria, hypothyroidism, early puberty)

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common cause of mitral stenosis?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
The most common cause of mitral stenosis is rheumatic heart disease. Mitral stenosis is the most common lesion in rheumatic heart disease.
In rheumatic mitral stenosis, calcification and fibrous bridging across the valvular commissures create fish mouth or buttonhole stenosis. Rheumatic mitral stenosis is associated with loud S1.
The most common causes of various valvular diseases are:
Aortic stenosis (AS) - calcification due to normal aging or congenitally bicuspid aortic valves
Aortic regurgitation (AR) - dilatation of the ascending aorta, often secondary to hypertension and/or aging
Mitral regurgitation (MR) - myxomatous degeneration (mitral valve prolapse)

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man presented with chest pain and exertional dyspnea for the past 2 months. He has no history of cardiac disease. Examination revealed an ejection systolic murmur. Transesophageal echocardiography was done, which revealed an aortic valve with 2 functional cusps and a valve area of 0.8 sq. cm. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?
options: It is due to abnormal fusion of valve commissures
Midline of larger cusp is major site of calcification
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario and echo findings are suggestive of calcific aortic stenosis secondary to bicuspid aortic valve (2 functional cusps). It is due to incomplete separation of valve commissures during development, not abnormal fusion.
In a congenitally bicuspid aortic valve, the 2 functional cusps are usually of unequal size. The larger cusp has a midline raphe that results from incomplete commissural separation during development. The raphe is frequently a major site of calcific deposits.
This condition is associated with mutations in the following areas:
Chromosomes 18q, 5q, and 13q
Chromosome 9q - loss-of-function mutations in NOTCH1 gene Late complications include:
Aortic stenosis or regurgitation
Infective endocarditis

Aortic dilation and/or dissection.
Predisposed to progressive calcification - Approximately 50% of cases of aortic stenosis in adults.
Note: Acquired bicuspid valves result from abnormal fusion of valve commissures because of an acquired deformity (rheumatic valve disease). It produces a conjoined cusp that is generally twice the size of the nonconjoined cusp.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman who came for a routine check-up was incidentally found to have a late systolic murmur with a mid-systolic click. Echocardiography revealed thickening and redundancy of mitral leaflets with bulging into the left atrium. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The clinical features and echocardiography findings are suggestive of mitral valve prolapse (MVP) or Barlow syndrome. It is not associated with degenerative calcified deposits (seen in calcific valvular degeneration, not MVP).
Barlow syndrome is more common in females. It may be an isolated condition or less commonly can be associated with connective tissue disorders like Marfan's syndrome.
In this condition, there is mitral annular dilatation with floppy mitral valve leaflets. They prolapse or balloon back into the left atrium during systole. The following pathological changes are seen:
Interchordal ballooning (hooding) of the mitral leaflets
Thick, rubbery, redundant leaflets
Thickened mural endocardium
The main histologic change is marked thickening of the spongiosa layer with deposition of mucoid called myxomatous degeneration.
Most individuals diagnosed with MVP are asymptomatic. On auscultation, a mid-systolic click, sometimes followed by a mid to late systolic murmur is heard. Chest pain mimicking angina and dyspnea occur rarely.
The complications include:
Infective endocarditis
Mitral insufficiency
Stroke or other systemic infarcts
Arrhythmias
Sudden cardiac death (rarely)

questions.stem: A 48-year-old man presented with dull aching abdominal pain and diarrhea for the past 2 months. On examination, his face and chest appeared flushed. In a 24-hour urine sample, 5HIAA levels were elevated. CT scan of the abdomen revealed a mass in the terminal ileum. Cardiac involvement in this syndrome is characterized by all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of carcinoid syndrome. Mitral stenosis is not a feature of cardiac involvement in this condition.
Carcinoid heart disease refers to the cardiac manifestations caused by the bioactive compounds released by carcinoid tumors. Classically, the endocardium and valves of the right heart are primarily affected.

Findings in carcinoid heart syndrome:
Endocardial plaque-like thickening and fibrosis
Tricuspid insufficiency
Pulmonary stenosis
No valve destruction
Myocardium not involved
The left side of the heart is less commonly affected because the pulmonary vascular bed degrades the mediators. However, left heart carcinoid lesions can occur in the setting of ASD or VSD, or in the case of primary pulmonary carcinoid tumors.

questions.stem: Which is the most commonly involved valve in carcinoid heart disease?
questions.explanation:
Carcinoid heart disease most commonly affects the tricuspid valve.
It usually affects right heart structures. The most common features are tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is admitted with fever and polyarthritis. He had a bout of streptococcal sore throat infection two weeks back. His ESR on admission was 80mm/hr and fever 3€°C. What is the mechanism of tissue injury in this condition?
options: Type II and type III hypersensitivity
Type II and type IV hypersensitivity
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with polyarthritis (1 major) along with fever and ESR elevated (2 minor) is suggestive of acute rheumatic fever. It is an example of type II hypersensitivity.
This condition classically occurs a few weeks after an episode of group A streptococcal pharyngitis or, less commonly, skin infections. The antibodies to streptococcal cell-wall antigen cross-react with myocardial antigen resulting in macrophage activation and inflammation.
Acute rheumatic carditis is a common manifestation of active RF and may progress over time to chronic rheumatic heart disease (RHD), mainly manifesting as valvular abnormalities. Damage to heart tissue may be caused by a combination of antibody and T-cell-mediated reactions.

questions.stem: Which is the least commonly affected heart valve in acute rheumatic fever?
questions.explanation: The least commonly affected valve in acute rheumatic fever is the pulmonary valve. The most commonly affected valve is the mitral valve.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman died due to cardiac failure. On autopsy, on the mitral valve, small warty vegetations were present along the lines of closure. There were also irregular thickenings in the left atrium. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario and the gross findings seen are diagnostic of rheumatic heart disease.
Inflammation of the endocardium and the left-sided valves results in fibrinoid necrosis within the cusps or tendinous cords. Overlying these necrotic foci and along the lines of closure are small (1 to 2 mm) warty vegetations.

[[IMG:1]]
Subendocardial lesions, exacerbated by regurgitant jets, can induce irregular thickenings called MacCallum plaques, usually in the left atrium.

questions.explanation:
