questions.stem: Which of the following is implicated in acute infective endocarditis?
questions.explanation:
Acute infective endocarditis is due to infection by highly virulent organisms like Staphylococcus aureus. It results in rapidly necrotizing and destructive lesions.
Infective endocarditis is classified into acute and subacute forms.
Acute - infection of a previously normal heart valve by a highly virulent organism
Subacute - infection in previously deformed valves by organisms of lower virulence (S.viridans,
S. epidermidis, HACEK)

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with severe rheumatic mitral stenosis underwent prosthetic mitral valve insertion. In the first 2 months following surgery, he is at the highest risk of infection with which of the following organisms?
questions.explanation:
Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase-negative Staphylococci (like S. epidermidis).
The following organisms are implicated in infective endocarditis following prosthetic valve surgery:
Early (< 2 months) - Staphylococcus aureus, Staphylococcus epidermidis
Intermediate (2-12 months) and late (> 12 months):
Streptococci and Staphylococcus aureus - more common
Enterococci and Staphylococcus epidermidis

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man presented with a high-grade fever, chills, and breathlessness for 4 days. He has no other known medical conditions but has a history of IV drug abuse. On examination, the following painful lesions were noted and a regurgitant murmur was heard on auscultation. All of the following are minor criteria for diagnosis of this condition except:  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given features and the image showing painful Osler nodes are suggestive of infective endocarditis. Echo showing a valve-related mass is a major criterion according to Duke’s criteria.
Infective endocarditis (IE) is a microbial infection of the heart valves or the mural endocardium. The aorta, aneurysms, other blood vessels, and prosthetic devices can also become infected. Most infections are bacterial.
Vegetations on heart valves are the classic hallmark of IE. They are friable, bulky, potentially destructive lesions. They contain fibrin, inflammatory cells, bacteria, or other organisms. The mitral valve is most commonly involved.
Complications of infective endocarditis:
Cardiac complications - valvular insufficiency or stenosis, myocardial ring abscess, suppurative pericarditis

Embolic complications - left-sided (brain, spleen, kidney) or right-sided lesion (lung infarct and abscess)
Renal complications - embolic infarcts, focal (more common) or diffuse glomerulonephritis (less common)

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true regarding the modified Duke’s criteria?
options: Single positive blood culture for HACEK group is a major criterion
Single positive blood culture for Coxiella Burnetti is a major criterion
Documentation of four minor criterion allows a clinical diagnosis
questions.explanation: Single positive blood culture for Coxiella burnetti is considered as one of the major criteria to establish the diagnosis of infective endocarditis.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presented with chest pain and breathlessness for 1 month. Examination revealed a regurgitant murmur. Transesophageal echocardiography revealed vegetations on both sides of mitral valve leaflets. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with vegetations on both sides of valve leaflets is suggestive of Libman–Sacks endocarditis. It is a feature of systemic lupus erythematosus.
The vegetations in this condition have the following features:
Small - 1 to 4 mm in diameter
Single or multiple
Sterile, pinkish vegetations
May be located on both sides valve leaflets
Associated with intense valvulitis - characterized by fibrinoid necrosis
Mitral valve is more frequently involved and regurgitation is the usual functional abnormality.

questions.stem: Large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves are seen in which condition?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
Large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves are seen in infective endocarditis.
Infective endocarditis is characterized by the presence of large, friable, irregular vegetations on heart valves. Aortic and mitral valves are the most commonly affected, however, in some cases, the right heart valves may be involved.
Vegetations may be single or multiple and may involve one or more valves. Embolization often occurs and may lead to septic infarcts or mycotic aneurysms at the site of lodgement due to the presence of virulent organisms in the emboli.

questions.stem: Match the following morphology of vegetations with the conditions in which they are found.
questions.explanation:
The rightly matched vegetations with the conditions that they are seen are as follows: 1-C, 2-A, 3-D, 4-B

Rheumatic heart disease often presents with rheumatic fever phase where small, warty 1- 2 mm vegetations, also called veruccae, extend along the lines of closure of the valve leaflets. The cardinal anatomical changes of the mitral valve in chronic RHD are:
Leaflet thickening
Commissural fusion and shortening
Thickening and fusion of the tendinous chords
Infective endocarditis has large, irregular, friable masses on the valve cusps that can extend onto the chordae. These vegetations can be single or multiple and may involve one or more
valves. They are potentially destructive lesions and contain fibrin, inflammatory cells, bacteria or other organisms. They can erode into the underlying myocardium and produce a ring abscess.
They are prone to embolisations, resulting in abscess formation wherever they lodge due to the presence of virulent organisms. Thus, it may lead to sequelae like septic infarcts or mycotic aneurysms.
Subacute infective endocarditis contains less destructive vegetations. They contain granulation tissue at their bases indicative of healing. Fibrosis, calcification and a chronic inflammatory infiltrate can develop over the time.
Nonbacterial thrombotic endocarditis is characterised by one or more small, 1-5 mm, sterile vegetations which are usually attached at the line of closure. They are seen associated with hypercoagulable states like chronic DIC or malignancy. They are loosely attached to the underlying valve and are non-destructive in nature. They do not cause any inflammatory reaction but they can be a source of systemic embolisation.
Libman-Sack's endocarditis has small- or medium-sized, 1- 4 mm, sterile vegetations associated with systemic lupus erythematosus. They may be present on one or both the sides of the leaflets, on the valve surface, chordae or anywhere on the endocardium. These vegetations develop due to immune complex deposition and complement activation. They cause intense valvulitis resulting in fibrinoid necrosis of the valve substance. Persistent injury to the valves can result in scarring and leaflet fusion.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis?
questions.explanation:
Vegetations in non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis (NBTE) are of 1 to 5 mm size.
NBTE is seen in patients with debilitating conditions such as cancer and sepsis or systemic hypercoagulable states. Hence it is also called marantic endocarditis.
There is the deposition of small sterile thrombi loosely attached to the leaflets of cardiac valves. They form single or multiple vegetations along the lines of closure of the leaflets or cusps. They are non-invasive and do not elicit an inflammatory reaction. It can be a source of systemic emboli.

questions.stem: What is the minimum amount of proteinuria required to diagnose a patient with nephrotic syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The minimum amount of proteinuria required to diagnose a patient with nephrotic syndrome is
3.5 g/day.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl is brought with complaints of generalized swelling of the body and frothy urine. Urinary examination revealed grade 3 proteinuria and the presence of hyaline and fatty casts. There were no red blood cells in the urine. Which of the following statements about her condition is true?
options: IgA nephropathy is the likely diagnosis.
It is associated with low C3 levels.
No IgG or C3 deposition is seen on renal biopsy.
Alport syndrome is the likely diagnosis.
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario in this child is strongly suggestive of nephrotic syndrome due to minimal change disease (MCD). It is characterized by the absence of immune deposits on biopsy and histopathological examination.
It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children (peaks between 2–6 years). Biopsy findings of MCD are as follows:
Light microscopy - glomeruli appear normal (hence called 'minimal change')
Immunofluorescence studies - no Ig or complement deposits
Electron microscopy - diffuse effacement of foot processes of visceral epithelial cells
(podocytopathy)

questions.stem: A 10-year-old boy is brought for a follow-up visit. He was diagnosed with nephrotic syndrome 3 months ago and had been started on a course of oral prednisolone. During the current visit, no improvement is noted with regards to facial puffiness and urine analysis reveals grade 3 proteinuria. Mutations in all of the following are associated with this condition except:
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. It can be caused due to mutations in the following components of the glomerular filtration barrier:
Nephrin, podocin - are molecular components of the slit diaphragm complex
Alpha-actinin 4 - is a component of the foot process cytoskeleton

[[IMG:1]]
Megalin is not a component of the glomerular filtration barrier. It is present in proximal convoluted tubular cells. Mutations in megalin may lead to some proteinuria but not nephrotic syndrome because glomerular filtration of proteins is not affected.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man presents with sudden onset flank pain and hematuria. Ultrasound reveals enlargement of both kidneys. He is a known case of membranous nephropathy. What is the likely pathophysiology for his current presentation?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario in a patient suffering from membranous nephropathy, which is a type of nephrotic syndrome, is suggestive of renal vein thrombosis. It is due to the loss of antithrombin III (an endogenous anticoagulant) in urine.
Renal vein thrombosis is most often a consequence of a hypercoagulable state. In adults, it is most commonly seen in patients with membranous nephropathy.

questions.stem: In a patient with nephrotic syndrome, all of the following are decreased except:
questions.explanation:
In nephrotic syndrome, there is an increase in fibrinogen levels.
The following proteins are increased in nephrotic syndrome:
Fibrinogen
Lipoproteins - due to increased synthesis
The following proteins are decreased in nephrotic syndrome as a consequence of selective proteinuria:
Albumin - the largest proportion of protein lost in nephrotic syndrome.
Transferrin
Cholecalciferol-binding protein
Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG)

Ferritin
Coagulation factors
Antithrombin III

questions.stem: A patient with radiologically confirmed reflux nephropathy develops nephrotic-range proteinuria. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nephrotic syndrome due to a secondary cause (reflux nephropathy). Secondary nephrotic syndrome in adults is most likely due to focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS).
FSGS is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults. It is a podocytopathy, with degeneration and focal disruption of visceral epithelial cells and effacement of foot processes. Glomerular hyalinosis and sclerosis are seen due to the entrapment of plasma proteins and increased extracellular matrix deposition.
FSGS is classified as follows:
Primary
Idiopathic FSGS
Secondary
HIV associated
Heroin addiction
Sickle cell disease
Obesity
Hypertensive nephropathy
Renal conditions
Focal glomerulonephritis (e.g. IgA nephropathy)
Renal ablation
Unilateral renal agenesis or renal dysplasia
Reflux nephropathy
Inherited
Mutated proteins of the slit diaphragm - podocin, alpha-actinin 4, TRPC6

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
Electron microscopy of FSGS shows:
Diffuse effacement of the podocyte foot processes
Focal detachment and degeneration of the epithelial cells
Absence of electron-dense deposits

questions.stem: Patients diagnosed with which variant of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis are likely to have the worst prognosis?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]]
questions.explanation:
The collapsing variant of focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) is associated with the worst prognosis.
There are 5 variants of FSGS:
Collapsing variant - poor prognosis
Glomerular tip variant - good prognosis
Cellular variant
Perihilar variant
Not otherwise specified - most common
Given below is a histological image of collapsing glomerulopathy showing the involvement of the entire glomerular tuft and proliferation of visceral epithelial cells.

[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]

questions.stem: Given below is an electron microscopy image showing deposits in the kidney. What could be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
[[IMG:4]]
The given electron microscopy image shows subepithelial deposits in the kidney which is suggestive of membranous nephropathy.
The following electron microscopy image shows subepithelial deposits in the kidney.
Membranous nephropathy is characterized by the diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall. It is due to the accumulation of deposits containing Ig along the subepithelial side of the basement membrane.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presents with complaints of facial puffiness and frothy urine. Given below is his renal biopsy findings. What is the likely diagnosis?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario and the histopathological image showing uniform, diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall are suggestive of membranous nephropathy.

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
Membranous nephropathy is one of the most common causes of nephrotic syndrome in the adults/elderly. It is a chronic immune-complex-mediated disease.
The following image of the glomerulus shows the characteristic spikes. The spikes are formed due to the presence of basement membrane material (have affinity to silver stain) in between the immune complex deposits (lack affinity to silver stain).

[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]

questions.stem: Mesangial deposits are seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Mesangial deposits are seen in the following conditions:
IgA nephropathy (Berger disease)
Henoch–Schonlein purpura
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
Lupus nephritis classes I and II
Resolving postinfectious glomerulonephritis

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man presented with complaints of blood in his urine. Urine analysis was positive for proteins and red cell casts. A renal biopsy was done as shown below. Immunofluorescence microscopy revealed granular deposits of C3 on either side of the glomerular basement membrane but was negative for IgG, C1q, and C4. What is the likely diagnosis?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]] [[IMG:4]] [[IMG:5]] [[IMG:6]]
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario, immunofluorescence findings, and the image showing proliferating mesangial cells and capillary endothelial cells are suggestive of membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis type 2 (MPGN type 2) or dense-deposit disease.

[[IMG:7]]
[[IMG:8]]
The following image shows bright deposits scattered along capillary walls and in the mesangium by immunofluorescence microscopy with antibodies to C3.

[[IMG:9]]
[[IMG:10]]
This condition belongs to a group of disorders called C3 glomerulopathies and primarily affects children and young adults. It is associated with a dysregulation in the alternative complement pathway. It is clinically and morphologically similar to MPGN type 1 but pathogenetically distinct from it.
In this condition, a circulating autoantibody called C3 nephritic factor is present,
which stabilizes the C3 convertase enzyme. The stabilized C3 convertase enhances C3 activation and consumption causing hypocomplementemia. Patients will have consistently decreased serum C3 levels, but normal C1 and C4 levels.
The prognosis is poor, with about half of these patients progressing to end-stage renal disease
(ESRD).

questions.stem: What is the most likely diagnosis based on the given serum electrophoresis image?
questions.explanation: The given electrophoresis shows hypoalbuminemia and increased alpha-2 globulin, which is classically seen in nephrotic syndrome.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of primary nephritic syndrome?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
IgA nephropathy (Berger disease) is the most common cause of primary nephritic syndrome in the world.
Nephritic syndrome is characterized by:
Acute onset of hematuria

[[IMG:2]]
Urinalysis - red cell casts
Diminished glomerular filtration rate (GFR) (oliguria)
Mild to moderate proteinuria
Hypertension
Azotemia

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man is being evaluated for hematuria after UTI. Histopathology showed mesangial widening and endocapillary proliferation. The following finding is seen on immunofluorescence, which was positive for C3 and negative for IgG. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario, histopathology findings of mesangial widening and endocapillary proliferation, as well as immunofluorescence showing mesangial deposits are suggestive of IgA nephropathy (Berger's disease).
It is the most common type of glomerulonephritis worldwide. It is characterized by recurrent hematuria/ nephritic syndrome and the presence of prominent IgA deposits in the mesangium. Patients generally present with gross hematuria after respiratory, gastrointestinal or urinary tract infection.
The systemic variant of IgA nephropathy is called Henoch–Schönlein purpura. It is a disorder of children which presents with similar renal manifestations with characteristic IgA deposits in the mesangium in about one-third of the patients.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old child abruptly develops fever, oliguria, periorbital edema and smoky cola-colored urine 2-weeks after recovery from sore throat. His renal biopsy image is given below. Which of the following statements is false about the given condition?  [[IMG:1]]
options: A rapidly progressive form with oliguria develops in 50% of children
It is a form of proliferative glomerulonephritis
Granular IgG and C3 deposits are seen on immunofluorescence
Dome-shaped subepithelial humps are seen on electron microscopy
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and histopathology image showing hypercellular glomeruli are suggestive of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN). Rapidly progressive disease with oliguria is very rare (< 1% of patients).

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type of diffuse proliferative glomerulonephritis. It is usually preceded by an acute streptococcal sore throat or impetigo around 1-4 weeks prior.
It usually presents with features of nephritic syndrome including:
Hematuria
Red cell casts in the urine
Azotemia, oliguria
Hypertension
Mild to moderate proteinuria
Edema
On microscopy, the following findings are seen:
Light microscopy - enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with influx of leucocytes (endocapillary proliferation)

[[IMG:4]]
Electron microscopy - subepithelial humps
Immunofluorescence - granular IgG and C3 deposits on glomerular basement membrane and mesangium
Majority (> 95%) of affected children eventually recover renal function with conservative therapy.

questions.stem: A pathologist is examining the following renal biopsy specimen. What does it show?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
options: Proliferating parietal and visceral epithelial cells and WBCs in Bowman space
Diffuse thickening of the glomerular capillary wall
Proliferating mesangial cells and increased matrix deposition in the mesangium
Proliferation of capillaries with fibrin deposition
questions.explanation:
The given image shows a crescent-shaped mass of proliferating parietal and visceral epithelial cells and leukocytes within the Bowman capsule. It is a characteristic feature of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) or crescentic glomerulonephritis.
RPGN is a type of nephritic syndrome associated with severe glomerular injury with necrosis and formation of crescents. It is usually immune-mediated and may be associated with
circulating anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCAs), anti-GBM antibodies, and antinuclear antibodies (ANA).
Injury to the glomerular capillary wall leads to the escape of procoagulant factors and cytokines in the Bowman space. This triggers:
Proliferation of glomerular epithelial cells - mostly parietal, but also some visceral cells
Recruitment of leukocytes and fibroblasts
Pathognomonic crescents - due to the circumferential accumulation of these cells and fibrin The crescents progressively compress the capillary tuft. This results in a rapid decline of
glomerular filtration rate (GFR) and, consequently, acute kidney injury (AKI). Thus, the degree of crescent formation correlates with the severity and the prognosis of the disease.

[[IMG:3]]

questions.stem: A patient with recurrent hemoptysis and renal failure underwent renal biopsy. It revealed the presence of crescents in most of the glomeruli. Immunofluorescence finding is shown in the image below. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario, histopathology findings, and immunofluorescence showing linear, dense, and smooth deposits are suggestive of Goodpasture's syndrome.
Goodpasture's syndrome is an anti-GBM (glomerular basement membrane) antibody-mediated disease. The antibodies are directed against the non-collagenous portion of the 3 chain of collagen type IV. As it is present in both the alveoli and GBM, it usually presents with pulmonary hemorrhage and renal failure. It makes up about 1/5 of cases of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.

[[IMG:1]]
Crescents with linear deposits of IgG and C3 in the glomerular basement membrane are seen on histopathology.
Note: Wegener's granulomatosis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis) causes the pauci-immune type of rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. There is an absence of immune complex deposition on immunofluorescence.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old otherwise healthy boy presents with complaints of hematuria. His father has also had similar complaints since childhood. Light microscopy of the renal biopsy specimen showed no abnormalities. Diffuse thinning of the glomerular basement membrane was seen on electron microscopy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with normal findings on light microscopy and diffuse thinning of the glomerular basement membrane on electron microscopy are highly suggestive of benign familial hematuria (thin basement membrane disease).
It is a type of hereditary nephritis manifested clinically by familial asymptomatic hematuria. The following are the differences between Alport's syndrome and benign familial hematuria.
Features | Alport's syndrome | Benign familial hematuria
Inheritance | X-linked (most common)Aut osomal inheritance | Autosomal inheritance
Affected protein | 5 chain of type IV collagen ( Most commonly) | 3 or 4 chains of type IV co llagen.
Hearing Loss | Present | Absent
Ocular abnormalities | Present | Absent
Features	Alport's syndrome	Benign familial hematuria | Features	Alport's syndrome	Benign familial hematuria | Features	Alport's syndrome	Benign familial hematuria
Progress to end-stage renal d isease | Yes | No
Electron microscopy | Irregularthickeningandthinni ngof basement membraneSpl itting and lamination of lami na densa -basket-weaveappea rance | Diffuse thinningof the glomer ular basement membrane
Prognosis | Poor | Good

questions.stem: What is the most common manifestation of Alport's syndrome?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
The most common manifestation of Alport syndrome is gross or microscopic hematuria, frequently accompanied by red cell casts.
Proteinuria and oliguria may develop later in the disease, and rarely, nephrotic syndrome develops. The deafness may be subtle requiring sensitive testing.
There are no significant light microscopy changes in Alport syndrome. On electron microscopy, the glomerular basement membrane shows:
Irregular foci of thickening, alternating with attenuation (thinning)
Pronounced splitting and lamination of the lamina densa - basket-weave appearance

questions.stem: A middle-aged male patient has proteinuria. Looking at the immunofluorescence image below, what is the diagnosis?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]]
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]
The given immunofluorescence staining of the kidney biopsy specimen shows positive staining for fibrinogen, IgG, IgA, IgM, C1q, C3,  chain, and k light chain. This is known as full-house effect. It is seen in lupus nephritis.

questions.stem: Urinary albumin excretion of how much is considered as microalbuminuria?
questions.explanation:
Urinary albumin excretion in the range of 30–300 mg/24 hours is called microalbuminuria. It is the hallmark of early diabetic nephropathy.
The terms microalbuminuria and macroalbuminuria are no longer used now. Proteinuria is currently classified as:
Type of Proteinuria | Total proteinuria (mg/day) | Albuminuria(mg/d ay)
Normal-range | <150Mainly Tamm-Horsfall p rotein (70-75 mg/day) | < 30
Moderately increas ed | 150-500 | 30-300
Severely increased | > 500 | > 300

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man presented with the blurring of vision. Urine examination showed proteinuria. Fundus examination showed dot and blot hemorrhages, microaneurysms, and cotton wool spots. Histopathology of the kidney was as shown below. What is your diagnosis?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]]
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:3]]
The given clinical scenario and histopathology image showing acellular periodic acid Schiff (PAS)-positive nodules are suggestive of Kimmelstiel–Wilson disease. It occurs in patients with diabetic nephropathy.
The following renal lesions are encountered in diabetic nephropathy:

[[IMG:4]]
Glomerular lesions -
Capillary basement membrane thickening
Diffuse mesangial sclerosis
Nodular glomerulosclerosis/ Kimmelstiel–Wilson disease
Intercapillary glomerulosclerosis
Renal vascular lesions - hyaline arteriolosclerosis
Pyelonephritis - necrotizing papillitis
Option A: In amyloidosis, glomerular deposits appear as thickenings of the mesangial matrix, forming interlacing broad ribbons of amyloid.
Option B: In focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, there is focal and segmental hyalinosis and sclerosis of the capillary wall with lipid droplets in the sclerosed area.
Option D: In lupus nephritis, immune complex deposits are seen in the mesangium or along the entire basement membrane (wire loop lesions), with mesangial cell proliferation.

questions.stem: A 51-year-old male patient came with complaints of hematuria to the clinic. On examination, he was normotensive and had pedal edema. Investigations revealed the patient had no glycosuria and had a creatinine of 9. His renal biopsy is shown below. Which of the following investigations should be done to identify the disease?
questions.explanation:
Based on the given clinical history and microscopy showing crescents, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis (RPGN) is suspected. Among the given options, anti- GBM antibody testing should be done, since it is a part of the work-up of RPGN.

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
Type 1 RPGN includes renal limited disease and Goodpasture's disease. In this condition, antibodies are produced against the non-collagenous domain of the 3 chain of collagen IV of the GBM.
Microscopy findings of Goodpasture's disease are:
Immunofluorescence - linear deposits of Ig and complement along the glomerular basement membrane
Electron microscopy - wrinkling of the glomerular basement membrane with focal disruptions without any immune complex deposition.
A variant of Goodpasture's disease with pulmonary involvement is known as Goodpasture's syndrome.
Option A: ANA testing is done if SLE is suspected. Electron microscopy will show immune complex deposits.
Option C: HIV RNA testing is done in immunodeficiency syndrome associated with weight loss. Electron microscopy will show diffuse podocyte injury with complete foot process effacement. Tubuloreticular inclusions will be seen in endothelial cells.
Option D: Urine electrophoresis is done if nephrotic syndrome is suspected.

questions.stem: Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis is seen in:
questions.explanation:
Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) is seen in HIV, SLE, CLL, and Hepatitis B.
MPGN is caused due to immune-mediated injury. It often presents with a nephritic-nephrotic picture.

The causes of MPGN are as follows:
Primary MPGN (Idiopathic)
Secondary MPGN
System lupus erythematosus (SLE)
1-antitrypsin deficiency
Infections - hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, schistosomiasis, endocarditis, infected ventriculoatrial shunts, chronic visceral abscesses
Malignancies - chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)
MPGN is characterized by the proliferation of cells predominantly in the mesangium and the capillary loops. Hence it is also called mesangiocapillary glomerulonephritis. There are 2 types of MPGN:
Type I - It is characterized by the deposition of immune complexes and mesangiocapillary proliferation.
Type II - It is now known as dense-deposit disease. It belongs to a group of disorders called C3 glomerulopathies.
Light microscopy findings of MPGN are as follows:
Lobular glomeruli with proliferating mesangial cells, capillary endothelium, and infiltrating leukocytes (endocapillary proliferation)
Duplication of the basement membrane gives a double contour or tram-track appearance. It is especially evident in silver or PAS stains.

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man was brought to the ER by his friends after they found him lying unconscious next to an empty antifreeze bottle. Investigations were significant for the following findings. This condition predominantly affects which part of the kidney?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of acute tubular necrosis (ATN) due to ingestion of ethylene glycol. Toxins usually result in ATN by causing damage to the proximal convoluted tubules (PCTs).
Ethylene glycol poisoning produces marked ballooning and hydropic or vacuolar degeneration of PCT. Calcium oxalate crystals are often also found in tubular lumens.

Direct toxic injury to the tubules in ATI can be caused by:
Endogenous agents: Myoglobin, hemoglobin, monoclonal light chains, bile/bilirubin
Exogenous agents: Drugs, radiocontrast dyes, heavy metals, and organic solvents

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with urinary frequency, urgency, and burning during urination of two days duration. Presence of which of the following additional findings would make you suspect pyelonephritis in this patient?
questions.explanation:
White blood cell casts are specific features of pyelonephritis. Neutrophil-rich casts (pus casts) indicate renal involvement because casts are formed only in tubules.
The urine contains many leukocytes (pyuria) derived from the inflammatory infiltrate. It is found in both upper and lower UTIs and cannot differentiate between them. Fever is also a non-specific finding.
Ascending infection is the most common cause of clinical pyelonephritis.
Note: Sterile pyuria is defined as white cells in the urine in the absence of significant bacterial growth. It is seen in renal TB.

questions.stem: What is the most common organism causing acute pyelonephritis?
questions.explanation:
The most common organism causing acute pyelonephritis is Escherichia coli. The organisms that cause acute pyelonephritis include:
E. coli
Proteus
Klebsiella
Enterobacter species
Mycobacteria - caseating granulomatous inflammation
Fungi - non-caseating granulomatous inflammation
Viruses (CMV and adenovirus) - immunocompromised people

questions.stem: Periglomerular fibrosis is considered typical of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Periglomerular fibrosis is considered typical of chronic pyelonephritis. Histopathological features of chronic pyelonephritis are:
Dilated tubules with flattened epithelium may be filled with casts resembling thyroid colloid (thyroidization)
Chronic interstitial inflammation and fibrosis in the cortex and medulla
Periglomerular fibrosis

[[IMG:1]]
Secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), usually several years after the scarring has occurred and often in the absence of continued infection or persistent vesicoureteral reflux

questions.stem: A pathologist noted the following microscopic finding while examining a slide of a kidney. What is the likely cause?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given image shows dilated tubules with flattened epithelium, filled with casts, resembling thyroid colloid (thyroidization). This is seen in chronic pyelonephritis.
Option A: In acute tubular necrosis, there is focal tubular epithelial necrosis, tubulorrhexis. Option C: In acute interstitial nephritis, there is patchy edema and mononuclear cell infiltrates. Option D: In systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), wire-loop lesions are seen.

[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: All of the following patients are at risk of developing renal papillary necrosis except:
options: A 14-year-old girl being treated for thalassemia major
A 60-year-old man with longstanding diabetes mellitus
A 46-year-old man with a history of analgesic abuse
A 24-year-old woman identified to have sickle cell trait
questions.explanation:
Necrotizing papillitis or acute papillary necrosis is not associated with thalassemia. Major causes of acute papillary necrosis include
Diabetes mellitus
Sickle cell disease or trait
Analgesic abuse nephropathy
Obstruction by calculi
Focally in renal tuberculosis

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman presented with recurrent episodes of flank pain and fever with chills. CECT abdomen showed dilated and enlarged left renal pelvis with the multiloculated calyces and resection of the kidney was done. The gross specimen showed large yellowish-orange nodules. Histological examination revealed foamy macrophages. Which of the following is associated with this condition?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The clinical features and histological findings are suggestive of xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis. It is associated with Proteus infection and obstructive uropathy.
Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis is a relatively rare form of chronic pyelonephritis characterized by the accumulation of foamy macrophages intermingled with plasma cells, lymphocytes, polymorphonuclear leukocytes, and occasional giant cells.
The lesions sometimes produce large, yellowish-orange nodules that may be grossly confused with renal cell carcinoma. CECT abdomen shows dilated and enlarged renal pelvis and calyces showing a multiloculated appearance referred to as the bear paw sign.

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]

questions.stem: Which of the following do not result in granular contracted kidneys?
questions.explanation:
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis and amyloidosis cause enlarged kidneys. Causes of contracted kidneys:
Symmetric
Chronic glomerulonephritis
Benign nephrosclerosis
Asymmetric
Chronic pyelonephritis Causes of enlarged kidneys:

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis
Amyloidosis
Polycystic kidney disease
Hydronephrosis (bilateral obstruction)
The following image shows the gross appearance in benign nephrosclerosis illustrating the fine, leathery granularity of the surface.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is not associated with malignant hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Image 4 shows a leather-grain appearance, which is seen in benign nephrosclerosis. Features of malignant hypertension:
Flea bitten kidney - small petechial hemorrhages on the cortical surface, leading to a mottled appearance
Fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles - cytologic detail is lost and the vessel wall takes on a smudgy eosinophilic appearance due to fibrin deposition
Onion-skinning (hyperplastic arterioles) - intimal thickening with the fine concentric layering of collagen & smooth muscles

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
The differential diagnosis for flea-bitten kidney includes:

[[IMG:4]]
Polyarteritis nodosa
Subacute bacterial endocarditis (SABE)
Malignant hypertension

questions.stem: Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome can be caused by all except:
questions.explanation:
Deficiency of ADAMTS13 leads to thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).
Two common pathogenetic triggers of thrombotic microangiopathies are:
Endothelial injury - HUS
Excessive platelet activation and aggregation - TTP

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy is brought with blood in the urine. His mother says he had bloody diarrhea, fever, and vomiting 10 days ago. His BP is 130/•0 mm Hg, and he is jaundiced. Investigations reveal a platelet count of 50,000 cells/cu mm, BUN of 35mg/dl, and creatinine of 3.5mg/dl. Which of the following cells would you expect to see in the peripheral smear?
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario is suggestive of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). It is characterized by the presence of schistocytes in peripheral smear. It indicates microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.

questions.stem: Cholemic nephrosis is associated with which of the following casts?
questions.explanation:
Cholemic nephrosis is associated with casts of bile.
In patients with acute or chronic liver disease with advanced liver failure, renal function may be impaired. This is called hepatorenal syndrome. This can be associated with highly elevated bilirubin levels with bile cast formation (also known as cholemic nephrosis) in distal nephron segments.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man died in a road traffic accident. On autopsy, the following appearance of the kidney was noted. Which of the following is not associated with this condition?  [[IMG:1]]
options: Cysts in liver, pancreas, and spleen
questions.explanation:
The gross image suggests that the patient had autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD). This condition is not associated with hepatic fibrosis. However, patients with autosomal recessive (childhood) polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) have congenital hepatic fibrosis.
ADPKD is associated with mutations in PKD1, encoding polycystin 1, and PKD2, encoding polycystin 2. The multiple expanding cysts of both kidneys ultimately destroy the renal parenchyma and cause renal failure. Cysts arise from the tubules throughout the nephron and, therefore, have variable lining epithelia.
The common extrarenal manifestations of ADPKD include:
Hepatic cysts - most common
Seminal vesicle cysts - can result in infertility
Arachnoid membrane cysts - usually asymptomatic, may increase the risk of subdural hematoma
Pancreatic cysts
Splenic cysts
Intracranial berry aneurysms
Subarachnoid hemorrhages
Mitral valve prolapse
There are very few case reports with lung cysts in ADPKD patients, but the association between ADPKD and lung cysts has not been proved. However, there is a three-fold increase in the incidence of bronchiectasis in ADPKD patients.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about the polycystin gene?
options: Polycystin-1 is most commonly involved in ADPKD
Polycystin-2 is a calcium ion channel
Mutation in polycystin-2 causes more severe form of ADPKD
Polycystin-1 is involved in cell interactions
questions.explanation:
The polycystin-2 mutation is less commonly involved and less severe.
Polycystin-1 is encoded by the PKD1 gene located on chromosome 16p13.3. It is expressed in tubular epithelial cells, particularly those of the distal nephron. It contains domains that are usually involved in cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions. Mutations in PKD1 account for about 85% of cases of ADPKD (autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease) and it causes a more severe form of the disease.
Polycystin-2 is an integral membrane protein that is expressed in all segments of the renal tubules and in many extrarenal tissues. It functions as a Ca2+ cation channel. Overall, it causes a less severe form of ADPKD disease.

questions.stem: What is the most common extrarenal site of cysts in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease?
questions.explanation:
The most common extrarenal site of cysts in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
(ADPKD) is the liver.
40% of individuals with autosomal-dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) have one to several cysts in the liver (polycystic liver disease) that are usually asymptomatic. The cysts are derived from the biliary epithelium.
Cysts occur much less frequently in the spleen, pancreas, and lungs. There are very few case reports with lung cysts in ADPKD patients, but the association between ADPKD and lung cysts has not been proved.

questions.stem: In patients with ADPKD, the mutated genes are located on which chromosomes?
questions.explanation:
The genes mutated in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) are located on chromosomes 16 and 4.
This condition occurs due to mutations of the PKD1 gene (chromosome 16) and PKD2 gene (on chromosome 4). These genes encode for polycystin 1 and 2 proteins respectively.

questions.stem: Mutations in fibrocystin are seen in which condition?
questions.explanation:
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (ARPKD) is caused by mutations in the PKHD1 gene on chromosome 6p21-p23 which encodes fibrocystin.
The gene is highly expressed in adult and fetal kidneys and also in the liver and pancreas. Fibrocystin has been localized to the primary cilium of tubular cells.
The serious manifestations of ARPKD are usually present at birth, and may cause death by renal failure. The following gross findings are seen:
Enlarged kidneys with smooth external appearance
Spongelike appearance due to numerous small cysts in the cortex and medulla
Dilated elongated channels at right angles to the cortical surface, completely replacing the medulla and cortex
On microscopic examination, there is cylindrical or, less commonly, saccular dilation of all collecting tubules with linning of cuboidal cells. In almost all cases, the liver has cysts associated with portal fibrosis and proliferation of the portal bile ducts, termed congenital hepatic fibrosis.

questions.stem: Hepatic fibrosis is a feature of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Hepatic fibrosis is a feature of childhood (autosomal recessive) polycystic kidney disease.

questions.stem: A routine urine examination of a 46-year-old woman shows thorn-apple crystals. Past history is significant for constipation and longstanding use of laxatives. What is the likely composition of these crystals?
questions.explanation: Ammonium biurate crystals appear as spheres with radial or concentric striations and irregular projections or thorns, referred to as thorn apples. They are seen in laxative abuse.

questions.stem: In patients with chronic kidney disease, what type of casts are seen?
questions.explanation:
Broad casts are seen in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD). They are also known as renal failure casts.
Broad casts are defined as those with a diameter 2-6 times that of normal casts. They indicate chronically damaged tubules or collecting ducts. They indicate a poor prognosis.

options: It constitutes 5% of all renal tumors
Cytogenetic testing of the tumor shows multiple chromosomal losses

A 36-year-old woman presented with intermittent suprapubic pain, increased urinary frequency, and dysuria for 2 months. A cystoscopy revealed the presence of Hunner ulcers. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Hunner ulcers are chronic mucosal ulcers that are characteristic of interstitial cystitis or chronic pelvic pain syndrome.
It is a rare idiopathic condition that occurs most frequently in women. It presents with intermittent severe suprapubic pain, urinary frequency, urgency, hematuria, and dysuria.
The following cystoscopic findings are seen in the bladder mucosa:
Fissures
Punctate hemorrhages (glomerulations)
The microscopic findings include:
Mucosal ulceration covered by fibrin and necrotic material
Increased numbers of mucosal mast cells
Submucosal edema

[[IMG:1]]
In later stages, transmural fibrosis may occur, leading to a contracted bladder. Biopsy must be done to rule out carcinoma in situ, which may clinically mimic interstitial cystitis.
The following image shows a Hunner's ulcer in a patient with interstitial cystitis.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old man presented with a history of recurrent UTIs and hematuria. Urine culture showed growth of E. coli. Flexible cystoscopy revealed yellow-brown soft plaques with a central umbilication. Microscopy of the plaque showed Michaelis-Gutmann bodies. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario with the presence of Michaelis-Gutmann bodies is suggestive of malakoplakia.
Malakoplakia is a chronic inflammatory reaction resulting from acquired defects in phagocyte function, commonly affecting the urinary bladder. It can also be seen in other organ systems like the gastrointestinal tract, female genital tract, and central nervous system.
It is seen in chronic bacterial infection, mostly by Escherichia coli or occasionally Proteus species.
Grossly, it presents as soft, yellow-brown, slightly raised mucosal plaques. Microscopically, the following findings are seen:
Large, foamy macrophages containing -
Abundant granular cytoplasm due to undigested bacterial products
Michaelis-Gutmann bodies - PAS-positive basophilic concretions due to iron and calcium deposits in lysosomes
Occasional multinucleated giant cells and lymphocytes
Note: Xanthogranulomatous cystitis is morphologically and probably pathogenetically similar to malakoplakia, but it lacks Michaelis–Gutmann bodies.

[[IMG:1]]

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of polypoid cystitis?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of polypoid cystitis is indwelling catheters.
Polypoid cystitis is an inflammatory lesion resulting from mucosal irritation. It may also be associated with radiation therapy and malignant tumors. It usually involves the posterior wall of the bladder.
Grossly, it may show bulbous or papillary appearance and may be confused with papillary urothelial carcinoma. Microscopically, the papillary projections are broad-based, non-branching, and without atypia. Stroma is edematous with minimal inflammation.
Options A and D: Adenovirus infection and the use of anti-cancer drugs like cyclophosphamide cause hemorrhagic cystitis.
Option B: Systemic allergic disorders cause eosinophilic cystitis.

questions.stem: A pathologist observed a metaplastic lesion in a biopsy sample taken from the bladder mucosa of a patient. Which of the following is not a differential diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Malakoplakia is not a metaplastic lesion of the bladder. It is a type of chronic granulomatous cystitis due to defective phagocytic function that may mimic malignancy.
Metaplastic lesions of the bladder include the following:
Nests of urothelium (Brunn nests) may grow downward into the lamina propria resulting in the following lesions -
Cystitis glandularis - epithelial cells in the center of the nest undergo metaplasia and take on a cuboidal or columnar appearance
Cystitis cystica - epithelial cells retract to produce cystic spaces lined by flattened urothelium
Squamous metaplasia - in response to injury, urothelium is replaced by stratified squamous epithelium.

Nephrogenic adenoma - due to implantation of shed renal tubular cells at sites of injured urothelium, resulting in replacement of urothelium by cuboidal epithelium with a papillary growth pattern

questions.stem: [[IMG:1]] What is the most common tumor of the urinary bladder?
questions.explanation:
The most common tumor of the urinary bladder is transitional cell carcinoma or urothelial carcinoma.
Other epithelial tumors like squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, and small cell carcinoma may also occur.
Sarcomas are distinctly uncommon in the bladder. However, the most common sarcoma in infancy or childhood is embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, and the most common sarcoma in the bladder in adults is leiomyosarcoma.

questions.stem: A 57-year-old man presented with chronic hematuria and dysuria. Microscopic examination of urine showed the following parasitic eggs. What type of bladder carcinoma is commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The image shows oval-shaped eggs with the terminal spine which is characteristic of Schistosoma haematobium. It is most commonly associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.
The ova are deposited in the bladder wall and incite a brisk chronic inflammatory response. This induces progressive mucosal squamous metaplasia and dysplasia and, in some instances, neoplasia.
Schistosomal infection can less frequently result in adenocarcinoma or transitional cell carcinoma.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a carcinogen for bladder cancer?
questions.explanation:
Isopropyl alcohol is not implicated in the causation of bladder cancer.
Benzidine, arylamines, and phenacetin are well-established risk factors for bladder cancer.

questions.stem: Which of the following genetic changes is not associated with bladder carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Activating mutation in HRAS (not NRAS) is responsible for bladder carcinoma. Genetic changes associated with carcinoma bladder:
Noninvasive low-grade papillary urothelial carcinoma is associated with:
Gain-of-function mutations of FGFR3 and HRAS genes
Chromosome 9p and 9q deletions

High-grade invasive urothelial carcinoma (either papillary or flat) is associated with:
Loss-of-function mutations of TP53 and RB genes
Note: Erdafitinib (kinase inhibitor) is the first targeted drug therapy approved by the FDA for the treatment of metastatic urothelial carcinoma especially in patients with mutations of FGFR3 or FGFR2.

questions.stem: The most consistent and persistent feature of bladder carcinoma is:
questions.explanation:
The most consistent and persistent feature of carcinoma bladder is painless hematuria. Bladder tumors produce a wide range of clinical features including:
Painless hematuria - classical feature and may be the only clinical manifestation
Irritative urinary symptoms (frequency, urgency, dysuria) - diffuse tumors or tumors at the bladder neck
Pyelonephritis or hydronephrosis - when the ureteral orifice is involved
Obstructive symptoms, palpable suprapubic mass, or lower extremity edema - late presentation with a large tumor mass
Weight loss and/or localized bone pain - metastatic disease

questions.stem: Which of the following is not included in the latest International Society of Urological Pathology grading of urothelial tumors?
options: Urothelial neoplasm of low malignant potential
questions.explanation:
International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) grading system classifies papillary urothelial carcinoma into 2 grades - low grade and high grade. The classification of papillary urothelial carcinoma into grades 1, 2, 3 was was part of the earlier WHO classification.
Grading of urothelial (transitional cell) tumors: WHO/ISUP grades:
Urothelial papilloma
Urothelial neoplasm of low malignant potential
Papillary urothelial carcinoma, low grade
Papillary urothelial carcinoma, high grade WHO grades (old classification):
Urothelial papilloma
Urothelial neoplasm of low malignant potential
Papillary urothelial carcinoma, grade 1
Papillary urothelial carcinoma, grade 2
Papillary urothelial carcinoma, grade 3

questions.stem: A 67-year-old chronic smoker with gross painless hematuria was diagnosed with infiltrating urothelial carcinoma. What is the most important prognostic factor for his condition?
questions.explanation:
The staging (extent of spread) at the time of initial diagnosis is the most important prognostic factor in infiltrating urothelial carcinoma.
The prognosis of bladder carcinoma depends on the histologic grade and the stage at diagnosis. As most infiltrating urothelial carcinomas are high-grade, staging becomes the major factor to determine the prognosis.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presented with purulent vaginal discharge associated with fever, malaise, and inguinal pain. A Pap smear revealed the following findings. What is the causative agent?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given image of Pap smear shows cells with ground glass nuclei, viral inclusions, multinucleation, and margination of chromatin. These findings are characteristic of herpes simplex infection.
Some infections of the female genital tract and their diagnostic features are given below:

[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: What are the cystic remnants of mesonephric ducts in the cervix and vagina called?
questions.explanation:
Cystic remnants of mesonephric ducts in the cervix and vagina are termed Gartner duct cysts.
The mesonephric (Wolffian) ducts normally regress in females. Its remnants may persist into adult life as epithelial inclusions adjacent to the ovaries, tubes, and uterus. In the cervix and
vagina, these ducts may be cystic and are termed Gartner duct cysts.
The following images show the embryological development of the mesonephric duct and its persistence into adult life.

questions.stem: The following histological image depicts a pathology in which of the following sites?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
The given histopathological image shows benign papillary projections covered with columnar secretory epithelium and underlying myoepithelial cells. These are commonly seen in papillary hidradenoma of the vulva.
It presents as a sharply circumscribed nodule, most commonly on the labia majora or interlabial folds. Like the breast, the vulva also contains modified apocrine sweat glands. Its histologic appearance is identical to that of intraductal papilloma of the breast.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old girl presents with a mass protruding from the anterior vaginal wall that appears like grape clusters. Histopathological examination reveals tadpole cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma (sarcoma botryoides).
It is an uncommon vaginal tumor composed of malignant embryonal rhabdomyoblasts. It is most frequently found in infants and in children < 5 years of age. They are locally invasive tumors that cause death by penetration into the peritoneal cavity or by obstruction of the urinary tract.
Grossly, polypoid, rounded, bulky masses that appear like grape clusters can be seen. On microscopy, small tumor cells with oval nuclei, and small protrusions of cytoplasm from one end resembling a tennis racket (tadpole cells) can be seen. Beneath the vaginal epithelium, the tumor cells are crowded in a cambium layer, in the dermis.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false regarding precursor squamous epithelial lesions of the cervix?
options: LSIL progress directly to invasive carcinoma
LSILs are 10 times more common than HSILs
HPV-16 is the most common HPV type in both LSIL and HSIL
They progress to invasive carcinoma over many years
questions.explanation:
Low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) does not progress directly to invasive carcinoma. They initially progress to a high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL), then invasive carcinoma.
The WHO currently recommends a 2-tier system of classification for cervical lesions - low and high-grade intraepithelial lesions (LSIL and HSIL). HPV-16 is the most common HPV type associated with both LSIL and HSIL
LSILs are 10 times more common than HSILs. Most of these lesions regress
spontaneously. Progression to invasive carcinoma is unpredictable and can take place over years.

questions.stem: What is the most common type of human papilloma virus causing cervical carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Human papillomavirus (HPV)-16 is the most common type of HPV causing cervical carcinoma. It accounts for almost 60% of cervical cancer cases.
The ability of HPV to act as a carcinogen depends on the viral proteins E6 and E7. These proteins interfere with the activity of tumor-suppressor proteins that regulate cell growth and survival.
E6 - binds with p53 gene and promote its degradation
E7 - binds with RB gene and promotes its degradation

questions.stem: A young woman comes to the gynecology OPD for cervical cancer screening. What is the staining technique used for this?
questions.explanation:
Cervical cancer screening test, commonly known as Pap smear, is stained using the Papanicolaou method.
The time for initiating Pap smear screening is 21 years, regardless of the age of first sexual intercourse.
The sample is collected using Ayre's spatula and endocervical brush. 2 samples are taken:
1st slide - prepared from a sample taken from portio vaginalis of the cervix
2nd slide - prepared from the sample taken from the endocervix (transformation zone) 95% ethanol is used as a fixative.
It is a highly specific test. Colposcopic examination and biopsy are recommended in case of abnormal Pap smear results.

questions.stem: Which of the following is incorrect about type I endometrial carcinoma?
options: It is associated with obesity and diabetes
Smoking is a high risk factor
It is caused by unopposed estrogen stimulation
questions.explanation:
Smoking is strongly associated with mucinous cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary, but not endometrial carcinoma.
Endometrial carcinoma is the most common invasive cancer of the female genital tract. Type 1 endometrial carcinoma shows endometrioid morphology and is associated with:
Unopposed estrogen exposure (endometrial hyperplasia)
Obesity
Diabetes mellitus
Hypertension
PTEN tumor-suppressor gene is mutated in approximately 20% of endometrial hyperplasias.
Genomic sequencing of endometrial carcinoma has revealed 4 major molecular subtypes of endometrioid and serous carcinomas:
Ultramutated/ POLE tumors - mutations in DNA polymerase  (POLE)
Hypermutated/ MSI (microsatellite instability) tumors - mutations involving mismatch repair genes
Copy number low/ MSS (microsatellite stable) tumors - mutations involving the PI3K/AKT pathway
Copy number high/ serous-like tumors - TP53 mutations and numerous genomic copy number variants

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a criterion to distinguish leiomyosarcoma from leiomyoma?
questions.explanation:
The size of the tumor is not a criterion to distinguish between leiomyosarcoma and leiomyoma. The following features are seen in leiomyosarcomas:
Mitotic index - 10 mitoses / 10 hpf
Nuclear atypia - in the presence of nuclear atypia, 5 mitoses / 10 hpf
Tumor cell necrosis -
Characterized by an abrupt transition from viable to non-viable areas
Within the necrotic zones, atypical cells can be seen

questions.stem: Histopathological examination of an ovarian mass sent to the pathology department revealed the following. Which of the following is false regarding this condition?  [[IMG:1]]
options: It is more common in women with low parity
The pathogenesis is related to family history and heritable mutations
High-grade tumors are associated with TP53 mutations
questions.explanation:
The given image denotes Psammoma bodies which are a histopathological finding seen in ovarian papillary serous cystadenoma and cystadenocarcinoma. These tumors are most
commonly bilateral.

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
The majority of serous tumors of the ovary are benign or borderline. But the serous carcinomas of the ovary include the most common malignant tumors of the ovary.
Nulliparity, family history, and heritable mutations play a role in the development of these tumors. Mutations in the oncogenes KRAS, BRAF, or ERBB2 result in low-grade tumors, and mutation in TP53 is associated with high-grade tumors.
There is a higher frequency of carcinoma in women with low parity. Women on oral contraceptive pills or those who have undergone tubal ligation are at a lower risk. The marker for ovarian tumors is CA-125.

questions.stem: Which of the following is false regarding mucinous tumors of the ovary?
options: It occurs principally in middle adult life
Mutation of the KRAS proto-oncogene is seen
questions.explanation:
The vast majority of mucinous tumors of the ovary are benign or borderline tumors (not malignant).
It occurs principally in middle adult life and is rare before puberty and after menopause. The surface of the ovary is rarely involved, they are rarely bilateral. It is associated with the mutation of KRAS proto-oncogene.

[[IMG:1]]
Grossly it is multiloculated and filled with sticky, gelatinous fluid (rich in glycoproteins).

questions.stem: [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]] A 30-year-old woman underwent an evaluation for an abdominal mass. A laparotomy was decided upon for the removal of the mass. The gross appearance of the mass is as follows. Histopathological examination revealed no malignant change. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario and image showing unilocular cystic space containing hair and sebaceous material are suggestive of mature teratoma.
Dermoid cysts or mature teratomas are benign tumors, usually found in young women during the active reproductive years. It is bilateral in 10% to 15% of cases.

[[IMG:4]]
[[IMG:5]]
Microscopically, the cyst wall is composed of tissues from all 3 germ layers. This includes stratified squamous epithelium, with underlying sebaceous glands, hair shafts, and other skin adnexal structures. Sometimes cartilage, bone, thyroid, and neural tissue can be seen.
About 1% of the dermoids undergo malignant transformation, most commonly to squamous cell carcinoma. It can also transform into other cancers (e.g., thyroid carcinoma, melanoma).
The component tissue of immature malignant teratomas resembles embryonal and immature fetal tissue. It often consists of primitive neuroepithelial cells. The tumor is found chiefly in prepubertal adolescents and young women, the mean age being 18 years.

[[IMG:6]]
Monodermal or specialized teratomas:
Struma ovarii - composed entirely of mature thyroid tissue, which may be functional and cause hyperthyroidism.
Ovarian carcinoid - arises from intestinal tissue, may be functional causing carcinoid syndrome in the absence of hepatic metastasis

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman presented to the gynecology OPD with a history of abdominal pain and distension of abdomen. Ultrasound imaging revealed tumor in the right ovary. Serum level of inhibin was raised. The histopathology of the tumor is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?  [[IMG:1]] [[IMG:2]] [[IMG:3]] [[IMG:4]] [[IMG:5]] [[IMG:6]]
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and histopathology showing Call-Exner bodies are suggestive of granulosa cell tumor.
Call-Exner bodies are small, distinctive, glandlike structures filled with an acidophilic material resembling immature follicles. Additionally, small, cuboidal to polygonal cells are seen which may grow in anastomosing cords, sheets, or strands.

[[IMG:7]]
[[IMG:8]]
Granulosa cell tumors are composed of cells that resemble granulosa cells of a developing ovarian follicle. It can be of adult and juvenile types. Elevated tissue and serum levels of inhibin, a product of granulosa cells, are associated with this tumor.
Mutations of the FOXL2 gene are seen in most adult granulosa cell tumors.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl, who is yet to attain her menarche, presents with an ovarian mass. Her serum biomarkers are normal except for elevated AFP. Staging laparotomy was performed and the histopathological image is given below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical features and the histopathological image showing Schiller Duval bodies are suggestive of endodermal sinus tumors. It is also known as yolk sac tumor.
The Schiller-Duval body is a glomerulus-like structure composed of a central blood vessel enveloped by tumor cells within a space that is also lined by tumor cells.
It is the second most common malignant tumor of germ cell origin. It is a unilateral tumor usually affecting children or young women.

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: Which of the following are sex cord-stromal tumors?
questions.explanation:
Sex cord-stromal tumors include the following:
Granulosa cell tumor
Sertoli cell tumor
Fibroma
Brenner tumor is an epithelial tumor and dysgerminoma is a germ cell tumor.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman presented with bilateral adnexal masses. Histopathological examination of the resected specimen showed sheets of mucin-producing signet-ring cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and histopathology findings are suggestive of metastatic carcinoma of the ovary or Krukenberg tumor.
It can arise from primary carcinomas of the stomach (most common), colon, appendix, and breast
(invasive lobular carcinoma). It is often bilateral and on microscopy shows mucin-laden signet-ring cells with eccentric hyperchromatic nuclei.

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
Metastatic tumors of the ovary include:
Tumors of Müllerian origin (most common) - the uterus, fallopian tube, contralateral ovary, or pelvic peritoneum
Tumors of extra-Müllerian tumors - breast and gastrointestinal tract carcinomas
Pseudomyxoma peritonei - derived from appendiceal tumors
Krukenberg tumor

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman was diagnosed with molar pregnancy and underwent suction and evacuation. The resected specimen is shown below. Histopathological examination revealed thin-walled, cystic structures consisting of hydropic villi with extensive trophoblastic proliferation along its entire circumference. Immunohistochemistry was negative for p57. Which of the following is false about this condition?  [[IMG:1]]
options: The genetic material is completely maternally derived
Embryo dies very early in development and therefore is usually not identified
It is associated with a 2.5% risk of subsequent choriocarcinoma
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and image showing grapelike vesicles are suggestive of a complete mole. It results from the fertilization of an egg that has lost its female chromosomes, and as a result, the genetic material is completely paternally derived.

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
The pathogenesis of complete mole is as follows:
Androgenesis (most common) - 46XX karyotype stemming from the duplication of the genetic material of 1 sperm
Dispermy - 46XX or 46XY karyotype due to fertilization of an empty egg by 2 sperms
Microscopically, thin-walled, cystic, grapelike structures consisting of hydropic villi are seen. Trophoblastic proliferation involving the entire circumference of the villi is seen.
The embryo dies very early in development and, therefore, is usually not identified. Patients have a 2.5% risk of subsequent choriocarcinoma and a 15% risk of the persistent or invasive mole.
The following image shows the pathogenesis of molar pregnancy.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman with a positive pregnancy test presented with vaginal bleeding in the first trimester. On examination, grape-like vesicles were noted in the vagina. A transvaginal ultrasound revealed the presence of fetal tissues. A suction evacuation was performed. What is the most likely karyotype of the evacuated material?
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
The given clinical scenario with grape-like vesicles in the vagina and the presence of fetal tissues on transvaginal ultrasound are suggestive of partial mole. The karyotype in a partial mole
is triploid (e.g., 69XXY) or occasionally tetraploid (92XXXY).
It results from the fertilization of an egg with 2 sperms. There is an increased risk of persistent molar disease but it is not associated with choriocarcinoma.
Given below is an image showing the karyotype of molar pregnancy.

questions.stem: What is the most common site of metastasis in gestational choriocarcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Lungs are the most common site of metastasis in gestational choriocarcinoma.
It is followed by the vagina, brain, liver, bone, and kidney in descending order of frequency.
Gestational choriocarcinomas are malignant neoplasm of trophoblastic cells derived from a previously normal or abnormal pregnancy, such as an extrauterine ectopic pregnancy. The hCG levels are elevated to levels above those encountered in hydatidiform moles. It
shows hematogenous spread. It is rapidly invasive and metastasizes widely.

Gestational choriocarcinomas are chemosensitive whereas non-gestational choriocarcinomas are chemoresistant.

questions.stem: The genetic profile of malignant mixed Müllerian tumors resembles that of:
questions.explanation:
Malignant mixed Müllerian tumors (MMMTs) are carcinosarcomas whose genetic profile closely resembles endometrial carcinomas.
They involve mutations in the same genes - PTEN, TP53, and PIK3CA. The usual genetic alterations found in sarcomas are absent in MMMTs.
MMMTs are endometrial adenocarcinomas with malignant mesenchymal components. The mesenchymal component may resemble uterine mesenchymal elements (stromal sarcoma, leiomyosarcoma) or contain heterologous malignant cell types (striated muscle, cartilage, adipose tissue, and bone).
It occurs in postmenopausal women and presents with bleeding. It is associated with a poor outcome.

questions.stem: Which of the following are the components of Meig's syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Meigs' syndrome triad includes the following:
Solid benign ovarian tumor (fibroma)
Right-sided hydrothorax
Ascites - disappears after the removal of the tumor Pseudo-Meigs' syndrome is characterized by the following:
Non-malignant ascites
Pleural effusion
Pelvic tumors - other than solid benign ovarian tumors
Note: Ovarian fibroma is also associated with nevoid basal cell carcinoma. This association is known as Gorlin syndrome.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman was operated for an ovarian mass and the sample was sent for histopathological examination. The findings are given below. Which of the following is false about the given condition? [[IMG:1]]
options: It expresses OCT-3, OCT4, and NANOG
It occurs in patients with gonadal dysgenesis
questions.explanation:
The given histopathological image shows large cells with clear cytoplasm (fried egg appearance), tumor cells arranged in sheets, and cords of fibrous stroma infiltrated by lymphocytes. These findings are suggestive of dysgerminoma. It is highly responsive to radiotherapy.

[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
Dysgerminomas are the ovarian counterparts of testicular seminoma. They may occur in childhood, but most commonly occur in the 2-3rd decades. It may occur in patients with gonadal dysgenesis, including pseudohermaphroditism. The majority of these tumors are unilateral. They express OCT-3, OCT4, and NANOG.
All dysgerminomas are malignant, but the degree of histologic atypia is variable. Only about
one-third of these lesions are aggressive. These neoplasms are responsive to chemoradiation, and overall survival exceeds 80%.

questions.stem: A young sexually active man presented with multiple polypoid growths over his penis. Histopathological image of an excised lesion is as shown below. What is the diagnosis?  [[IMG:1]]
questions.explanation:
The given histopathological image showing papillary (villous) architecture with acanthosis, hyperkeratosis and koilocytosis of squamous epithelium, are characteristic findings of condyloma acuminatum.
Koilocytes have a prominent cell membrane, hyperchromatic resinoid nucleus, and perinuclear halo.
Grossly, they consist of single or multiple sessile or pedunculated, red papillary excrescences on the coronal sulcus, and the inner surface of the prepuce.
Option A: Condyloma lata is a maculopapular/nodular lesion seen in secondary syphilis.
Option B: Bowen's disease is carcinoma in situ of the penis characterized by the hyperproliferative epidermis and dysplastic epithelium.
Option D: Verrucous carcinoma / very well-differentiated squamous cell carcinoma, shows hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, and keratin pearls.

questions.stem: All of the following are true regarding Bowen's disease except:
options: Marked dysplasia and hyperproliferative epidermis are seen
Virtually never develops into an invasive carcinoma
questions.explanation:
[[IMG:1]]
Bowen's disease starts as a premalignant lesion and transforms into infiltrating squamous cell carcinoma in approximately 10% of patients, usually over a span of many years.
Bowen's disease occurs in the genital region of both men and women, usually in those older than age 35 years. These lesions have a strong association with infection by high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV), most commonly type 16.
Grossly, it appears as a solitary, thickened, gray-white, and opaque plaque.
The below histological image of Bowen's disease shows dysplastic cells with large hyperchromatic nuclei, koilocytic atypia and an intact basement membrane.
Premalignant lesions of invasive penile SCC:

[[IMG:2]]
Erythroplasia of Queyrat
Condyloma acuminatum
Bowen's disease
Bowenoid papulosis occurs in young, sexually active adults. It presents as multiple reddish-brown papular lesions and it is histologically indistinguishable from Bowen's disease, but virtually never develops into invasive carcinoma.

questions.stem: The biopsy of a resected inguinal mass from a patient shows marked fibrotic changes with prominent Leydig cells and hypoplastic Sertoli cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given histopathological features are strongly suggestive of cryptorchidism. Cryptorchidism is histopathologically characterized by the following:
Testicular atrophy: thickening of the basement membrane, arrested germ cell development, marked hyalinization
Tubules showing Sertoli cells but no spermatogenesis
Increase in the interstitial Leydig cells.
Cryptorchidism is the failure of the descent of the intra-abdominal testes into the scrotal sac. It is the most common congenital abnormality of the genitourinary tract. The testes can arrest anywhere during descent, and the most common site is the inguinal region.
Phases of testicular descent:
Transabdominal phase: Testes come to lie in the lower abdomen or pelvis. This phase of descent is regulated by Mullerian-inhibiting substances.
Inguinoscrotal phase: Testes descend along the inguinal canal and reach the scrotal sac. This phase of the descent is regulated by androgen-induced calcitonin gene-related peptide from the
genitofemoral nerve.
The exact pathogenesis remains unknown, however, deficiency in gonadotropins and Mullerian-inhibiting substance (MIS) and increased expression of estradiol in the placenta are thought to play a role. It is associated with testicular atrophy and dysfunction, which result in
sterility. Cryptorchid testes carry a 3–5-fold higher risk for testicular cancer (usually seminoma).

questions.stem: Testicular atrophy is not seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Torsion testis does not cause testicular atrophy. It may cause intense congestion to widespread hemorrhage to testicular infarction.

Causes of testicular atrophy:
Progressive atherosclerotic narrowing of the blood supply in old age
End-stage of an inflammatory orchitis
Cryptorchidism - associated with progressive tubular atrophy and sterility
Hypopituitarism
Generalized malnutrition or cachexia
Irradiation
Prolonged administration of antiandrogens (treatment for advanced carcinoma of the prostate)
Liver cirrhosis - may cause testicular atrophy as a result of increased levels of circulating endogenous estrogens not metabolized by the diseased liver
Exhaustion atrophy, which may follow persistent stimulation by high levels of the follicle-stimulating pituitary hormone
Occasionally occurs as a primary failure of genetic origins, such as in Klinefelter (XXY)
syndrome
The histological image below of testicular atrophy shows small tubules with few or no germ cells, thickening of the basement membrane of the spermatic tubules, and prominent Leydig cells. The near-normal seminiferous tubules are seen side-by-side with atrophic seminiferous tubules.

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man undergoes testicular biopsy as part of infertility work-up. Sperm count shows oligospermia. Microscopy shows only Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules. What is the most likely finding seen in the condition?
questions.explanation:
The above clinical scenario depicts that the patient is having Sertoli cell-only syndrome, and patients with this syndrome will have increased levels of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH).
The below image shows normal histology of testis:
In normal males, as spermatogenesis and testosterone production increase, the Sertoli cells produce inhibin, which inhibits the release of FSH. The Sertoli cells are supporting cells that are under the action of FSH. Leydig cells, which are present in the interstitial spaces, are under the action of luteinizing hormone(LH) and produce testosterone. Testosterone has a feedback inhibition on LH.

[[IMG:1]]
In Sertoli cell-only syndrome, within the seminiferous tubules, only Sertoli cells are seen and no germ cells. Hence, there are no spermatozoa and there is no feedback inhibition, which results in increased FSH levels. So, testosterone levels, and LH levels remain unaffected since Leydig cells are not affected. Hence, the patient will have male secondary sexual characters.
The most important indication of testicular biopsy is infertility workup.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old boy presents with acute onset of testicular pain. On examination, the left testis is enlarged, tender and positioned higher than the right at an unusual angle. Pain is not relieved on elevation of the scrotum. What histopathological changes can be seen in this condition?
options: Marked fibrosis with prominent Leydig cells and hypoplastic Sertoli cells
Dysplastic cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, koilocytic atypia
Intense congestion, hemorrhage, and areas of infarction
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is testicular torsion. The pathological changes range from intense congestion to widespread hemorrhage to testicular infarction. In advanced stages, the testis is markedly enlarged and consists entirely of soft, necrotic, hemorrhagic tissue.

[[IMG:1]]
[[IMG:2]]
[[IMG:3]]
[[IMG:4]]
Adult torsion is typically seen in adolescence and presents with the sudden onset of testicular pain. Neonatal torsion can occur either in utero or shortly after birth and the cause is unknown.
It results from a bilateral anatomic defect that leads to increased mobility of the testes (bell-clapper□ abnormality). Twisting of the spermatic cord typically cuts off the venous drainage of the testis. But, thick-walled arteries remain patent, producing intense vascular engorgement, followed by hemorrhagic infarction. If the testis is manually untwisted within approximately 6 hours of the onset of torsion, there is a good chance that the testis will remain viable.

questions.stem: Which of the following infections primarily affects the testis?
questions.explanation:
Syphilis and mumps affect the testis primarily and later spread to surrounding structures.
Syphilis can affect both the testis and epididymis, but invariably, the testis is involved first as gummas and diffuse interstitial inflammation.
